topic: The contrarian case against a redesigned Gujarat 7/12 land-records citizen portal: ICTD critique, channel reality, legal standing, exclusion, source-data quality, privacy, and prior art

claims.claim: The Supreme Court of India held that a mutation entry in the revenue record 'does not confer any right, title or interest in favour of the person' and exists 'only for the fiscal purpose' of collecting land revenue; disputed title must be crystallised by a civil court before mutation follows.
claims.source_name: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors., Supreme Court of India, 6 Sept 2021 (LL 2021 SC 430)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the single most dangerous fact for the project's framing. A 7/12 extract is NOT proof of ownership, not even in certified form. Any copy that says or implies 'this is your land' is legally wrong. The UI must state, in Gujarati, that the RoR is a presumptive fiscal record, not a title. It also reframes the product: the honest value is 'see what the state currently has recorded about this parcel and whether it is wrong', not 'prove you own it'.

claims.claim: Gujarat's own rural re-survey (2009–2018), covering roughly 93% of rural Gujarat (2.58 lakh sq km), was halted in August 2018 after ~12,000 of 18,501 villages were promulgated, because private agencies relied on old maps and old records instead of the mandated DGPS/ETS ground measurement. By December 2021, 5.28 lakh survey numbers had complaints registered against them; 1.68 lakh verification applications were received in 2020–21, of which 90,000+ were disposed of by March 2022. Officials estimated 15–20% of landowners approached offices for corrections. State cost ~Rs 370 crore against a union allocation of Rs 54.66 crore.
claims.figure: 5,28,000 survey numbers with complaints; 15–20% of landowners seeking correction
claims.source_name: Article 14 — 'How Gujarat's Rural Land Digitisation Programme Was Botched, Starting A Fresh Trail Of Land Litigation'
claims.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Gujarat-specific attack on the project. The areas and boundaries you will render beautifully are, for a material share of Gujarat parcels, known to be wrong — and the state knows it. Presenting bad numbers in a cleaner, more confident, more trustworthy-looking layout is an active harm: it increases the credence a semi-literate user places in a figure the government itself is currently correcting. This must be surfaced in-product, not in a footnote.

claims.claim: Solomon Benjamin et al. found that Karnataka's Bhoomi land-records digitisation increased corruption and bribery, substantially increased the time taken for land transactions, and facilitated very large players in Bangalore's land market to capture vast quantities of land — by centralising records away from villages to districts. Poorer users could not afford the 'expediters who understand the system'; electronic access was often slower than paper because of computer malfunction and power cuts.
claims.source_name: Benjamin, S., Bhuvaneswari, R., Rajan, P. & Manjunath (2007), 'Bhoomi: E-Governance, Or, An Anti-Politics Machine Necessary to Globalize Bangalore?' CASUM-m Working Paper
claims.why_it_matters: The canonical counter-case: the best-known Indian land-records digitisation, celebrated as an e-governance success, was found by field researchers to have net-harmed small holders and net-helped land aggregators. It is the precedent a hostile judge will cite. Note the evidence is qualitative fieldwork, not a controlled study — say so before someone else does, but do not dismiss it: no one has produced a stronger counter-study.

claims.claim: Toyama's amplification thesis: technology is a magnifier of existing institutional intent and capacity, not a substitute for it. Three mechanisms — differential access, differential capacity, differential motivation — mean 'the greater one's capacity, the more technology delivers... technology helps the rich get proportionately richer, thus widening, not narrowing, the gaps'. He names 'appropriate design', 'participatory design' and 'human-centered design' explicitly as banners under which the 'myth of scale' is charged.
claims.source_name: Kentaro Toyama, 'Technology as Amplifier in International Development', iConference 2011 (ACM)
claims.why_it_matters: Toyama pre-emptively names your defence. 'But I did human-centred design and it's context-appropriate' is the exact move he labels the myth of scale. The only response that survives is to design the tool to amplify a human who already has intent and capacity — the talati, the Village Computer Entrepreneur, the literate son/nephew — rather than to claim you have replaced them.

claims.claim: Richard Heeks' widely cited estimate for e-government projects in developing/transitional countries: ~35% are total failures, ~50% are partial failures, ~15% succeed — attributed to 'design–reality gaps' between the system's assumptions and local organisational reality.
claims.source_name: Richard Heeks, 'Most eGovernment-for-Development Projects Fail: How Can Risks be Reduced?' / eGovernment for Development, University of Manchester IDPM
claims.why_it_matters: The base rate. An outsider-built prototype with no institutional owner, no budget line and no revenue department buy-in sits in the worst cell of Heeks' model — maximum design-reality gap. Honest framing: state the base rate yourself and explain what specifically about your design narrows the gap (it does not replace any government process; it fails safe to the official channel).

claims.claim: Women constitute barely 14% of landowners in rural India and own 11% of agricultural land; 84% of landowning rural households have no female owner at all, nine years after the 2005 Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act. 87.5% of plots are owned by individual men, 10.2% by individual women, 2.3% jointly.
claims.figure: 14% of landowners; 11% of land; 84% of households with no woman owner
claims.source_name: Agarwal, B., Anthwal, P. & Mahesh, M. (2021), 'How Many and Which Women Own Land in India? Inter-gender and Intra-gender Gaps', Journal of Development Studies
claims.why_it_matters: A portal indexed by owner name and survey number is structurally blind to ~half the adult population of a landowning household. 'Accessible to Gujarati-first rural users' is not the same as 'reaches women'. Do not claim gender inclusion you cannot deliver; if anything, an interface that makes the recorded owner list more legible to the household is a genuine, modest, honest gender claim — a woman can see she is not on it.

claims.claim: NFHS-5 (2019–21) records that only ~48.8% of women in Gujarat have ever used the internet — among the five lowest states; nationally ~47% of rural women own a mobile phone versus 69% of urban women; fewer than 3 in 10 rural Indian women have ever used the internet.
claims.figure: 48.8% of Gujarat women ever used the internet; 47% rural women own a phone
claims.source_name: National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) 2019–21, IIPS/MoHFW — as reported by FACTLY and IndiaSpend
claims.why_it_matters: Sets a hard ceiling on 'digital by default' reach in exactly your target segment. The number I report is secondary reporting of the NFHS fact sheets — pull the Gujarat state fact sheet directly before you put a figure on a slide. It also argues for a share-out-of-app path (a plain image/PDF that travels by WhatsApp to whoever is literate) rather than assuming the user opens the app themselves.

claims.claim: Gujarat delivers rural government services primarily through an assisted, staffed counter, not through citizens using websites: Digital Seva Setu (launched Oct 2020) offers 321 services across 14,112 gram panchayats in 248 talukas, staffed by Village Computer Entrepreneurs (VCEs) who submit applications on behalf of citizens; 27,13,079 people used it in 2023–24 and 34,99,261 in 2024–25.
claims.figure: 14,112 gram panchayats; 321 services; ~35 lakh users in 2024-25
claims.source_name: Government of Gujarat / MyGov and press reporting on Digital Seva Setu
claims.why_it_matters: This is the best available evidence on the 'is the interface even the bottleneck' question, and it cuts against the project: the state's own answer to rural digital access is a human operator at a panchayat counter. If the dominant channel is assisted, the highest-value redesign target is the VCE's screen and the talati's workflow, not the farmer's phone. Reframe the product as an assisted-mode tool and this objection becomes a strength.

claims.claim: Gujarat already issues a digitally signed, legally usable Record of Rights online through the iORA portal (iora.gujarat.gov.in) for a nominal fee (reported at ~Rs 5–15 per village form); the free AnyRoR view is explicitly not accepted for court, registration or banking. A private company (Landeed) resells the same digitally signed Gujarat SatBara/7-12 for Rs 199 per document with a 1-hour-to-3-day turnaround.
claims.figure: Rs 5–15 official vs Rs 199 private resale
claims.source_name: Landeed product page for Gujarat certified SatBara/RoR; secondary guides on iORA digitally signed RoR
claims.why_it_matters: Potentially fatal to the read-only-viewer premise, and I could not verify the official fee from a government page — verify on iora.gujarat.gov.in yourself before you present. If it holds: the legally usable copy is ALREADY online and cheap, so a prettier free viewer adds no legal capability. But the Rs 199 vs Rs 15 spread is your evidence that people will pay a 13x markup to avoid the state's interface — the friction is real and monetisable, and what is being sold is the errand, not the document.

claims.claim: India's land titling is presumptive, not conclusive: the state does not guarantee title. Impact assessments cited by Vidhi found 34% ownership-and-possession discrepancies in rural Shimla and 6% in Baddi (Himachal Pradesh), and in Maharashtra area discrepancies against GPS/ETS measurement were flagged in more than half the properties surveyed, even though ownership concordance with the record office was near-perfect (101 of 102 parcels).
claims.figure: 34% (rural Shimla) and 6% (Baddi) ownership/possession discrepancy; >50% of Maharashtra parcels with area discrepancy
claims.source_name: Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, 'Is land digitisation enough?'
claims.why_it_matters: Quantifies the 'clearer presentation of bad data' risk. Note the shape of the error: WHO is recorded is mostly right; HOW MUCH and WHERE is frequently wrong. That is a precise, defensible design instruction — render owner names with normal confidence and render area/boundary with an explicit uncertainty treatment. These are small non-Gujarat samples; do not generalise them to a national error rate.

claims.claim: Only 39% of spatial (map) data had been verified nationally and only 26% of maps were linked to the Record of Rights, against 86% computerisation of textual land records — i.e. the textual record and the map are largely unreconciled. Real-time RoR/map update stood at 15%, and survey/re-survey was complete in 9% of villages (35% of area).
claims.figure: 86% textual computerised vs 39% spatial verified, 26% maps linked to RoR, 9% of villages re-surveyed
claims.source_name: PRS Legislative Research, 'Land Records and Titles in India', citing Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development
claims.why_it_matters: Directly supports the CLAUDE.md finding that parcel geometry is not buildable from the available sheets — it is not a Gujarat quirk, it is the national state of the data. It also means any UI that visually juxtaposes a record and a map implies a linkage that mostly does not exist. Figures are 2017; get the current DILRMP dashboard numbers before quoting.

claims.claim: In Andhra Pradesh, digitisation of the Adangal automated Column 13 (which records the actual cultivator) to show cultivator and owner as the same person, erasing recorded tenancy; reporting documents tribal and Dalit farmers losing claims and welfare-scheme eligibility through altered or deleted record columns and NRI claims over tribal land.
claims.source_name: Pulitzer Center, 'In Andhra Pradesh, Software Flaws Aid Land Grab From Tribal and Dalit Farmers'
claims.why_it_matters: The best documented case of digital-first land records causing concrete harm to the exact population you name as beneficiaries — and the mechanism is a schema/defaulting decision made by a developer, not by a corrupt official. It is a direct warning about your own normalisation and identity-merge logic: a rule that fuses or defaults a field is a land-rights decision. (Your project already learned this once: stripping characters from survey numbers fused 250 different parcels.) I could not retrieve the article body — it 403s to automated fetch — so verify the Column 13 detail before citing it on stage.

claims.claim: Official Indian tenancy statistics are known to be a large undercount: NSSO's 70th Round (2013) recorded ~10.1% of land leased-in and ~14% of rural households (21.3 million) leasing in land, but tenancy is largely informal or concealed because restrictive leasing law makes it unsafe to record, so sharecroppers' rights 'do not appear either in official records or in official surveys'.
claims.figure: 10.1% of land leased-in officially recorded; widely held to be a substantial undercount
claims.source_name: NSSO 70th Round Land and Livestock Holdings; ActionAid India, 'The Status of Tenant Farmers/Sharecroppers (Bataidars)'
claims.why_it_matters: The cultivator who most needs the record — the tenant seeking crop loans and compensation — is precisely the person the record does not contain. A VF-12 crop record viewer is therefore not a farmer's tool, it is a landowner's tool. Say that explicitly rather than letting a judge find it.

claims.claim: The widely repeated 'two-thirds / 66% of civil cases in India relate to land' figure traces to Daksh's Access to Justice Survey: ~9,000–9,329 litigants interviewed across ~300–305 district courts in 24 states, November 2015 – February 2016, which found two-thirds of CIVIL cases IN DISTRICT COURTS related to land and property. PRS separately attributes a similar claim to a 2007 World Bank study. The popular rendering — '66% of all court cases in India are land disputes' — is not what either source measured.
claims.figure: ~66% of civil cases in district courts (Daksh, 2015-16 litigant survey)
claims.source_name: DAKSH, Access to Justice Survey (2015–16)
claims.why_it_matters: You will be tempted to open with this number. It has a real primary source, but it is a litigant survey of civil district-court cases, not a census of Indian litigation, and it excludes criminal matters and cases without a private party. State it with its scope attached ('two-thirds of civil cases in district courts, per a 2015-16 survey of 9,000 litigants') and you gain credibility; state it as '66% of court cases in India' and any informed judge can dismantle your framing in one question.

claims.claim: 'About 70% of land in the developing world is undocumented' — repeated in reporting on Indian land digitisation, attributed loosely to development-sector sources with no originating dataset given.
claims.source_name: Dawn / Thomson Reuters Foundation, 'As India pushes towards digitising land records, is it putting its poor at risk?'
claims.why_it_matters: A representative example of the genre. I could not trace it to any originating study. Do not use it. Its presence in an otherwise good article is a reminder to trace every number in your deck.

claims.claim: Named experts warn specifically that digitisation empowers the already-empowered. Namita Wahi (CPR): 'Technology has the potential to be empowering, but it is possible that it will empower those who are already empowered more than those who are currently disempowered.' Usha Ramanathan: 'For the government, digitisation makes it easier to administer and go to market. But what is the use of an open registry for poor communities and small and marginalised farmers who cannot access it?' Amy Coughenor (Cadasta): 'having digital records doesn't take away the need to accurately and fairly document land in the first place.'
claims.source_name: Dawn / Thomson Reuters Foundation reporting
claims.why_it_matters: These are the exact sentences a judge with domain knowledge will quote at you. Having them in your own deck, answered, is worth more than any feature. Ramanathan's question is the hardest one in the whole research set: what IS the use of an open registry for people who cannot access it?

claims.claim: Telangana's Dharani land-records portal, a flagship digitisation, generated over six lakh grievances after a complaint feature was opened, with 2.45 lakh Dharani-related cases pending; common defects were wrong survey numbers, wrong owner names, wrong land classification, mismatched e-passbooks, and patta land wrongly entered as notional khata. Farmers were charged Rs 1,000 per correction application and some could not mortgage land for loans.
claims.figure: 6,00,000+ grievances; 2,45,000 pending cases; Rs 1,000 per correction
claims.source_name: The South First / Deccan Chronicle reporting on Dharani
claims.why_it_matters: A second, recent, large-scale instance of the same failure mode as Gujarat's re-survey — and evidence that the correction pathway, not the viewing pathway, is where citizen pain concentrates. A portal that shows the record but offers no route to fix it is addressing the smaller half of the problem.

claims.claim: Indian government portals holding citizen land and welfare data have a documented record of leaking identifiers: CIS found ~130–135 million Aadhaar numbers and ~100 million bank account numbers publicly exposed across four government portals, in one case reachable by changing a URL parameter from 'nologin' to 'login'.
claims.figure: 130–135 million Aadhaar numbers, ~100 million bank accounts, 4 portals
claims.source_name: Sinha, A. & Kodali, S., 'Information Security Practices of Aadhaar (or lack thereof)', Centre for Internet and Society
claims.why_it_matters: Grounds the privacy objection in Indian fact rather than principle. It also cuts at your architecture: if you cache or mirror land data anywhere (a unified DB, a synced app store, an exported Documents tree), you have created a second copy of a dataset whose first copy has a poor security record — with none of the state's legal cover. Be able to say exactly where the data lives and who can read it.

claims.claim: A well-funded private incumbent already occupies this space: Landeed (founded 2022, Y Combinator / Draper Associates / Bayhouse) has raised $19.3M across four rounds for Indian property title search and sells Gujarat digitally signed 7/12 at Rs 199 per document, targeting loan, mortgage and litigation use cases; it explicitly states it 'is not a government entity and is not affiliated with any government agency'.
claims.source_name: Dealroom / Tracxn / Landeed product pages
claims.why_it_matters: Answers 'why has nobody done this': somebody has, with $19M, and they went B2B/transactional rather than free-consumer-Gujarati. That is a market signal, not a coincidence — the willingness to pay sits with lawyers, banks and buyers, not with the farmer checking his own khata. Your honest differentiation is the segment nobody can monetise, which is also why it needs to be a public-interest tool rather than a startup pitch.

claims.claim: The free-viewer niche for AnyRoR is already saturated by unofficial SEO clones and wrapper apps: at minimum anyror.in, anyror.site, anyror.org, anyror.co, anyrorgujarat.org, anyrorgujarat.co, gujaratanyror.in and www-anyror.com, plus Play Store apps such as 'Gujarat 7/12 8a Any Land info'. Each carries a disclaimer that it is 'not affiliated, associated, authorized, or endorsed by the Government of Gujarat'.
claims.source_name: AnyRoR clone-site disclaimers (representative example)
claims.why_it_matters: Two consequences. First, 'nobody has built a nicer front end' is false — many have, badly, for ad revenue, and they dominate search. Second, your product will be visually and functionally indistinguishable from them to a first-time rural user, which is a trust problem that no amount of typography solves. Distribution and provenance, not interface quality, are the binding constraints.

claims.claim: Every reviewed critique converges on the same institutional diagnosis rather than an interface diagnosis: the Bhoomi loopholes analysis attributes failure to un-updated paper records at source, Village Accountants' limited capacity, Revenue Inspectors unable to validate, illiterate farmers' dependence on intermediaries, and the absence of any safeguard against coercion or false entry during computerisation.
claims.source_name: Accountability Initiative, 'Loopholes: Land ownership and the Bhoomi Project'
claims.why_it_matters: None of the five named failure modes is an interface problem. This is the cleanest statement of the core objection: the bottleneck is upstream of any screen. The only honest response is to scope the claim — you are not fixing land administration, you are removing a specific, measurable access tax (five chained dropdowns, a CAPTCHA on public data, session fragility, desktop-only output) — and to be able to measure that tax.

design_rules.rule: Put a permanent, Gujarati-first provenance strip on every record view: source portal, the date the state promulgated/last updated that record, and the date YOU fetched it. Never show a record without both dates.
design_rules.rationale: Gujarat's re-survey was halted mid-programme; ~12,000 of 18,501 villages were promulgated and 5.28 lakh survey numbers carry complaints. Whether a given village's figures come from the pre-2009 record or the disputed 2009–18 re-survey is decision-relevant and currently invisible.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Clean-UI instinct to hide metadata chrome and show only the 'content'. Here the metadata IS the content.

design_rules.rule: Label your own rendering 'MAHITI MATE — information only, not a legal document' in Gujarati, permanently and non-dismissibly, and end every record view with a single primary action that hands off to the official signed copy (iORA / e-Dhara Kendra), naming the fee and what it is accepted for.
design_rules.rationale: Online AnyRoR output has no legal standing; the digitally signed RoR from iORA does, and a private reseller charges Rs 199 for it. A beautiful viewer that a user mistakes for a usable document creates a wasted trip to a bank.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Wanting the app to feel like a complete, self-sufficient product. It should feel deliberately incomplete at exactly the legal boundary.

design_rules.rule: State the presumptive-title fact in the product, not just the pitch: a one-line Gujarati explainer on the 7/12 view that the RoR is a fiscal record and confers no title, with the Supreme Court holding available behind a tap.
design_rules.rationale: Jitendra Singh v. State of MP (2021): mutation entry confers no right, title or interest; it is for fiscal purpose only. A product that implies otherwise misinforms users about their legal position.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The emotionally compelling hackathon narrative 'now farmers can prove their land is theirs'. That narrative is legally false.

design_rules.rule: Render area and boundary figures with visibly lower confidence than owner names — different weight, an explicit uncertainty marker, and a tap-through explaining the re-survey. Do not right-align areas into a crisp numeric column that reads as authoritative.
design_rules.rationale: The error profile is asymmetric: ownership concordance with the record office was 101/102 parcels in Maharashtra while area discrepancies were flagged in over half; Himachal showed 34% ownership/possession discrepancy in one sample. Who is mostly right; how much and where is often wrong.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Typographic consistency — the mono-numeral treatment that makes survey numbers and areas look equally solid.

design_rules.rule: Build the correction pathway, not just the viewing pathway: from any field, a 'this is wrong' flow that produces the actual application the user must file, names the office (e-Dhara Kendra / Mamlatdar), and states the fee and expected timeline.
design_rules.rationale: 1.68 lakh Gujarat verification applications in 2020–21; 5.28 lakh disputed survey numbers; Telangana's Dharani generated 6 lakh+ grievances at Rs 1,000 per correction. Citizen pain concentrates at correction, not at lookup.
design_rules.conflicts_with: 'Read-only viewer' scoping, which is the easy build and the weaker product.

design_rules.rule: Ship an explicit assisted mode designed for an operator serving a queue — a VCE, talati, shopkeeper or literate relative — with fast re-entry, multi-parcel session, print/share-out, and no assumption the person holding the phone is the landowner.
design_rules.rationale: Gujarat's own rural delivery model is 14,112 gram panchayat counters with Village Computer Entrepreneurs serving ~35 lakh people in 2024–25; Toyama's telecentre finding is that a capable, motivated local champion is the single best predictor of success.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The disintermediation story ('cut out the middleman'). The evidence says amplify the intermediary instead.

design_rules.rule: Refuse to build owner-name search, whole-village enumeration, and bulk export — and say on stage that you refused, naming the Bhoomi finding as the reason.
design_rules.rationale: Benjamin et al. found Bhoomi's centralisation helped large players capture land; the incumbent's five dropdowns and CAPTCHA function, accidentally, as a rate limiter on exactly that. Your speed and offline capability are the same capability a land aggregator wants.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The single most demo-friendly feature you could build, and the one judges will ask for.

design_rules.rule: Make the local data store parcel-scoped and user-initiated: cache only records the user explicitly looked up, keep them on-device, never sync a village-wide corpus to a server, and be able to state in one sentence where every byte lives.
design_rules.rationale: CIS documented ~130–135 million Aadhaar numbers exposed across four government portals. A mirrored land dataset held by a private app carries the same risk profile with none of the state's legal cover.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Pre-fetching a whole village for offline speed — the obvious performance win, and the wrong one.

design_rules.rule: Treat every normalisation, merge and defaulting rule as a land-rights decision requiring a test vector, not a data-cleaning convenience. Never collapse two distinct entities to make a join work.
design_rules.rationale: Andhra Pradesh's Adangal digitisation defaulted Column 13 so owner and cultivator became the same person, erasing recorded tenancy. This project has already reproduced the failure class once: stripping characters from survey numbers fused 250 distinct parcels onto shared keys.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Nothing — but it is routinely violated under deadline, which is when it happens.

design_rules.rule: Name the non-users on the record view: state that the record lists recorded owners only, and that tenants, sharecroppers and unrecorded heirs will not appear even when they farm the land.
design_rules.rationale: Women are ~14% of landowners and 84% of landowning households have no female owner (Agarwal et al. 2021); official tenancy is ~10% of land and is agreed to be a large undercount because concealed leasing is unsafe to record.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Claiming the product 'serves farmers'. It serves recorded landowners. Those are different populations.

design_rules.rule: Give every record a path out of the app that survives on someone else's phone: a single plain image or PDF, legible at low resolution, shareable on WhatsApp, self-describing without the app installed.
design_rules.rationale: Only ~48.8% of Gujarat women have ever used the internet and ~47% of rural women own a phone; the decision-maker and the device-holder are frequently different people in the same household.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Deep-link/app-only sharing flows that assume the recipient installs anything.

design_rules.rule: Report a measured before/after on the access tax as your primary quantitative claim — taps, seconds, bytes, and failure rate to reach a named parcel on the incumbent versus yours, on a throttled connection and a low-end device — and present it as the ONLY thing you claim to have improved.
design_rules.rationale: Every institutional critique in this set (Bhoomi loopholes, Heeks' design–reality gap, Toyama's amplification) is unanswerable at the level of 'we fixed land administration' and fully answerable at the level of 'we removed a specific measurable friction'. Scope discipline is the defence.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The temptation to claim impact on litigation, corruption or farmer incomes, none of which you can evidence.

design_rules.rule: Open the honesty section by naming the strongest objection yourself — 'the interface is probably not the bottleneck, and here is the evidence' — and present the Digital Seva Setu counter-channel data before a judge raises it.
design_rules.rationale: I could not find any data on the portal-versus-counter channel split for Gujarat land records; the honest position is that the premise is unverified. Conceding an unverified premise is stronger than defending it badly.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Pitch convention, which rewards confident problem framing.

design_rules.rule: State the e-government base rate against yourself: ~35% total failure, ~50% partial failure in developing-country e-government (Heeks), then name the specific design-reality gaps you closed — no new government process required, fails safe to the official channel, no data the state does not already publish.
design_rules.rationale: Heeks' design–reality gap model predicts failure for outsider-built systems that assume organisational change. A design that requires zero institutional change has a structurally narrower gap, and that is a real, defensible engineering claim.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Roadmap slides promising government adoption, which widen the gap you just claimed to have narrowed.

design_rules.rule: Differentiate on provenance and trust signals rather than aesthetics: no ads, no data collection, no account, an open method note describing exactly how records are fetched, and visible non-affiliation with the Government of Gujarat.
design_rules.rationale: At least eight AnyRoR lookalike domains and multiple Play Store wrappers already occupy the free-viewer niche, all carrying non-affiliation disclaimers. A first-time rural user cannot distinguish you from them on visual quality alone.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Assuming design quality is itself a trust signal to this audience.

design_rules.rule: Attach scope to every statistic in the deck. Say 'two-thirds of civil cases in district courts, per a 2015-16 DAKSH survey of ~9,000 litigants across 24 states' — never '66% of court cases in India are land disputes'. Drop the '70% of land in the developing world is undocumented' claim entirely.
design_rules.rationale: The 66% figure has a genuine primary source but a much narrower scope than its popular rendering; the 70% figure could not be traced to any originating study.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Every deck in this category, which is precisely why scoped numbers read as credible.

gaps: CRITICAL GAP — the central question of the assignment is unanswered. I found no data anywhere on the channel split for land-record requests in Gujarat or any comparable state: what share of 7/12 requests go through the AnyRoR website versus a talati, an e-Dhara Kendra counter, a VCE at a gram panchayat, a CSC, a lawyer or a middleman. The 'e-Dhara has issued 47 million RoRs and e-Gram 13 million' figure appears in commercial SEO content with no traceable government source and should NOT be used. Gujarat's Digital Seva Setu volumes (~27.1 lakh users in 2023-24, ~35 lakh in 2024-25) are the closest proxy and are indicative only — they cover 321 services, not land records specifically. Treat the premise 'the interface is the bottleneck' as unverified, and consider that the cheapest way to close this gap is primary research you can actually do: ask ten people in Bharoda, Sundalpura and Valetva where they last got a 7/12 and what it cost them. Ten honest interviews beat any statistic you could cite.

I could not verify from any government source that iORA issues a digitally signed RoR online, nor its fee. The Rs 5–15 figure comes only from commercial guides and SEO sites. Landeed selling a 'digitally signed SatBara' at Rs 199 corroborates that such a document exists and is obtainable, but not that a citizen can self-serve it online cheaply. This is load-bearing for the certified-copy objection — verify it on iora.gujarat.gov.in yourself before presenting either way.

No evidence found of any legal action, cease-and-desist, takedown or IP-blocking against a private party scraping or re-presenting Indian government land-records data. This is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence — my search engines were exhausted or blocked before I could search this properly. Given that eight-plus SEO clone sites and multiple Play Store wrappers operate openly and a $19M-funded startup resells the documents commercially, the practical enforcement risk appears low, but I could not establish the legal position on Crown/government copyright, the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy, or IT Act s.43 as applied to automated access. Do not assert 'this is legal' on stage.

Could not retrieve the NCAER Land Records and Services Index (N-LRSI) scores — Gujarat's rank, its digitisation-versus-quality split, or the accessibility sub-index introduced in 2021. This is the single most relevant benchmark for the project and the report PDF is downloadable from ncaer.org. Get it; it may either strongly support you (poor quality/accessibility scores) or undercut you (Gujarat scoring well).

The Pulitzer Center Andhra Pradesh article and the Benjamin et al. Bhoomi working paper both 403'd to automated fetch. I am relying on secondary summaries for the Column 13 tenancy-erasure mechanism and for Bhoomi's quantitative findings. Both are central to the strongest objections — read the originals before quoting them.

Sources conflict on the provenance of the two-thirds land-litigation figure: PRS attributes it to a 2007 World Bank study, while the traceable primary source is DAKSH's 2015-16 Access to Justice Survey of district-court litigants. I could not locate the World Bank document. Cite DAKSH with its scope, not the World Bank attribution.

No quantitative evidence found of harm caused specifically by a land-records WEBSITE being easy to use — the documented harms (Bhoomi, Dharani, Andhra Pradesh) all stem from digitisation of the underlying record, not from front-end quality. This is genuinely helpful to you and should be said plainly: the privacy objection to a better viewer is an argument from mechanism and precedent, not from a measured case. It is still strong enough to justify the refusals in the design rules.

No Indian study found that isolates interface quality as a variable in government-service uptake. Every study conflates interface with the whole socio-technical deployment. This means neither you nor your critic can produce direct evidence on the project's core hypothesis — which is itself worth saying out loud, and is an argument for shipping a measurable friction claim rather than an impact claim.

The digitisation percentages I report are from September 2017 via PRS and are certainly stale — the government claimed ~95% rural digitisation by late 2024. Refresh before quoting.

topic: European land registries from a citizen's point of view — borrowable patterns for a redesigned Gujarat 7/12 (AnyRoR) portal, covering HM Land Registry (UK), Netherlands Kadaster, Sweden Lantmäteriet, Norway Kartverket, Denmark tinglysning, Finland Maanmittauslaitos, and the Estonian e-Land Register / X-Road

claims.claim: Estonian law forbids erasing or striking through register text. A change is made by deleting the previous entry and making a new one; the deleted part must remain permanently reproducible; deleted entries are shown only if separately requested; and when shown they must be visually distinguishable from valid entries.
claims.source_name: Land Register Act (Kinnistusraamatuseadus), Republic of Estonia — consolidated English text, §§25, 26(2), 77¹
claims.why_it_matters: This is the exact legal-grade version of the tombstone model already built in the irmsc identity layer, and it settles the chain-of-title UI question: history is never a separate 'history page', it is the same ledger with superseded rows hidden by default and revealed by one explicit control, rendered differently from live rows.

claims.claim: Estonian entries are numbered per division in the order made, and a change or deletion entry takes the number of the entry it refers to — so an amendment is visibly bound to what it amended.
claims.source_name: Land Register Act (Estonia), §25 Numbering of entries
claims.why_it_matters: Gives a numbering scheme for a VF-6 mutation ledger where a correction renders as a child of the entry it corrects, instead of as an unrelated new row.

claims.claim: An Estonian register part has a title plus four divisions: I 'Composition of the property' (cadastral code, purpose, location, area, and — explicitly — combining/dividing of real estates and separating/merging parts), II 'Owner', III 'Encumbrances and restrictions', IV 'Mortgages'.
claims.source_name: Land Register Act (Estonia), §§11(4), 13–16
claims.why_it_matters: Splits and mergers are a first-class register entry in Division I, not derived metadata — the direct precedent for surfacing parcel lineage on the parcel tile rather than burying it in a merge log.

claims.claim: In the Estonian register, cadastral code, intended purpose, location and area are supplied by the state land cadastre and the Act states they 'are not entries within the meaning of the Property Rights Act or this Act' — i.e. they sit on the same page as legally guaranteed data but are formally labelled as not guaranteed.
claims.source_name: Land Register Act (Estonia), §13(2)
claims.why_it_matters: A statutory precedent for visually separating guaranteed fields from informational fields pulled from another system — exactly the problem of showing jantri rates and map links beside VF-7 rights data.

claims.claim: Estonian publicity is split by layer: anyone may consult a register part and take printouts with no reason given, but the underlying real-estate file (the documents) requires a legitimate interest — and an owner can digitally authorise a named third party to view their file through the website, revocable through the website.
claims.source_name: Land Register Act (Estonia), §74 Publicity of the land register
claims.why_it_matters: A two-tier publicity model (summary open to all, documents gated) plus owner-granted delegation — a better answer than a CAPTCHA for the public/private tension, and it fits rural reality where a son or a talati acts for the owner.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry's free 'Search for land and property information' service was used 19.9 million times in FY2024-25, against 6.8 million paid 'Views of the register' and 1.1 million MapSearch — the free tier is roughly three times the paid tier. Total daily requests across these services: 215,000.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Annual Report and Accounts 2024 to 2025 — Performance report
claims.why_it_matters: Hard evidence that a free, no-account 'what is here' tier carries the citizen journey while paid official copies serve professionals — the strongest argument for making the Gujarat 7/12 read path free and unauthenticated.

claims.claim: 89% of HM Land Registry's 23 million+ guaranteed information requests in FY2024-25 were automated and available instantly; 99.8% of pre-completion requests were returned within three working days (target 99%).
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Annual Report and Accounts 2024 to 2025 — Performance report
claims.why_it_matters: A published, target-versus-actual SLA on an information service — the end-to-end/process metric a hackathon judge wants to see proposed, and a realistic benchmark to claim (instant for the cached majority, hours for the rest).

claims.claim: HM Land Registry's register holds more than 27 million titles covering over 89% of the land area of England and Wales, and its digital register has been 'fully open to the public' since 1990.
claims.figure: 27 million titles; 89% of land area; open since 1990
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Annual Report and Accounts 2024 to 2025 — Performance report
claims.why_it_matters: Useful comparator scale, and the '89% coverage' framing is an honest way to state that a register is incomplete without undermining it — a model for stating Gujarat coverage gaps.

claims.claim: On GOV.UK a citizen gets a free property summary (address, description, tenure, restrictive covenants, easements); the title register is £7, the title plan £7, and a posted official copy £11. Downloaded copies explicitly 'cannot be used as proof of ownership' — only the posted official copy is legal evidence.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK — Search for land and property information
claims.why_it_matters: The tiering to copy: free informational view, cheap unofficial download, paid legally-evidential copy — with the evidential status stated on the artefact itself. Directly solves 'is this screen the same as the paper 7/12'.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry raised electronic copy prices from £3 to £7 and postal copies from £7 to £11 on 9 December 2024, and publicly warns that private resellers repackage the same information at higher cost.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry blog — 'Are you paying too much for HM Land Registry services?'
claims.why_it_matters: The reseller problem is the same one AnyRoR has (paid 7/12 middlemen in every village). The registry's counter-move is to name the official price on its own site — cheap to copy.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry's bulk data catalogue prices each dataset explicitly and states whether an API exists: INSPIRE index polygons free/Open Government Licence/no API; Price Paid Data free/OGL/no API; Transaction Data free/OGL/no API; UK companies and Overseas companies that own property free, own licence, API yes; Registered Leases and Restrictive Covenants fee-dependent, API yes; National Polygon Service £20,000 + VAT a year, API yes.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry — Use land and property data (datasets catalogue)
claims.why_it_matters: Shows the actual open/closed line a best-in-class registry draws: geometry indexes and price data open; the authoritative full polygon-plus-title product priced for commercial reuse. A defensible model for what a Gujarat portal could open first.

claims.claim: Price Paid Data covers more than 24 million records of residential sales in England and Wales back to January 1995, updated monthly, published under Open Government Licence v3.0, also as a 4-star linked-data set of over 400 million triples with a public SPARQL endpoint.
claims.figure: 24 million records; 400 million triples; since Jan 1995
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Open Data
claims.why_it_matters: Proof that transaction prices can be fully open without publishing buyer/seller identity — the template for opening Gujarat sale-deed values while keeping names gated.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry publishes a plain-language accuracy disclaimer on its own open data: 'We strive to ensure that our public data is as accurate as possible but cannot guarantee that it is free from errors or fit for your purpose or use. Reports are based on data collected at the time a property transaction is registered with us and will not necessarily be up to date.'
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Open Data
claims.why_it_matters: Ready-made wording for the honesty requirement: a state registry saying out loud that its own data may be wrong and stale, without hedging the whole product into uselessness.

claims.claim: Since launching its 'Use land and property data' platform in 2020, HM Land Registry reports more than 1.5 million data downloads, which it states generates 'an economic benefit of £370 million per year'.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Annual Report and Accounts 2024 to 2025 — Performance report
claims.why_it_matters: Quotable open-data benefit figure, but it is the agency's own estimate with no methodology shown in the report — cite it as a claim by HMLR, not as a measured fact.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry runs a free 'Property Alert' service: email alerts on significant activity (e.g. a new mortgage) for up to 10 monitored properties, and you do not have to own a property to monitor it — you can monitor a relative's. HMLR reports 669 fraudulent registrations prevented since 2009.
claims.figure: free; up to 10 properties; 669 frauds prevented since 2009
claims.source_name: GOV.UK — Property Alert (HM Land Registry) and HMLR Annual Report 2024-25
claims.why_it_matters: A high-value, low-cost feature for exactly the Gujarat fraud problem (benami mutations, forged entries), and the 'monitor a relative's property' rule fits migrant families watching ancestral land from another city.

claims.claim: Anyone may inspect the register or caution register of any individual title, its title plan, and documents referred to in the register, without giving a reason — the open register under the Land Registration Act 2002 s.66. The privacy carve-out is the 'exempt information document' regime (application on form EX2, with notice to interested parties).
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Practice guide 11: inspection and application for official copies
claims.why_it_matters: The clean statement that public land data needs no justification to read — the direct rebuttal to AnyRoR's CAPTCHA-on-public-data. Privacy is handled by exempting specific documents, not by obstructing everyone.

claims.claim: An HM Land Registry title register is split into three parts: Property register (the land and estate, freehold/leasehold), Proprietorship register (current legal owners, class of title, restrictions on dealing, price last paid), Charges register (mortgages and other burdens). It shows the current state, not a chain of title; previous editions must be ordered separately on form HC1, and HMLR only holds electronic registers from 4 May 1993 and electronic title plans from 13 October 2003.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry form HC1 and Practice guide 11; LexisNexis guidance on register contents
claims.why_it_matters: Important negative finding: the UK, often held up as best in class, does NOT show chain of title in its citizen UI. If you show ownership history inline you are ahead of HMLR, not behind it — and you should say so.

claims.claim: In the Netherlands, viewing your own cadastral data is free: 'Inzicht in de eigen kadastrale gegevens is gratis', and Kadaster's Eigenaarsinformatie product ('what property is registered in my name, and what restrictions apply') is delivered free through the national citizen portal MijnOverheid.nl with DigiD login. Third-party extracts are paid.
claims.source_name: Geobasisregistraties.nl — Basisregistratie Kadaster; Kadaster — Eigenaarsinformatie
claims.why_it_matters: The 'my holdings' view — one authenticated screen listing every parcel you own across villages — is free everywhere in Europe and is the single most useful screen for a farmer with scattered survey numbers. It is also the natural home for the stamp strip.

claims.claim: Kadaster's paid citizen products are priced in single euros: Eigendomsinformatie and Hypotheekinformatie €3.70 via the webshop (€22.25 by post), Koopsominformatie from €3.70, and a price-by-SMS product at €1.50 charged only if information is actually available for that address.
claims.source_name: Kadaster.nl — Eigendomsinformatie, Hypotheekinformatie, Koopsominformatie product pages
claims.why_it_matters: Two patterns worth copying: an order of magnitude cheaper online than by post (pricing that pushes people to the cheap channel), and never charging when the lookup returns nothing.

claims.claim: The Dutch Basisregistratie Kadaster (BRK) has exactly two components — the cadastral registration and the cadastral map — and is deliberately linked to the other base registries: BAG (addresses and buildings), the Handelsregister (companies) and BRP (persons), so that the rightful holder of any dwelling or commercial building can be resolved by key rather than by name matching.
claims.source_name: Geobasisregistraties.nl — Basisregistratie Kadaster
claims.why_it_matters: The Dutch 'stelsel van basisregistraties' (register once, use many times, one authoritative source per concept, joined by identifiers) is the end-to-end architecture story: it is why Kadaster never has to fuzzy-match owner names, and it is the argument for a place-id and person-id layer under a Gujarat portal.

claims.claim: A Dutch parcel is identified by cadastral municipality + section + parcel number, and the parcel number CHANGES whenever the boundary changes (split or merge). Kadaster sells 'filiatieonderzoek' at €60 per object to trace the relationship between old and new parcel numbers — either which parcels a current parcel came from, or which parcels a former parcel became. Research cannot go back before 1 April 1838.
claims.source_name: Kadaster — Vroegere percelen opvragen (filiatieonderzoek)
claims.why_it_matters: Key finding on parcel identity: the Dutch approach is a NEW identifier on every boundary change plus an explicit, bidirectional lineage service. That is the opposite of Gujarat's mutating suffixes (845/અ, 2/1/p1/p) and validates the irmsc merge layer as a lineage graph — parent-of / child-of edges, queryable in both directions.

claims.claim: Kadaster publishes live service metrics in the footer of every page: average call-centre wait 32 seconds, customer rating 7.8, 73% helped immediately.
claims.source_name: Kadaster.nl (site-wide contact panel)
claims.why_it_matters: Radical, cheap transparency — the registry publishes its own service quality on the page where you might need help. A near-zero-cost honesty feature for a hackathon build (show live scrape success rate, last-sync time, source uptime).

claims.claim: Dutch cadastral personal data is public by law, but can be shielded on request: for people in the state protection system (Kadasterbesluit art. 37a) and for at-risk professions under signed covenants with the bailiffs' body (KBvG), the bar association (NOvA), the Public Prosecution Service (OM), the Council for the Judiciary (RvdR), the journalists' union (NVJ) and the Police. Notaries, bailiffs and administrative bodies still receive the shielded data because their statutory duties require it.
claims.source_name: Kadaster — Laten afschermen persoonsgegevens
claims.why_it_matters: The mature answer to public-vs-private: publish by default, shield named at-risk individuals by exception, and keep the shielded data flowing to the officials who legally need it. Far better than the blanket obstruction a CAPTCHA provides.

claims.claim: In the Netherlands only residential WOZ values are public, via the national WOZ-waardeloket (legal basis Wet WOZ art. 40b(1)); non-residential values require a demonstrated 'justified interest' (art. 40(1)-(2)); and the underlying valuation report is available only to the property's own interested party, never to third parties comparing properties.
claims.source_name: Waarderingskamer — Vraagbaak Wet WOZ, hoofdstuk 7: openbare en niet-openbare WOZ-gegevens
claims.why_it_matters: A worked example of publishing a government valuation figure while withholding the workings — and of the stated reason for publishing it (letting citizens check their own assessment against neighbours), which is the honest framing for showing jantri.

claims.claim: Kadaster's public WOZ explainer follows a fixed disclosure template: it names the responsible body (the municipality, not Kadaster), states the purpose (property tax, water board levies, income tax), gives the valuation reference date ('the amount the dwelling should fetch on 1 January of the preceding year'), gives the objection route and the 6-week deadline, states 'we cannot change these figures for you', and lists the two reasons a value may be missing.
claims.figure: reference date 1 Jan of preceding year; 6-week objection window
claims.source_name: Kadaster — WOZ-waarde van een huis
claims.why_it_matters: This is the template to copy verbatim for the jantri stamp-duty floor: purpose, owner of the number, as-of date, challenge route, and 'not us, not changeable here'. It stops a tax figure from reading as a market valuation without a hedging paragraph.

claims.claim: Sweden's 'Vem äger fastigheten' owner-lookup is free but hard-gated for privacy: BankID login required; the user must attest a lawful purpose (private processing, or dealing in registered property) under lagen (2000:224) om fastighetsregister; each user is limited to FIVE searches per 24 hours explicitly to satisfy GDPR; and the user must log in from within the EU/EEA/Switzerland because of the GDPR third-country transfer ban.
claims.source_name: Lantmäteriet — Vem äger fastigheten
claims.why_it_matters: The best real-world answer to 'public data, but stop bulk harvesting': identity + purpose attestation + a hard per-person rate limit, applied to owner NAMES only. It is what a CAPTCHA is pretending to do, done properly — and it leaves the parcel data itself fully open.

claims.claim: Lantmäteriet's 'Min fastighet' is free with BankID and covers only the user's own properties, site leaseholds, joint facilities and joint units — showing area, mortgages, taxeringsvärde (tax assessment value), servitudes and land-use plans. People with protected identity are removed from the service entirely and must be served by phone.
claims.source_name: Lantmäteriet — Min fastighet
claims.why_it_matters: Confirms the free 'my holdings' tier again, and honestly documents its cost: the privacy carve-out breaks self-service for the most vulnerable users. Worth naming as a limitation rather than repeating silently.

claims.claim: Lantmäteriet explains lookup FAILURE by its underlying data cause: if you own a property but nothing appears in Min fastighet, it is probably because your personnummer is missing from the register's inskrivningsdel — since it is not a mandatory field when applying for lagfart — and it tells you how to supply it.
claims.source_name: Lantmäteriet — Min fastighet
claims.why_it_matters: The single most copyable micro-pattern in this whole report for AnyRoR, where 'no record found' is the default failure. Naming the specific registry defect that caused the empty result converts a dead end into an actionable next step.

claims.claim: A Swedish property designation (fastighetsbeteckning) has exactly three parts — municipality, then trakt/kvarter name, then a register number, e.g. 'Stockholm Söder 75:2' or 'Gävle Abborren 1' — and the service tells the user that a no-hit almost certainly means one of the three parts is missing from what they typed.
claims.source_name: Lantmäteriet — Vem äger fastigheten
claims.why_it_matters: A structured identifier taught to the citizen in one sentence, with the failure mode explained in terms of the structure. The Gujarat equivalent (district / taluka / village / survey with suffix) can be taught the same way instead of via five chained dropdowns.

claims.claim: The Swedish fastighetsregister is organised in parts — allmänna delen (designations, boundaries, and property-law actions such as avstyckning/subdivision and sammanläggning/merger, plus tidigare fastighetsbeteckning, the previous designation), inskrivningsdelen (title/lagfart, mortgages, leases; ~3.2 million properties, updated daily on workdays), adressdelen, byggnadsdelen (~7 million buildings), and taxeringsuppgifter supplied annually each July by the Swedish Tax Agency.
claims.figure: ~3.2M properties; ~7M buildings; tax values annually in July
claims.source_name: Lantmäteriet — Fastighetsregistret: registrets innehåll
claims.why_it_matters: Two things to borrow: 'previous designation' is a first-class stored field (not a computed guess), and the tax-assessment value lives in a clearly separate, differently-updated part of the register — reinforcing that valuation data must be visually and temporally separated from rights data.

claims.claim: Denmark's tingbog (land register) is searchable free by anyone. Without login you get summary information; with MitID you see the most, including purchase price, mortgage terms and servitude text. A control labelled 'Vis historiske adkomster' (show historical titles) reveals previous owners, when they bought, and what they paid.
claims.source_name: Videncentret Bolius — 'Se din nabos tinglysning – gratis' (citing Tinglysningsretten)
claims.why_it_matters: The closest thing found to a chain-of-title feature in a live public citizen UI: history is a labelled toggle on the same page as the current owner, not a separate paid product. This is the established pattern to copy for the VF-6 mutation view.

claims.claim: Danish land-register searching became free on 1 July 2013; before that a lookup on someone else's property cost DKK 30–120 and access to underlying documents DKK 175. The registration duty (tinglysningsafgift) was raised in compensation — as of January 2024, DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the purchase sum to register a deed.
claims.figure: free since 1 July 2013; previously DKK 30–120 per search; duty DKK 1,850 + 0.6%
claims.source_name: Videncentret Bolius (citing Tinglysningsretten)
claims.why_it_matters: The funding model for free access — recover cost at the transaction, not at the lookup — is exactly the argument for making 7/12 reads free in Gujarat. But the date conflicts with a secondary claim of a 2014 parliamentary decision, so trace it before quoting.

claims.claim: Finland is the counter-example on citizen cost: the National Land Survey charges €20.08 excl. VAT (€25.20 incl.) for ownership and address information on 1–6 register units, €3.35/€4.20 per unit beyond that, and its contractual real-property data interface carries a minimum fee of €247.40 excl. VAT (€310.49 incl.) per year.
claims.figure: €25.20 incl. VAT for a basic ownership lookup
claims.source_name: National Land Survey of Finland — Price list: property ownership and address information
claims.why_it_matters: Guards against the 'Nordic = free and open' cliché. Finland is highly digital and still charges more than €25 for a basic ownership lookup, so 'Europe does it free' is not a safe blanket claim in a submission.

claims.claim: Estonia's e-Land Register portal authenticates private persons by ID card or Mobile-ID. Viewing your own registered immovables and their documents is free; queries on other people's immovables are charged per query, or by monthly invoice under a contract. Data is exchanged with other Estonian registers over X-Road.
claims.source_name: Centre of Registers and Information Systems (RIK) — E-Land Register portal
claims.why_it_matters: Confirms the free-own / paid-other split a third time, across three unrelated jurisdictions — strong enough to treat as the established European default rather than one country's quirk. Fee amounts are not published on the page.

claims.claim: X-Road, Estonia's data-exchange layer, is reported to carry 2.2 billion transactions per year across 3,000+ e-services with 52,000 organisations as indirect users; all outgoing data is digitally signed and encrypted and all incoming data authenticated and logged; it is deployed in over 20 countries and federated with Finland since February 2018.
claims.source_name: e-Estonia — X-Road
claims.why_it_matters: The right architectural reference for the backend story (registers talk over a signed, logged, authenticated bus rather than by scraping each other), but e-estonia.com is a government promotion site and the figures are self-reported with no methodology — attribute, do not assert.

claims.claim: The Estonian land cadastre and the land register are deliberately two registers with two identifiers: cadastral register number (a numeric code per cadastral unit, held by the Land and Spatial Development Board) and registered immovable number (per immovable in the land register, held by Tartu County Court's Land Registry Department). Subdivision and merger of cadastral units are formal, separately-documented procedures.
claims.source_name: Estonian Land and Spatial Development Board — Geoportal, Landowner's Guide
claims.why_it_matters: Separating the SPATIAL identity of a piece of ground from the LEGAL identity of the rights over it is what lets Estonia renumber a parcel on subdivision without breaking the title. Gujarat conflates the two in the survey number, which is precisely why the merge layer was needed.

claims.claim: GOV.UK's service manual and design system prescribe: start with one thing per page; run a question protocol so every question is justified; mark optional fields '(optional)' and never mark mandatory fields with asterisks; allow 'I do not know' where valid; always include a Back link without breaking the browser back button; and never ask for the same information twice in one journey. The stated benefits include easier comprehension, easier mobile use, faster error recovery, incremental save, and per-question analytics.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK Design System — Question pages pattern; GOV.UK Service Manual — Form structure
claims.why_it_matters: The direct antidote to AnyRoR's five chained dropdowns on one page. Note the honesty caveat: the service manual justifies one-thing-per-page with a single example (Register to Vote) and general principles, not cited empirical studies — so present it as an established government convention, not a proven finding.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry measures customer satisfaction only via a quarterly survey of PROFESSIONAL customers rating 8-10, with Information Services and Land Charges highest at nearly 90%. No citizen-facing satisfaction metric appears in the annual report.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry Annual Report and Accounts 2024 to 2025 — Performance report
claims.why_it_matters: A gap you can claim: even the best-resourced registry in this set publishes no usability measure for ordinary citizens. Proposing one (task completion for a first-time rural user) is genuine product thinking, not table stakes.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry's Digital Street project completed a blockchain-based transfer of a semi-detached house in Gillingham, Kent on 6 March 2019 using R3's Corda with Mishcon de Reya, MyHomeMove, Shieldpay, Yoti and HMRC. It was framed as a proof of concept, with no plan to adopt the technology, and a research horizon to 2030.
claims.source_name: Computer Weekly / Legal Futures / UKAuthority reporting on HM Land Registry Digital Street
claims.why_it_matters: Useful as a cautionary reference: the flagship registry blockchain experiment moved exactly one property and was never adopted. Cite it if a judge asks 'why not blockchain'; do not cite it as a working pattern. No published evaluation was found.

design_rules.rule: Make the entire read path free and unauthenticated — no CAPTCHA, no session, no account — and reserve authentication for (a) the 'my holdings' view and (b) legally evidential copies. Put a persistent line on every record saying which tier it is: 'Informational copy. Not proof of ownership.'
design_rules.rationale: HMLR's free tier ran 19.9M times in FY2024-25 against 6.8M paid register views, so the free tier IS the citizen journey; PG11/LRA 2002 s.66 confirms anyone may inspect a register without giving a reason; and GOV.UK states outright that a downloaded copy cannot be used as proof of ownership. Estonia's §74 draws the same line: the register part is open to all, the underlying file needs legitimate interest.
design_rules.conflicts_with: AnyRoR's CAPTCHA and server-side session on data that is legally public. Also conflicts with the instinct to gate everything behind a login 'for security'.

design_rules.rule: Build a free, authenticated 'My land' screen that lists every parcel held in the user's name across all villages, with the 4-slot stamp strip per parcel. Make this, not search, the app's home screen for a signed-in user.
design_rules.rationale: All four systems that offer a free tier converge on exactly this: Kadaster's Eigenaarsinformatie is free via MijnOverheid/DigiD ('inzicht in de eigen kadastrale gegevens is gratis'), Lantmäteriet's Min fastighet is free with BankID, Kartverket shows only your own properties on login, and Estonia's e-Land Register is free for your own immovables and charged for others'. Three unrelated jurisdictions landing on the same split makes it the European default, not a quirk.
design_rules.conflicts_with: AnyRoR's model, where every retrieval starts from geography and a farmer with parcels in three villages must run the cascade three times.

design_rules.rule: Render ownership history as ONE ledger, not two screens. Superseded rows stay in place, hidden behind a single explicit control ('Show superseded entries'), and when shown they render visibly differently (struck/dimmed/dashed) from live rows. A correction row carries the number of the row it corrects and renders indented under it.
design_rules.rationale: This is Estonian statute, not fashion: Land Register Act §77¹ requires that a change be made by deleting the old entry and adding a new one, that the deleted part remain permanently reproducible, that deleted entries appear only on separate request, and that when reproduced they be distinguishable from valid entries; §25 gives a change/delete entry the number of the entry it refers to; §26(2) forbids erasing. Denmark ships the same idea in a live public UI as the 'Vis historiske adkomster' toggle showing previous owners, dates and prices.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The common instinct to build a separate 'History' tab or an animated timeline. No system found does either; they all keep history inline in the ledger. It also conflicts with physical deletion — which the irmsc tombstone rule already forbids.

design_rules.rule: Do not derive parcel lineage — store it as an explicit, bidirectional, first-class relation (parent-of / child-of) and render it on the parcel tile itself as 'Formed from 845' / 'Split into 845/અ, 845/બ', each a tappable link.
design_rules.rationale: Estonia records combining, dividing, separating and merging of real estates as entries in Division I of the register part (§13(1)6) — lineage is register content, not metadata. Kadaster assigns a NEW parcel number on every boundary change and sells filiatieonderzoek (€60/object) as an explicitly bidirectional lookup: which parcels this one came from, or which parcels a former one became. Sweden stores 'tidigare fastighetsbeteckning' as a stored field in the allmänna delen.
design_rules.conflicts_with: String-munging the survey number to infer relationships. The irmsc probe-tokenizer result (stripping characters fused 250 different surveys onto one uid) is the empirical proof that inference fails; Europe's answer is that lineage is authored data.

design_rules.rule: Separate the spatial identity of the ground from the legal identity of the rights over it, with two identifiers and two lifecycles. The parcel identifier may change on a boundary event; the rights record persists and points at whichever parcel identifier is current.
design_rules.rationale: Estonia runs exactly two registers with two numbers — cadastral register number (Land and Spatial Development Board) and registered immovable number (Tartu County Court) — which is what lets a parcel be renumbered on subdivision without breaking title. The Netherlands does the same by splitting BRK into cadastral registration plus cadastral map.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Gujarat's survey number, which carries both meanings at once — which is precisely why suffixes like 845/અ and part-parcels like 2/1/p1/p produce identity collisions.

design_rules.rule: Visually mark every field that is informational rather than legally guaranteed — area, map link, jantri rate, crop data — with a distinct treatment (a muted label plus source attribution) and never let it share styling with rights data.
design_rules.rationale: Estonian Land Register Act §13(2) states in statute that cadastral code, purpose, location and area — sitting on the same register page as the owner and the mortgages — 'are not entries within the meaning of the Property Rights Act or this Act'. A best-in-class register puts the guaranteed/not-guaranteed boundary in law and shows it on the page.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Flattening every field into one uniform data table, which is what AnyRoR's photo-of-paper output does.

design_rules.rule: Present the jantri figure using the full Kadaster WOZ disclosure template, in this order: what it is FOR (stamp-duty floor), WHO sets it (the state government, not this app), the AS-OF date (ASR-2011 with the 15/04/2023 doubling applied), how to CHALLENGE it, and 'we cannot change this figure here'. Add the two reasons it may be absent. Never place it next to any figure that could read as a market price, and never render area × rate unless the area is actually known.
design_rules.rationale: Kadaster's WOZ page follows precisely this template — responsible body, purpose (property tax/water levies/income tax), reference date ('the amount the dwelling should fetch on 1 January of the preceding year'), 6-week objection deadline, 'we cannot change these figures for you', plus the two reasons a value can be missing. The Dutch legislature also published residential WOZ values specifically so citizens could check their own assessment, which is the honest framing for showing an official rate at all.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The common product urge to show a headline 'estimated property value'. Every European system that publishes an official figure labels it by its tax purpose and by who is accountable for it.

design_rules.rule: Protect owner NAMES with identity plus purpose attestation plus a hard per-person rate limit — not with a CAPTCHA. Leave parcel geometry, area, survey identity and mutation events fully open. If names must be shown to anonymous users, show them only for the parcel the user already identified, never in a searchable-by-name index.
design_rules.rationale: Lantmäteriet's owner lookup is free but requires BankID, an attested lawful purpose under lagen (2000:224), a login from within the EU/EEA/Switzerland, and caps every user at five searches per 24 hours explicitly to satisfy GDPR. That is what a CAPTCHA pretends to do, done properly: it stops bulk harvesting of personal data while leaving the land data itself open (cf. HMLR PG11 — anyone may inspect a register with no reason given).
design_rules.conflicts_with: AnyRoR's CAPTCHA, which blocks everyone equally and stops nobody determined (the irmsc CNN solves it at 98.7%), while the personal data behind it stays bulk-scrapeable.

design_rules.rule: Ship a named-individual shielding mechanism from day one: a documented route by which a person at risk can have their name suppressed from public view, with the data still flowing to officials who need it (talati, registrar, courts). Say in the UI that the mechanism exists.
design_rules.rationale: Kadaster shields personal data under Kadasterbesluit art. 37a for people in the state protection system and, via signed covenants, for journalists (NVJ), lawyers (NOvA), judges (RvdR), prosecutors (OM), bailiffs (KBvG) and police — while notaries, bailiffs and administrative bodies still receive the shielded data. Sweden's equivalent is blunter and worse: protected-identity people are removed from Min fastighet entirely and must phone in.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Treating 'the data is public by law' as the end of the privacy conversation. Publish-by-default plus exception-by-name is the mature position; the Swedish carve-out also shows the cost of doing it crudely.

design_rules.rule: Replace the five chained dropdowns with one thing per page: one question, one heading, one Continue, a Back link that does not break the browser back button, and a summary/check-answers page before the fetch. Ask nothing twice; pre-fill anything already known.
design_rules.rationale: GOV.UK Design System question-pages pattern and the service manual's form-structure guidance: start with one thing per page, run a question protocol, always include a Back link, allow 'I do not know', mark optional fields '(optional)' and never asterisk mandatory ones, and never ask for the same information twice in one journey — with mobile use and error recovery given as explicit reasons.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Nothing in the incumbent — but be honest in the write-up that GDS justifies this convention with principles and one worked example (Register to Vote), not cited empirical studies.

design_rules.rule: Teach the identifier's structure in one sentence, and explain a no-result in terms of that structure — 'a survey number here is village + number + optional suffix; no match usually means the suffix is missing or written differently'.
design_rules.rationale: Lantmäteriet does exactly this: it states that a fastighetsbeteckning has three parts with two worked examples ('Stockholm Söder 75:2', 'Gävle Abborren 1') and then says a no-hit probably means one of the three parts is missing from what you typed.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Generic 'No records found' — the single most common and least useful outcome on AnyRoR.

design_rules.rule: Never return a bare empty state. Every 'not found' must name the most likely underlying data cause and give the next action. E.g. 'This survey exists in VF-7 but has no VF-12 crop record for this year — crop entries are filed after the season by the talati.'
design_rules.rationale: Lantmäteriet's Min fastighet explains that if you own property and nothing shows, it is probably because your personnummer is missing from the inskrivningsdel, since it is not a mandatory field when applying for lagfart — and tells you how to fix it. Kadaster does the same for a missing WOZ value, listing the two possible causes. Both convert a dead end into a next step.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Treating empty results as an edge case. On a register with real coverage gaps it is a primary journey.

design_rules.rule: Charge nothing for a lookup that returns nothing, and price the online channel an order of magnitude below the offline one.
design_rules.rationale: Kadaster's SMS price product charges €1.50 'only if information is available for the address', and its Eigendomsinformatie is €3.70 online versus €22.25 by post. Denmark went further and made lookups free from 1 July 2013, recovering the cost at the transaction instead (registration duty raised to DKK 1,850 + 0.6% of the purchase sum).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Per-query pricing at the point of curiosity, which is what pushes Gujarat farmers to paid middlemen. Note the Danish date is from a secondary source and should be traced before being quoted.

design_rules.rule: Ship a free 'watch this survey number' alert: notify the user when any new mutation, charge or entry touches a parcel they follow, with no requirement that they own it — so a migrant son can watch ancestral land.
design_rules.rationale: HMLR's Property Alert is free, covers up to 10 properties, explicitly allows monitoring a relative's property, and alerts on significant activity such as a new mortgage; HMLR reports 669 fraudulent registrations prevented since 2009. This is the highest-leverage feature per unit of build effort found in the whole survey.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Nothing — AnyRoR has no equivalent, which is the point.

design_rules.rule: Publish your own service quality on the page: last successful sync per source, current scrape success rate, and what is stale. Do it in the footer of every screen, not on a hidden status page.
design_rules.rationale: Kadaster prints average call wait (32 s), customer rating (7.8) and first-contact resolution (73%) in the contact panel of every page. HMLR publishes target-versus-actual SLAs (99% target, 99.8% achieved; 89% of 23M requests automated and instant) in its annual report. Both are near-zero-cost honesty.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Hiding degradation. For a hackathon judged partly on honesty about mocked parts, a live 'what is real, what is cached, what is mocked' panel is the cheapest credibility available.

design_rules.rule: Copy HMLR's data disclaimer wording onto any bulk or derived output: state that the data may contain errors, may not be fit for the user's purpose, and reflects the state at the time of registration rather than today.
design_rules.rationale: HMLR publishes exactly that on landregistry.data.gov.uk for its own open data. A state registry admitting its data may be wrong and stale, in plain words, without hedging the product into uselessness, is the tone to imitate.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The urge to present scraped register data as authoritative because it came from a government source.

design_rules.rule: Draw the open-data line as: geometry, parcel identity, area and anonymised transaction values fully open under a named licence with a documented API; owner identity gated; the authoritative full-fidelity product priced for commercial reuse.
design_rules.rationale: That is literally HMLR's catalogue: INSPIRE index polygons free/OGL, Price Paid Data free/OGL (24M records since 1995, plus a 400M-triple linked-data set with public SPARQL), Transaction Data free/OGL, company-ownership datasets free with API, and the National Polygon Service — the authoritative geometry-plus-title product — at £20,000 + VAT a year with an API.
design_rules.conflicts_with: An all-or-nothing open-data position. The nuance (open the index, price the authoritative join) is what makes the proposal survive contact with a revenue-collecting department.

design_rules.rule: Frame the backend as registers talking over a signed, logged, authenticated bus with one authoritative source per concept (place, person, parcel, right), joined by stable identifiers — not as one system scraping another.
design_rules.rationale: The Dutch stelsel van basisregistraties links BRK to BAG, the Handelsregister and BRP by key, which is why Kadaster never fuzzy-matches owner names; Estonia's X-Road signs, encrypts, authenticates and logs every exchange (reported 2.2B transactions/yr, 3,000+ services, though self-reported by a government promotion site).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Presenting a scraper as the architecture. Scraping is the honest interim; the target architecture should be stated as the base-registry model, with the scraper named as the shim.

design_rules.rule: State plainly in the submission that showing ownership history inline puts you AHEAD of HM Land Registry, and that no system surveyed publishes a citizen usability metric.
design_rules.rationale: HMLR's title register shows only the current proprietorship state; previous editions must be ordered separately on form HC1, and HMLR only holds electronic registers from 4 May 1993 and electronic title plans from 13 October 2003.
