Its published satisfaction measure surveys professional customers only (~90% for Information Services), with no citizen-facing measure in the annual report.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The assumption that European registries are ahead on every axis. On chain of title in the citizen UI, only Denmark's free tingbog toggle clearly is.

design_rules.rule: Do not propose blockchain. If asked, cite the reference case and move on.
design_rules.rationale: HM Land Registry's Digital Street completed exactly one blockchain property transfer (Gillingham, Kent, 6 March 2019, on R3 Corda with Mishcon de Reya, Shieldpay, Yoti and HMRC), framed it as a proof of concept, stated no adoption plans, and set a research horizon to 2030. No published evaluation was found.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The hackathon instinct to reach for a ledger technology when the actual problems are access, identity and presentation.

gaps: Kartverket.no (Norway) was unreachable from this environment on every attempt (network error via curl and WebFetch alike), so all Norwegian claims rest on search-engine summaries of Kartverket pages rather than pages I read. Treat Norway as unverified: I could not confirm what Se eiendom/Eiendomsregisteret shows without login, whether ID-porten is required, what is free, or how matrikkelnummer (gnr/bnr/fnr/snr) behaves across splits and mergers.

Denmark's free-search date conflicts between sources: Bolius (citing Tinglysningsretten) says free since 1 July 2013 with prior fees of DKK 30-120 per search and DKK 175 for documents; a separate secondary source says a broad Folketing majority decided in 2014 to open free unrestricted access. Neither is a primary legal source. domstol.dk and tinglysning.dk both blocked automated access (Cloudflare interstitial), so I could not reach Tinglysningsretten or Retsinformation to settle it. Do not quote the date without tracing it to the amending act.

No published USABILITY metric was found for any system — no SUS scores, task-completion rates, time-on-task, or before/after redesign studies. HMLR publishes volume and SLA data plus a satisfaction survey of professional customers only. Everything I found is adoption/throughput, not usability. If you need a usability number for the submission, you will have to generate it yourself from testing.

No screenshots or visual descriptions of how chain of title is actually laid out on screen were obtainable — the live services (search-property-information.service.gov.uk, tinglysning.dk, kinnistusraamat.rik.ee) all sit behind JavaScript interstitials or bot protection, and I did not attempt interaction per the read-only constraint. The chain-of-title findings are therefore from statute (Estonia §77¹, §25) and from a Danish consumer explainer describing the 'Vis historiske adkomster' control, not from seeing the UI.

Estonian e-Land Register FEE AMOUNTS are not published on the RIK portal page — it states own-property-free / other-property-paid but gives no figures. Similarly I could not verify the Estonian Land Register's search-by-person-name policy or whether an anonymous user can query at all.

Kadaster's public map viewer specifics were not verified first-hand: I confirmed the BRK data model and the product/price pages, but not what the free kadastralekaart viewer actually renders, nor Kadaster's developer APIs (api.kadaster.nl / BRK Bevragen / PDOK WFS availability and whether they are open or key-gated). The Kadaster price figures (€3.70 / €22.25 / €1.50) come from a search-engine extraction of the product pages, not from the price text as I read it.

Denmark's official property valuation (ejendomsvurdering) caveat language could not be retrieved — vurderingsportalen.dk blocked automated access. The valuation-caveat rule therefore rests entirely on the Dutch WOZ material. Sweden's taxeringsvärde was confirmed as present in the register but I could not reach Skatteverket to confirm the commonly repeated '75% of market value' rule; treat that ratio as unverified folklore until sourced.

Firecrawl was unavailable (HTTP 402, credits exhausted) and the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was consumed early, so later research was limited to direct fetches of URLs I already knew. Several sites (use-land-property-data initially, kartverket.no, tinglysning.dk, domstol.dk, vurderingsportalen.dk, skatteverket.se, riigiteataja.ee's JS-rendered consolidated text) resisted automated reading; the Estonian statute was recovered instead from the FAO FAOLEX English PDF, which is a translation and should be checked against riigiteataja.ee before being quoted verbatim in a legal context.

The £370 million/year economic benefit HMLR attributes to its open-data platform is published without methodology in the annual report. It is the agency's own estimate. I could not find the underlying study.

topic: Government portal redesigns and their measured impact — evidence base for a Gujarat 7/12 land-records citizen portal (GOV.UK/GDS, USDS/18F, Estonia, Singapore, India), plus pattern-level evidence on cascading dropdowns, one-thing-per-page, CAPTCHA, legal-document presentation, progressive disclosure and offline-first delivery

claims.claim: The UK Government Service Manual states outright: "There are security, privacy, usability and accessibility issues associated with CAPTCHAs. You must not use them unless you both: limit their use to cases where you detect suspicious activity ... [and] have evidence to show that alternative solutions will not work for your service." It names rate and connection limiting, honey pots, and transaction monitoring as the alternatives, and warns "Advances in computer imaging and the use of CAPTCHA farms means some bots will still be able to access your service."
claims.source_name: GOV.UK Service Manual — Using CAPTCHAs (Government Digital Service)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the single strongest citation for deleting AnyRoR's CAPTCHA. It is a standing government-wide policy instruction, not an opinion piece, and it pre-specifies the replacement (rate limiting + honeypots + transaction monitoring) so the proposal is not 'remove the guard', it is 'swap a user-facing guard for a server-side one'.

claims.claim: Measured head-to-head, bots beat humans at every deployed CAPTCHA type. Distorted-text CAPTCHA: humans take 9–15.3 seconds at 50–84% accuracy; bots take under 1 second at 99.8% accuracy. reCAPTCHA image: humans 15–26 s at 81%; bots 17.5 s at 85%. reCAPTCHA checkbox: humans 3.1–4.9 s at 71–85%; bots 1.4 s at 100%. Study: 1,400 participants solving 14,000 unmodified, currently-deployed CAPTCHAs.
claims.figure: humans 50–84% vs bots 99.8% on distorted text
claims.source_name: Searles, Nakatsuka, Ozturk, Paverd, Tsudik, Enkoji — "An Empirical Study & Evaluation of Modern CAPTCHAs", USENIX Security 2023 (arXiv:2307.12108), Table 3
claims.why_it_matters: Kills the security justification. AnyRoR's CAPTCHA is a distorted-text CAPTCHA — the exact category where the measured human/bot gap is most inverted. It is a tax on the farmer and a rounding error to a scraper. (Your own project already proves this: your CNN solves it at 98.7%.)

claims.claim: In the same USENIX study, a dedicated abandonment experiment measured a 30% task-abandonment rate among participants who encountered CAPTCHAs during account creation — and this was among paid participants. The authors call "the trend of average users' unwillingness to solve a CAPTCHA during account creation (even for monetary compensation) ... a relevant finding for websites that choose to protect account creation (and/or account access) using CAPTCHAs." An earlier study they cite (Bursztein et al.) found 18%–45% abandonment.
claims.source_name: Searles et al., USENIX Security 2023, §6 Measuring User Abandonment
claims.why_it_matters: Converts the CAPTCHA argument from 'annoying' to a quantified funnel loss. If ~30% of paid, motivated, literate MTurk workers abandon at a CAPTCHA, the drop-off for a semi-literate Gujarati farmer facing Latin-script distorted text is plausibly worse — and you can say that as an inference, clearly labelled.

claims.claim: Non-native English speakers are measurably penalised by Latin-script CAPTCHAs. In a 318,000-CAPTCHA study across the 21 most-used schemes, schemes using real or pseudo English words "are solved far faster (up to 30%) by native English speakers", and the authors conclude "captcha schemes that rely on extensive experience with a single language can be biased against users who are not native speakers of that language." For audio CAPTCHAs based on spelling English words, non-native solving time was 18.39 seconds — 7.4 seconds (57%) longer than native speakers.
claims.figure: up to 30% slower; audio 57% slower for non-native speakers
claims.source_name: Bursztein, Bethard, Fabry, Mitchell, Jurafsky — "How Good Are Humans at Solving CAPTCHAs? A Large Scale Evaluation", IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2010
claims.why_it_matters: This is the specific, citable evidence that a Latin-alphabet CAPTCHA is a language test for a Gujarati-first user. It is the strongest equity argument you have, and it is peer-reviewed and measured, not asserted.

claims.claim: Baseline human failure rates on CAPTCHAs are high even for motivated, educated users: three independent humans agreed on the same answer only 71% of the time for image CAPTCHAs and only 31.2% of the time for audio CAPTCHAs. Median image solve time 9.8 s; audio 28.4 s. Scheme-to-scheme variation is enormous (93% agreement on the best scheme, 35% on the worst).
claims.source_name: Bursztein et al., IEEE S&P 2010
claims.why_it_matters: The 31.2% audio number destroys the standard 'we provide an audio alternative' defence, which is exactly the mitigation WCAG 1.1.1 and GIGW 3.0 nominally require. The accessible fallback is itself measurably broken.

claims.claim: W3C's position paper is "Inaccessibility of CAPTCHA: Alternatives to Visual Turing Tests on the Web", W3C Group Draft Note, 16 December 2021 (editors Hollier, Sajka, White, Cooper). Current stable URL: w3.org/TR/turingtest/. It states that "the very nature of the interactive task inherently excludes many people with disabilities, resulting in a denial of service to these users", that "traditional CAPTCHAs have generally presumed that all web users can read and transcribe English-based words and characters, thus making the test inaccessible to a large number of non-English speaking web users worldwide", and that "a design pattern that expects multiple attempts from users as a matter of course is arguably inaccessible by design to persons living with an anxiety disorder as well as to many living with a range of other cognitive and learning disabilities."
claims.source_name: W3C Accessible Platform Architectures WG — Inaccessibility of CAPTCHA
claims.why_it_matters: This is the document you were asked to find, and the wording about non-English users maps directly onto your users. Note the status honestly: it is a Group Draft Note, not a W3C Recommendation — do not call it a standard. The 2005 version is the one most people cite; cite the 2021 one.

claims.claim: The often-quoted "32 seconds to complete a CAPTCHA" figure in the W3C note is sourced to a Cloudflare engineering blog post, not to a study, and the W3C note itself immediately concedes "reliable estimates are not readily available" for the time cost borne by disabled users.
claims.source_name: W3C, Inaccessibility of CAPTCHA (citing Cloudflare 'attestation' post)
claims.why_it_matters: You asked for numbers that do not hold up. Use the USENIX per-type timings (9–15 s, 15–26 s) instead of the round 32-second figure; the 32 s number is a vendor estimate travelling as a W3C fact.

claims.claim: The GOV.UK Design System says the select (dropdown) component "should only be used as a last resort in public-facing services because research shows that some users find selects very difficult to use." The documented failure modes from GDS user research are: users unable to close the select; users trying to type into it; users confusing focused items with selected items; users trying to pinch-zoom options on small devices; and users not understanding that they can scroll to see more items. Recommended replacement: "try asking users questions which will allow you to present them with fewer options" — or use radios.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK Design System — Select component
claims.why_it_matters: This is the design-system-level authority for deleting the five-level cascade. Note that four of the five documented failure modes are specifically small-screen/touch failures — i.e. exactly your device profile. One select is 'last resort'; five chained selects is five last resorts, each blocking the next.

claims.claim: The anti-dropdown position originates in GDS user research recorded on video, not in a published controlled experiment. Alice Bartlett's GDS talk "Burn your select tags" (EpicFEL 2014) is the origin artefact — "Native select boxes are rubbish and I have the user research videos to prove it" — and GDS's own Design System page links to a video of users struggling rather than to a study. Luke Wroblewski's "Dropdowns Should be the UI of Last Resort" is the other widely-cited source and is likewise practitioner analysis.
claims.source_name: Alice Bartlett, "Burn your select tags" (GDS), EpicFEL 2014; LukeW, "Dropdowns Should be the UI of Last Resort"
claims.why_it_matters: Honesty requirement. Say 'the strongest anti-dropdown evidence is government user research and design-system policy, not a randomised trial'. A judge who knows the literature will respect the caveat; overclaiming here is the easiest way to lose credibility.

claims.claim: GDS's own "one thing per page" guidance publishes NO quantitative evidence. The originating post (Tim Paul, 3 July 2015) gives three qualitative reasons — "low-confidence users find them easier to use", "they work well on mobile devices", "they're better at handling things like errors, branches, loops and saving progress" — and a commenter's request for A/B data is answered with the observation that this would require a high-volume service to build both versions. The Design System pattern page likewise says only "Asking just one question per page helps users understand what you're asking them to do" and "User research will tell you when you can group pages together."
claims.source_name: GDS Design Notes blog, "One thing per page"; GOV.UK Design System, Question pages pattern
claims.why_it_matters: You asked what GDS actually found and measured. The answer is: they researched it extensively in qualitative sessions and never published numbers. Frame one-thing-per-page as 'the standard the UK government holds itself to', not as 'proven to raise completion by X%'. There is a real accessibility rationale you CAN assert: with one question per page the label/legend becomes the page heading, so screen readers do not double-announce.

claims.claim: GDS's own lessons-learned review found the flagship Exemplar Programme only half-worked. Of 25 services picked in 2012 for end-to-end redesign, 15 were live by March 2015 and 5 more in trial; GDS identified positive net present value for only 12 of the 22 exemplars for which data existed (10 had costs exceeding benefits, 3 had no data at all); only 6 live exemplars and 2 trials had produced an integrated service; and "in nearly two-thirds of the exemplars, GDS found that improvements in online services did not result in existing systems being reconfigured or becoming more efficient."
claims.figure: 12 of 22 positive NPV; 6 of 25 truly integrated
claims.source_name: National Audit Office, "Digital transformation in government", HC 1059, Session 2016-17, paras 10–11 and 3.2–3.5
claims.why_it_matters: The most useful sober counterweight in the whole file. The named failure mode — a good new front-end bolted onto an unchanged back office — is precisely the accusation a judge will level at a hackathon land-records portal. Pre-empt it by name and show what you would change behind the form.

claims.claim: The NAO's 2023 verdict on a decade of UK digital transformation: "our work over the past decade has shown that, across government, attempts at digital transformation have had little lasting success", and "government's own analysis in 2022 found simple online citizen transactions have been prioritised for transformation and more complicated services have been left behind. In developing digital 'front-ends', changes to legacy systems and processes that could reduce costs are often overlooked." Eleven cross-government digital strategies were launched over 25 years, all seeking to address the same usability, efficiency and legacy problems.
claims.source_name: National Audit Office, "Digital transformation in government: addressing the barriers to efficiency", HC 1171, Session 2022-23, paras 6–7
claims.why_it_matters: Direct ammunition for criterion 5 (end-to-end) and criterion 6 (honesty). The most credible thing you can say is: 'the UK's national audit office says the standard failure of projects exactly like this one is a pretty front-end over an untouched legacy system; here is what our proposal does about the back end, and here is what it honestly does not.'

claims.claim: GOV.UK Verify, the UK's flagship shared-platform programme, failed every published target. Against a 2016 business case target of 25 million users by 2020 and 46 connected services by March 2018: 3.6 million users by February 2019 (trend projection 5.4 million by 2020) and 19 connected services, 11 of which also offered an alternative login. Verification success rate was 48% against a projected 90%. Cost was at least £154 million to September 2018 (an underestimate — it excludes departments' own reconfiguration costs). Forecast four-year benefits were cut from £873 million to £217 million, a 75% reduction, and the NAO wrote: "we have not been able to replicate or validate GDS's estimated benefits on the evidence made available to us."
claims.figure: 48% success rate vs 90% target; benefits cut 75%
claims.source_name: National Audit Office, "Investigation into Verify", HC 1926, Session 2017-19, Key findings 1–7 and paras 1.16–1.21
claims.why_it_matters: The 48% figure is the perfect analogy for a CAPTCHA or login wall on public data: a gate that turns away more than half the people who reach it is not a security feature, it is the service failing. Also note the NAO's second-order point — even the 48% metric flatters, because it excludes people who dropped out before starting and does not check whether verified users could actually reach the service they wanted.

claims.claim: The UK's headline savings numbers are self-reported and only partly assured. GDS reported £1.3 billion of savings from digital spending controls over five years to April 2016; the Government Internal Audit Agency gave only "moderate assurance" for 2015-16 "because claimed savings are based on business case projections and the actual cost reductions will not be realised and confirmed until each project is completed". The NAO's earlier assessment was that "less than half (41%) of spending control savings were likely to be sustainable over the longer term."
claims.source_name: National Audit Office, "Digital transformation in government", HC 1059, paras 4.4–4.5 and Figure 10 notes
claims.why_it_matters: If you cite GDS savings at all, cite them with this caveat attached. It is the difference between a claim a judge can attack and one they cannot.

claims.claim: The famous "£1.7–1.8 billion a year" UK digital savings figure is a 2012 ex-ante projection, not a measured outcome, and it is conditional on an 82% digital take-up assumption that was never met. The Digital Efficiency Report (6 November 2012) states the average digital transaction costs about 20× less than telephone, 30× less than post and 50× less than face-to-face (worked example from the Driving Standards Agency: digital £0.22, telephone £4.11, post £6.62), derived from two methods (bottom-up case studies of 17 services; top-down accounts analysis), excluding transitional and investment costs and services under 10,000 transactions/year.
claims.source_name: UK Cabinet Office / GDS, "Digital Efficiency Report"
claims.why_it_matters: The 50×-cheaper-than-a-counter-visit ratio is the best single argument for why a working online 7/12 matters economically — but present it as a 2012 UK modelling exercise with stated caveats, not as a law of nature, and never transplant the pound figures to India.

claims.claim: GOV.UK's own savings claim drifted downward as it was restated: at launch (17 October 2012) the Cabinet Office said GOV.UK "will also cost taxpayers up to £70 million less per year than the services it replaces"; one year on (18 October 2013) the figure quoted was £50 million annually from replacing Directgov and Business Link. Neither figure was independently verified by the NAO. The one-year-on release does report hard traffic numbers: 425 million visits and 1.2 billion page views in year one, ~9 million visits/week, ~6 million unique visitors/week, 20% from mobile, ~2,000 government websites consolidated to one domain, all 24 ministerial departments migrated, 1,500+ application changes in year one.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK press releases, Cabinet Office
claims.why_it_matters: A small, precise example of benefit inflation you can cite while promising not to do it yourself. The traffic and consolidation numbers, by contrast, are countable outputs and safe to quote.

claims.claim: IRS Direct File's pilot published unusually good, methodologically-disclosed satisfaction data: 15,082 survey responses (13% completion rate; 26% among Spanish speakers), 90% rated the experience Excellent or Above Average, Net Promoter Score +74, 86% said the experience increased their trust in the IRS, and 90% of those who used customer support rated it Excellent or Above Average. Funnel: 3,340,500 started the eligibility checker → 677,663 completed it → 423,450 signed into an IRS account → 395,483 started a return → 161,042 submitted → 140,803 accepted (goal was 100,000). Users reported filing in under an hour, often 30 minutes; Treasury estimated $5.6m saved in preparation fees; pilot cost $24.6m.
claims.source_name: IRS, "Direct File Pilot Program Filing Season 2024 After Action Report" (Publication 5969)
claims.why_it_matters: The best model in the file for how to report your own numbers. Crucially the IRS also states the limitation itself: "as a completion survey, administered after submitting or resubmitting a tax return, it does not capture the views of taxpayers who decided not to use Direct File." Copy that sentence pattern verbatim for your own demo metrics.

claims.claim: IRS Direct File was cancelled despite those results. The IRS told state revenue departments "IRS Direct File will not be available in Filing Season 2026. No launch date has been set for the future." Treasury cited "low participation and relatively high costs and burdens on the federal government", estimating $41 million to operate for tax year 2024, or at least $138 per return. Separately, FedScoop reported the IRS spent $16.2 million on the service in FY2025 against a $61.2 million projection, partly because development was halted in mid-March 2025.
claims.source_name: Federal News Network / Nextgov / Tax Notes reporting on IRS notification to states; Treasury statements
claims.why_it_matters: Directly bears on how you frame permanence. A service with 90% satisfaction and +74 NPS was killed on cost-per-transaction grounds. If you claim your portal is sustainable, you must show a per-transaction cost story, not just a satisfaction story.

claims.claim: 18F, the US federal digital services consultancy that co-created the U.S. Web Design System, was shut down on 28 February 2025 and all its employees terminated; GSA's Federal Acquisition Service commissioner said the administration determined 18F to be non-essential under the Workforce Optimization Initiative executive order. Around 80 former staff filed a class appeal with the Merit Systems Protection Board in May 2025 alleging the shutdown was retaliatory and did not follow reduction-in-force requirements.
claims.source_name: Federal News Network; Nextgov/FCW
claims.why_it_matters: Frame institutional claims carefully. Do not write 'like the USDS/18F model, this will endure'. The honest framing is: the artefacts persist (USWDS is still maintained by GSA TTS; the design principles outlived the org) while the institutions did not.

claims.claim: GSA's Inspector General found that GSA "misled customer agencies" about Login.gov's compliance with NIST SP 800-63-3, and that despite officials asserting IAL2 compliance, "Login.gov has never included a physical or biometric comparison for its customer agencies." GSA "knowingly billed IAL2 customer agencies over $10 million for services, including alleged IAL2 services that did not meet IAL2 standards", and did not notify customers until 3 February 2022 — after a Wired article — although officials should have done so from 2019.
claims.source_name: GSA Office of Inspector General, report JE23-003
claims.why_it_matters: The best available case study in what happens when a government digital team overstates a compliance claim. Use it to justify a hard rule in your submission: state the assurance level of every claim, and label mocked components explicitly rather than by omission.

claims.claim: Healthcare.gov's cost grew far beyond plan before its failed October 2013 launch: obligations for the Federally Facilitated Marketplace contract rose from $56 million (September 2011) to $209 million (February 2014), and the Federal Data Services Hub from $30 million to $85 million; a successor contract awarded at $91 million in January 2014 exceeded $175 million by June 2014. GAO attributed this to unclear and changing requirements, inadequate acquisition planning, and postponed readiness assessments, and noted the site launched "without verification of performance requirements".
claims.source_name: U.S. Government Accountability Office, GAO-14-694
claims.why_it_matters: The canonical government-IT failure that produced USDS. Use it as the 'why a small team shipping a working thing matters' story — but cite GAO, not the popular retellings.

claims.claim: Estonia's celebrated savings figures rest on an unvalidated rule of thumb, not a study. e-Estonia's own explainer states the calculation: roughly 1.3 billion X-Road queries in a year, of which citizens submit only about 3%, and "assuming that each of the human-based queries saves 15 minutes of someone's working time, those requests have saved more than 1100 working years last year alone." No researcher, institution or published study is named for the 15-minute assumption. The companion article concedes that the remaining ~1.28 billion machine-to-machine queries are "a more notorious task" to value. The commonly cited "820 years" figure appears in the same family of posts with no methodology or citation at all.
claims.source_name: e-Estonia (Estonian Information System Authority / e-Estonia Briefing Centre)
claims.why_it_matters: You explicitly asked for famous numbers that do not survive tracing. This is one. The figure also drifts (820 / 1,100 / 1,345 / 1,400) across official pages, which is itself the tell. Do not cite it; if you must mention Estonia's savings, cite the methodology and let the reader judge.

claims.claim: Estonia's "saves 2% of GDP a year" claim is a political statement repeated as data. It is attributed to Estonian officials (including the Prime Minister, speaking at the International Peace Institute in 2016 — "Estonia saves two percent of GDP by signing things digitally") and to secondary compilations such as the e-Estonia Guide and OECD material. I could not locate an originating study, dataset or audit that derives it.
claims.source_name: International Peace Institute event report quoting Estonia's Prime Minister; e-Estonia Guide
claims.why_it_matters: The second famous number that does not trace. Both Estonia claims are widely used in Indian govtech decks; leaving them out and saying why is a credibility asset in an honesty-scored hackathon.

claims.claim: Singapore publishes modest, dated, checkable figures rather than dramatic ones: "99% of all transactions between citizens and the government can be completed online" (2023) and "high citizen and business satisfaction with Government Digital Services at 83% in 2023". Context figures: 99% of resident households connected to the internet (2022); 95% of SMEs have adopted at least one digital technology.
claims.source_name: Smart Nation Singapore — Achievements
claims.why_it_matters: Note what Singapore's own top-line satisfaction number is: 83%, not 95%. It is a useful realism anchor for what a genuinely well-run digital government scores, and a warning against promising better.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed audit of 65 Indian central-ministry e-government websites against WCAG 2.1 found an accessibility error rate of 89.23% at Level A and 78.46% at Level AA (0.00% at AAA), with 655 errors in total (542 Level A, 113 Level AA; mean 8.34 Level A errors per site). The three most-violated checkpoints were 1.4.3 contrast (45 of 65 sites), F54 mouse-only event handlers (42), and F24 inconsistent colours (39). Notably, 31 of 65 sites had HTML form controls with no label (F68) and 24 had no lang attribute (3.1.1). Conclusion: "the majority of e-government websites do not meet Level A conformance with WCAG 2.1."
claims.figure: 89.23% Level A error rate across 65 sites
claims.source_name: Surjit Paul, "Accessibility analysis using WCAG 2.1: evidence from Indian e-government websites", Universal Access in the Information Society (2022)
claims.why_it_matters: The peer-reviewed baseline for 'the incumbent is broken' — and it is Indian, current and specific. F68 (unlabelled form controls) at 31/65 is the exact defect class an AnyRoR-style cascade exhibits. Caveat to state: this was automated-tool testing, which catches only machine-detectable failures, so it is a floor, not a ceiling.

claims.claim: India already has a binding standard that AnyRoR-style portals breach. GIGW 3.0 (Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps, NIC/MeitY) is built "in accordance with level AA of WCAG 2.1" and grounded in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 and the IT Act 2000. Three checkpoints bite directly: (a) the WCAG 1.1.1(e) CAPTCHA clause requires text alternatives AND "alternative forms of CAPTCHA using output modes for different types of sensory perception ... to accommodate different disabilities"; (b) checkpoint 5.4.9 requires "Documents are provided either in HTML or other accessible formats" and that "the accessible version of all scanned documents is made available"; (c) checkpoint 5.4.10 requires the site to be "bilingual with a prominent language selection link", using Unicode, with language choice offered "prior to entering the website". Compliance is certifiable through STQC's Certified Quality Website scheme.
claims.source_name: NIC / MeitY, Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps (GIGW) 3.0
claims.why_it_matters: This is your compliance argument in Indian law and Indian standards, not borrowed from the UK. A single-modality image CAPTCHA fails 1.1.1(e); a 7/12 delivered as an image of paper fails 5.4.9; an English-only cascade fails 5.4.10. Note honestly that GIGW is issued as guidelines to be 'followed and implemented on priority' rather than as a statute with penalties — the enforceable hook is the RPwD Act 2016.

claims.claim: Maharashtra already ships the exact two-tier pattern for the same document. The free Mahabhulekh 7/12 view carries the notice "सुचना : या संकेतस्थळावर दर्शविलेली माहिती ही कोणत्याही शासकीय अथवा कायदेशीर बाबींसाठी वापरता येणार नाही" ("Notice: the information displayed on this website cannot be used for any governmental or legal matters"), while the separate Digitally Signed 7/12 service states "Digitally signed 7/12, 8A and Property Card can be used for all official and legal purposes" / "डिजिटल स्वाक्षरीत ७/१२, ८अ आणि प्रॉपर्टी कार्ड सर्व शासकीय व कायदेशीर बाबींसाठी वापरता येईल", paid through a prepaid deposit via SBI ePay.
claims.figure: two tiers: informational vs digitally signed
claims.source_name: Mahabhulekh (bhulekh.mahabhumi.gov.in) and Digital Satbara (digitalsatbara.mahabhumi.gov.in), Government of Maharashtra
claims.why_it_matters: The single most directly transferable finding in this report. It solves your hardest product question — how to make a legal document readable without altering its legal meaning — with an existing Indian government precedent in a neighbouring state, and it gives you the exact disclaimer wording in an Indian language, so you are not inventing legal copy.

claims.claim: HM Land Registry's equivalent split is statutory: an "official copy" of the register is admissible in evidence to the same extent as the original, and is obtained through a specific application (forms OC1 for the register/plan, OC2 for documents), distinct from the free or unofficial views of title information offered through the property search service.
claims.source_name: HM Land Registry forms and guidance on GOV.UK (Official copies of register or plan (OC1); Official copies of documents (OC2); Search for land and property information)
claims.why_it_matters: Confirms the two-tier pattern is a registry norm across jurisdictions, not a Maharashtra quirk. I could not retrieve Practice Guide 11's exact wording (see gaps), so cite the Maharashtra example for verbatim language and this one only as corroboration.

claims.claim: DigiLocker reports 70+ crore (700+ million) registered users and 900+ crore (9+ billion) issued documents, with issuer counts published per state (Gujarat: 110+ issuers).
claims.source_name: DigiLocker (MeitY), homepage counters
claims.why_it_matters: Establishes that a national distribution and verification rail for a signed 7/12 already exists and already reaches Gujarat. Caveat honestly: 'registered users' includes accounts auto-created during bulk issuance (e.g. exam results), so it overstates active use; treat it as reach, not engagement.

claims.claim: Offline-first is a proven government pattern at national scale, not a hackathon flourish. The DHIS2 Android Capture app keeps a synchronised local database on the device, works fully offline and syncs automatically when connectivity returns, with configurable sync budgets (e.g. up to 500 active enrollments, 1,000 most recent events, 500 datasets) and offline search against the local database. DHIS2 is used by ministries of health in 80 low- and middle-income countries, in more than 100 countries including NGO programmes, covering countries where 3.2 billion people (40% of the world's population) live.
claims.source_name: DHIS2 (University of Oslo) — Android app and In Action pages
claims.why_it_matters: The precedent that lets you propose offline-first without hand-waving, and it supplies concrete sync-budget numbers you can imitate (cache a bounded, prioritised working set rather than 'everything'). Note the honest limit: DHIS2 Android is a field-worker data-capture app, not a mass citizen-facing portal, so the analogy is architectural rather than exact.

claims.claim: UK public sector accessibility is legally mandatory: under the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018, in force since 23 September 2018, public sector websites and apps must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and publish an accessibility statement; the Government Digital Service monitors compliance annually and the Equality and Human Rights Commission enforces, with non-compliance also breaching the Equality Act 2010.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK guidance, "Understanding accessibility requirements for public sector bodies"
claims.why_it_matters: Useful as the comparator that makes the Indian position look weak by contrast, and as the model for what you would ask Gujarat to adopt: a named standard, a published statement, an annual monitor and an enforcer.

claims.claim: Progressive disclosure has no published quantitative evidence base in its canonical source. Nielsen's article (3 December 2006) defines it as "initially, show users only a few of the most important options. Offer a larger set of specialized options upon request" and claims improvements in learnability, efficiency and error rate, but reports no error percentages, learning times or satisfaction scores.
claims.source_name: Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group, "Progressive Disclosure"
claims.why_it_matters: Second honesty flag on a pattern you will use anyway. Present progressive disclosure as an established convention with a stated design rationale, not as an evidence-backed intervention.

claims.claim: The GOV.UK replacement for long option lists is a lookup/search, not a better dropdown. The addresses pattern tells services to let users "enter their postcode and select their address from a list", and to accept messy input rather than reject it: "It's easier for users if you accept and ignore unwanted characters. This is better than rejecting the input and telling the user they have not provided a valid postcode." GDS also maintains a dedicated accessible-autocomplete component, built "after studying many existing solutions and prototyping patches to fix user experience or accessibility issues", following WAI-ARIA practices and tested with assistive technology.
claims.source_name: GOV.UK Design System — Addresses pattern; alphagov/accessible-autocomplete
claims.why_it_matters: This is the concrete answer to 'what replaces the five-level cascade': one forgiving text field that resolves an identifier, with an accessible autocomplete for disambiguation. The 'accept and ignore unwanted characters' rule is directly applicable to Gujarati survey numbers (spaces, slashes, hyphens, Gujarati letters).

claims.claim: Verify's take-up shortfall was visible years before it was admitted: the September 2015 business case predicted 4.4 million users by end of March 2017; the October 2016 business case cut that to 1.8 million; the actual figure in February 2017 was 1.1 million (including 185,000 unverified 'basic' accounts that could not access live services). In 2014 GDS expected over 100 departmental services on Verify by 2016; in February 2017 there were 12, nine of which also offered another route in.
claims.source_name: National Audit Office, "Digital transformation in government", HC 1059, paras 4.23–4.25 and Figure 13
claims.why_it_matters: Shows how projections were quietly rebased rather than abandoned. If your submission forecasts adoption, forecast it once, publish the assumption, and say what would falsify it.

claims.claim: The U.S. Web Design System is maintained by GSA's Technology Transformation Services after being created in 2015 by 18F and USDS, and reports supporting "dozens of agencies and nearly 200 sites". It publishes no measured outcome metrics on its about page; its statutory anchor is the 21st Century Integrated Digital Experience Act (referenced only via sample contract language on the site itself).
claims.source_name: U.S. Web Design System — About
claims.why_it_matters: Tempering fact: even the most-cited government design system publishes adoption counts, not impact measurements. Do not promise your design system will produce measured gains; promise consistency and say that is what design systems demonstrably deliver.

design_rules.rule: Delete the five-level cascade and replace it with a single forgiving search box that resolves a survey to a canonical place identity, with an accessible autocomplete for disambiguation. Accept messy input (spaces, slashes, hyphens, Gujarati and Latin digits, Gujarati letters in survey numbers) and normalise silently rather than rejecting it. Keep the cascade only as a secondary 'browse' path for users who do not know what to type.
design_rules.rationale: GOV.UK's Design System says select "should only be used as a last resort in public-facing services because research shows that some users find selects very difficult to use", and four of its five documented failure modes (can't close it, can't scroll it, can't pinch-zoom it, confuses focus with selection) are small-screen touch failures — your exact device profile. GOV.UK's own replacement is a lookup: postcode in, address list out, with the explicit rule to "accept and ignore unwanted characters" rather than reject input. Chaining five selects multiplies the failure: each one is a server round trip that must succeed before the next renders.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The near-universal Indian government portal convention of district → taluka → village → record type → survey, and the intuition that dropdowns 'prevent invalid input'. They do not prevent invalid input; they prevent input.

design_rules.rule: Remove the CAPTCHA entirely for read access to public land records, and replace it server-side with rate and connection limiting, honeypot fields, and transaction monitoring. Document this swap explicitly in the submission as a security decision with a named replacement, not as a deletion.
design_rules.rationale: The GOV.UK Service Manual states "You must not use them unless you both: limit their use to cases where you detect suspicious activity [and] have evidence to show that alternative solutions will not work", and names exactly those three replacements. AnyRoR's CAPTCHA is unconditional, not triggered by suspicious activity, so it fails the first test on its face. It also cannot pass the second: distorted-text CAPTCHAs are solved by bots in under 1 second at 99.8% accuracy versus humans at 9–15.3 seconds and 50–84% accuracy (USENIX Security 2023) — and your own project's CNN reproduces that result at 98.7% on this specific CAPTCHA.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The standard Indian government assumption that a CAPTCHA is a load-shedding and anti-scraping control. It is neither: it stops the citizen and not the scraper, and rate limiting does the load-shedding job better.

design_rules.rule: If any human challenge survives (e.g. on a write path or bulk export), it must never be a single-modality Latin-script image. GIGW 3.0 adopts WCAG 2.1 1.1.1(e), which requires text alternatives plus "alternative forms of CAPTCHA using output modes for different types of sensory perception". State in the submission that even a compliant audio alternative is measurably broken — three humans agree on an audio CAPTCHA only 31.2% of the time.
design_rules.rationale: GIGW 3.0 is India's own standard and is built to WCAG 2.1 Level AA; a single image challenge fails it. Bursztein et al. (IEEE S&P 2010) measured 31.2% three-way agreement on audio CAPTCHAs versus 71% on image, so the mandated fallback does not rescue the pattern.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The common mitigation of 'add an audio CAPTCHA button and call it accessible'.

design_rules.rule: Ship two clearly-labelled tiers of the same record: a free, fast, readable, screen-reader-friendly HTML view marked as informational only, and a paid or authenticated digitally-signed PDF marked as valid for official and legal purposes. Use Maharashtra's wording as the model, translated for Gujarat: the free view says the information "cannot be used for any governmental or legal matters"; the signed copy says it "can be used for all official and legal purposes". Put the disclaimer at the top of the readable view and inside the rendered document, not in a footer.
design_rules.rationale: This is the only pattern I found that solves 'make the legal document readable without altering its legal meaning' — and Maharashtra already runs it for the identical document (7/12 / Satbara) at bhulekh.mahabhumi.gov.in versus digitalsatbara.mahabhumi.gov.in. HM Land Registry runs the same split (official copies via OC1/OC2 versus the free property search view). It lets you restructure, translate and progressively disclose the readable tier as aggressively as you like, because the legal artefact is a separate, byte-identical signed object.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The instinct to make one artefact that is both beautiful and legally authoritative. Do not restructure the legally-operative document; restructure the view and keep the signed original untouched.

design_rules.rule: Distribute the signed copy through DigiLocker rather than inventing a delivery mechanism, and make the readable view work without any account at all. Reserve identity checks for the signed-copy path only.
design_rules.rationale: DigiLocker reports 70+ crore registered users, 900+ crore issued documents and 110+ issuers in Gujarat, so the rail already reaches your users. Verify's collapse is the counter-example: an identity gate in front of a service produced a 48% verification success rate against a 90% target, and the NAO noted the metric does not even count people who dropped out before starting or people who verified but still could not reach the service. Never put an identity wall in front of data that is legally public.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The 'login first, then browse' architecture of most Indian government portals.

design_rules.rule: Structure every input step as one question per page, with the question as the page heading (so the label/legend is the h1 and screen readers do not announce it twice), a visible back link, and state preserved on the server or in local storage so a dropped connection never costs progress. Present this as the standard the UK government holds itself to — not as a measured conversion improvement.
design_rules.rationale: GOV.UK's Question pages pattern says "Start by asking one question per page" and gives the screen-reader duplication rationale explicitly. But GDS has published no quantitative evidence for the pattern: the originating 2015 post offers only three qualitative reasons and a commenter's request for A/B data goes unanswered. Claiming a completion-rate uplift would be inventing a number.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The desire to quote a percentage improvement for one-thing-per-page. There isn't one in the public record.

design_rules.rule: Build offline-first with a bounded, prioritised cache rather than 'cache everything': cache the user's own surveys and their most recently viewed villages, cap the working set explicitly, sync automatically when connectivity returns, and make search fall back to the local store when offline. Publish the cache budget as a number.
design_rules.rationale: DHIS2's Android Capture app is the proven government-scale precedent — a local synchronised database, automatic sync on reconnect, offline search against the local store, with explicit sync budgets (up to 500 active enrollments, the 1,000 most recent events, 500 datasets). It is used by ministries of health in 80 low- and middle-income countries, covering countries where 3.2 billion people live.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Framing offline support as a nice-to-have PWA checkbox. The precedent shows it is an architecture decision about what you cache and how much, made up front.

design_rules.rule: Publish the record as structured HTML with real semantics — labelled form controls, a lang attribute on every page and on every Gujarati string, a real table with headers for the record body — and never as an image of paper. Provide a text/data representation of anything scanned.
design_rules.rationale: GIGW 3.0 checkpoint 5.4.9 requires that "documents are provided either in HTML or other accessible formats" and that "the accessible version of all scanned documents is made available". The measured baseline for Indian ministry sites is dire: 89.23% Level A error rate across 65 sites, with 31 of 65 having form controls with no label and 24 of 65 missing a lang attribute (Paul 2022). Fixing exactly these two defects moves you past most of the incumbent estate.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The prevailing 'output that amounts to a photo of paper' convention across state land-records portals.

design_rules.rule: Make the language setting govern app chrome only and never the land data, and offer language choice before the user reaches the form. Keep Gujarati numerals in the record with a Latin helper line.
design_rules.rationale: GIGW 3.0 checkpoint 5.4.10 requires the site to be "bilingual with a prominent language selection link", Unicode-based, with the language option offered "prior to entering the website", justified because "a large part [of the population] is more comfortable in regional languages versus English". Translating land data would alter the record; translating chrome does not. (This also matches the rule already in your project's CLAUDE.md.)

design_rules.rule: Use progressive disclosure for the record body — show ownership, area and current status first, put mutation history, crop entries and encumbrance detail behind expandable sections — but describe it in the write-up as an established convention, not an evidence-backed intervention.
design_rules.rationale: The canonical source (Nielsen, 2006) defines the pattern and claims learnability, efficiency and error-rate benefits but publishes no measured outcomes. The convention is sound; the evidence base is not quantified, and a judge checking will find that.

design_rules.rule: In the honesty section, state a per-transaction cost and an operating model, not just satisfaction. Name what happens to the service if nobody funds it.
design_rules.rationale: IRS Direct File scored 90% Excellent/Above Average and NPS +74 with 140,803 accepted returns, and was still cancelled for Filing Season 2026 on cost-per-transaction grounds (Treasury citing ~$138 per return). Satisfaction did not save it. 18F was deleted outright in February 2025. Institutional permanence is not implied by quality.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The hackathon habit of ending on adoption and delight metrics.

design_rules.rule: Report your own demo metrics the way the IRS reported Direct File's: give the full funnel, give the survey response rate, and state the survey's blind spot in one sentence — e.g. 'this is a completion survey and does not capture people who gave up before finishing'.
design_rules.rationale: The Direct File after-action report publishes the whole funnel (3,340,500 started the eligibility checker → 140,803 accepted returns), the response rate (13%, 15,082 responses) and then says plainly that "as a completion survey ... it does not capture the views of taxpayers who decided not to use Direct File". That single sentence is why the report reads as credible. Copy the move.

design_rules.rule: Label every mocked, stubbed or scraped component explicitly and in place — on the screen, not only in the README — and state the assurance level of every compliance claim you make.
design_rules.rationale: GSA's Inspector General found GSA "misled customer agencies" about Login.gov meeting NIST IAL2 and billed them over $10 million for services that did not meet the claimed standard, having known since 2019 and disclosed only after press coverage. Overstated compliance is the specific failure mode that destroys government digital teams' credibility.

design_rules.rule: Devote a section of the submission to the back end — what data source you read, how records are identified across scrapes, what would have to change in the registry's systems for this to be real — and explicitly concede what your prototype does not fix.
design_rules.rationale: The NAO's decade verdict is that "attempts at digital transformation have had little lasting success" because "simple online citizen transactions have been prioritised ... In developing digital 'front-ends', changes to legacy systems and processes that could reduce costs are often overlooked." GDS's own exemplar review found positive NPV for only 12 of 22 exemplars and true end-to-end integration in only 6 of 25. A front-end-only land-records redesign is the textbook version of this failure; naming it first is the only defence.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Presenting UI polish as transformation.

design_rules.rule: Do not cite Estonia's '2% of GDP' or '820 years of work saved', and do not cite '£1.7–1.8 billion a year' as a realised UK saving. If you want a channel-cost argument, cite the Digital Efficiency Report's ratio (digital ≈ 20× cheaper than phone, 50× cheaper than face-to-face) with its stated caveats: 2012 UK data, excludes transition and investment costs, assumes 82% digital take-up.
design_rules.rationale: The Estonia figures trace to an unattributed 15-minute-per-query assumption applied to 3% of X-Road traffic, and the number itself drifts across official pages (820 / 1,100 / 1,345 / 1,400 years). The 2% of GDP claim traces to political statements, not a study. The £1.7–1.8bn figure is an ex-ante projection conditional on a take-up rate that was never achieved, and GDS's separately claimed £1.3bn of controls savings carried only 'moderate assurance', with the NAO judging 41% likely to be sustainable.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Every govtech deck ever assembled.

design_rules.rule: Do not claim a completion-rate or task-time improvement over AnyRoR unless you measure it yourself with a small moderated test, and report n honestly (e.g. 'we tested with 6 people; this is directional, not statistical').
design_rules.rationale: There is no published baseline for AnyRoR task completion, and the anti-dropdown evidence base is design-system policy and GDS user-research video, not controlled trials. A measured n=6 stated as n=6 is worth more to an honesty-scored panel than a borrowed percentage.

gaps: No published usability or task-completion study of AnyRoR specifically, or of any Indian state land-records portal, exists that I could find. The closest peer-reviewed evidence is Paul (2022) on 65 central-ministry sites, which is automated accessibility testing, not task-based usability testing. Any before/after claim you make about AnyRoR must come from your own testing.

There is no published controlled experiment showing cascading dependent dropdowns cause measurable task failure. The evidence is (a) GOV.UK Design System policy, (b) GDS user-research video, (c) practitioner analysis (Wroblewski, Bartlett). My OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar searches for controlled dropdown-vs-search comparisons returned nothing usable. This is the weakest link in your strongest argument — state it.

GDS has never published quantitative evidence for one-thing-per-page. A commenter on the 2015 post explicitly asked for A/B data and the answer was that it would require a high-volume service to build both versions. Nobody appears to have done it.
Progressive disclosure has no quantified outcome data in Nielsen's canonical article or anything I could reach.

I could not retrieve HM Land Registry Practice Guide 11 (the exact statutory wording and marking rules for 'official copies'). The GOV.UK URLs 404 and the GOV.UK search API does not surface it. The Maharashtra Digital Satbara / Mahabhulekh pair is a better and more relevant source anyway, and I did get its wording verbatim in Marathi and English.

Singapore: I could not reach GovTech's annual reports or the underlying Digital Government Perception Survey, so the 83% satisfaction and 99% online-transaction figures come from the Smart Nation achievements page rather than the survey report. Singpass user counts and LifeSG adoption numbers are unverified.

India: UMANG publishes no server-rendered statistics (it is a JS app and returns 403 to fetchers), so I have no verified figure for its services, users or transactions. NPCI's UPI product-statistics page returns 403. IRCTC: I found no published redesign study or before/after metrics at all. The National Portal (india.gov.in) likewise has no published usability evaluation I could locate.

DigiLocker's legal-parity statement (commonly cited as Rule 9A of the Information Technology (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries Providing Digital Locker Facilities) Rules, 2016) could not be verified from a primary source — digilocker.gov.in/about and the MeitY rules PDF both 403/404'd. Verify this yourself before asserting the legal equivalence of a DigiLocker-issued 7/12.

Estonia: I could not locate the World Bank study that a secondary source claims underpins the X-Road savings estimate (the 'one in three queries replaces an in-person visit, each saving 15 minutes' assumption). The Estonian National Audit Office has audited X-Road reliability, not the savings claims. Treat all Estonian savings figures as unsourced until someone produces that study.

The '53% of mobile visits are abandoned if load takes over 3 seconds' figure (Google/DoubleClick 2016) could not be traced — the original Think with Google page now 301s to a generic landing page and web.archive.org is unfetchable from this environment. Do not cite it; if you need a performance argument, measure your own page weight and time-to-interactive on a throttled connection and report that.

Research method constraint worth knowing: Firecrawl was out of credits (HTTP 402) and the WebSearch budget was exhausted 200/200 partway through, so the later half of this research ran on direct primary-URL fetches, the GOV.UK public search API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar. Several avenues (general web search for failure case studies beyond those named, Indian state portal comparisons, PWA deployments other than DHIS2) are therefore under-explored rather than absent. Notably, DuckDuckGo served a CAPTCHA challenge that blocked automated research — while I was researching CAPTCHA inaccessibility.

Not investigated because they sit in another agent's lane but relevant to your framing: Indian land-litigation statistics (widely repeated and, in my experience, poorly sourced), the Bhoomi/Karnataka digitisation impact literature (PDFs for it were already present in the shared scratchpad), and Gujarat-specific legal status of the RoR as a public record.

topic: Commonwealth/Asian land registries and measured land-records reform outcomes — evidence base for a redesigned Gujarat 7/12 citizen portal

claims.claim: The World Bank's own Independent Evaluation Group found that its interventions in the 'Registering Property' area were, on average, 28 percentage points LESS likely to achieve their objectives than interventions in other Doing Business areas — statistically significant at the 1% level. Verbatim: 'The estimated average marginal effect for Registering Property is negative and statistically significant at the 1% level, which implies that, on average, interventions related to that DB area are likely to be less successful by 28 percentage points than interventions in other areas.'
claims.source_name: IEG, 'The Development Effectiveness of the Use of Doing Business Indicators, Fiscal Years 2010–20 — An Independent Evaluation', World Bank
claims.why_it_matters: This is the single most useful honesty claim available. Land-registry reform is the World Bank's WORST-performing reform area, by its own independent evaluator. Any hackathon pitch that says 'digitise the records and outcomes follow' is contradicted by the best available meta-evidence. Put this on a slide and it converts criterion 6 (honesty) from a liability into the strongest part of the submission.

claims.claim: The same IEG evaluation, a systematic literature review of at least 103 studies, found that 'Evidence gaps, where the reforms have little or no rigorous evidence, appear on the topics of registering property and getting electricity.' Rigorous outcome evidence is concentrated in starting a business, trading across borders, getting credit and protecting minority investors — not property registration.
claims.figure: 103 studies reviewed; registering property = evidence gap
claims.source_name: IEG, 'The Development Effectiveness of the Use of Doing Business Indicators, FY2010–20', Appendix F
claims.why_it_matters: Tells you not to promise economic outcomes (credit access, investment, GDP) from a portal. Promise the things you can actually measure: time-to-answer, cost, successful-retrieval rate, correction turnaround. Scope your claims to what the evidence supports.

claims.claim: An Independent Review of Cambodia's World Bank-financed Land Management and Administration Project (Feb 2006), quoted in the Inspection Panel's investigation report, found: 'at least a fifth of households (19.6%) in 13 of the adjudication areas visited are being adversely affected by the systematic land titling process, usually through the refusal to register land in household possession or use.'
claims.source_name: World Bank Inspection Panel, 'Cambodia — Land Management and Administration Project: Investigation Report' (Report No. 58016-KH)
claims.why_it_matters: The hardest number anywhere on 'digitisation dispossesses'. It is not an NGO assertion — it is a World Bank Inspection Panel finding. One in five households in surveyed titling areas were HARMED, mostly by the system refusing to record land they actually held. This is exactly the failure mode a Gujarat portal must design against: a record that says 'no entry' is read by everyone as 'no right'.

claims.claim: The Cambodia Inspection Panel found that the project's headline performance target of issuing one million titles drove systematic exclusion of contested parcels: 'The current interpretation, reinforced by the Project's performance target of issuing one million titles, is simply that the Project will not title lands in areas where disputes are likely… it was referred by some as "going for the low-hanging fruits". However, the Panel notes that there is no reference in any key project documents to principles for determining "areas where disputes are likely" or procedures for how to excise such areas.'
claims.source_name: World Bank Inspection Panel, Cambodia LMAP Investigation Report, paras 153–155
claims.why_it_matters: A coverage KPI ('X lakh records digitised') mechanically selects for the easy, uncontested parcels and skips exactly the ones that need adjudication. If the portal shows a coverage figure, it must also show the denominator and the skipped set, or it will lie the same way.

claims.claim: In the Boeung Kak Lake case, about 4,250 families lived in the declared adjudication area; the requesters estimated more than 1,500 families had already been evicted; and during the Panel process, Bank Management's own field review 'identified at least 2,600 more families who had been evicted or are at risk of eviction in Project areas'. The Panel concluded 'design flaws in the Project led to arbitrary exclusion of lands from the titling process and denied residents the opportunity to claim and formalize their pre-existing rights.'
claims.source_name: World Bank Inspection Panel, Cambodia LMAP Investigation Report
claims.why_it_matters: Concrete human scale for the dispossession risk. Also note the mechanism: land was re-classified as state public land, which removed it from adjudication, which removed the residents' claim. A portal that renders 'state land' or 'no record' as a flat fact, with no visible provenance or challenge route, participates in that mechanism.

claims.claim: The Cambodia Panel's own land expert (Geoffrey Payne) concluded that titling 'has proved effective in areas where competition for land is at a relatively low level and where disputes are therefore limited, but ineffective and, in some circumstances, counter-productive, in increasing tenure security in areas where the increase in land values is significant and where this may attract predatory interest.'
claims.source_name: World Bank Inspection Panel, Cambodia LMAP Investigation Report, para ~294
claims.why_it_matters: Formalisation helps least, and can hurt, exactly where land is becoming valuable — i.e. peri-urban Gujarat. Argues for building the portal around dispute visibility and correction, not around asserting clean title.

claims.claim: Rwanda's Land Tenure Regularisation pilot evaluation found a small but statistically significant REDUCTION of eight percentage points in the likelihood that legally unmarried women would become documented owners — because Rwandan law protects property rights only within registered marriages, so consensual unions, customary and religious marriages and polygamous unions were not recognised at registration.
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger & Goldstein, 'Environmental and Gender Impacts of Land Tenure Regularization in Africa: Pilot Evidence from Rwanda', World Bank Case Study (No. 73154)
claims.why_it_matters: The cleanest measured case of digitisation actively stripping rights. The registry only had a slot for legally recognised relationships, so everyone outside that slot lost standing. Directly transferable: any Gujarat schema decision about who can appear in an owner field (co-widows, unpartitioned heirs, oral tenants, sharecroppers) has a distributional consequence.

claims.claim: The Rwanda pilot's positive findings, same study: households in LTR areas were almost 10 percentage points more likely to make soil-conservation investments (about double the change in the control group); female-headed households showed a 19 percentage point increase; legally married women (76% of sampled couples) were 17 percentage points more likely to be regarded as joint owners; landholders were 9 pp more likely to know who would inherit the parcel and children 13 pp more likely to inherit (boys 10.2 pp, girls 9.6 pp). Design: geographic/spatial discontinuity across four pilot cell boundaries, 3,554 households and ~6,330 parcels, surveyed 2010, 2.5 years after LTR start.
claims.figure: +10pp investment; +19pp female-headed; +17pp joint ownership; n=3,554 households
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger & Goldstein, World Bank Case Study No. 73154 (journal version: Journal of Development Economics 110:262–275)
claims.why_it_matters: The best 'this actually works' numbers in the whole field, from a credible quasi-experiment. Use these as the upside case — but always paired with the -8pp finding, which is in the same paper.

claims.claim: The same Rwanda pilot found NO statistically significant effect on perceived expropriation risk: 'a negative relationship between LTR and the subjective expropriation risk (for the purpose of public interest) was observed even if it was not statistically significant.'
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger & Goldstein, World Bank Case Study No. 73154
claims.why_it_matters: Registration reduced fear of your neighbour, not fear of the state. A portal cannot promise protection from acquisition; it can only promise you can see and prove what is recorded.

claims.claim: Rwanda's LTR reduced land-market activity, and the paper attributes this partly to a fee-structure change: the transfer fee moved 'from a rate of six percent of the property value to a flat fee of RwF 20,000 during the pilot', which 'could easily exceed 25 percent of the land value of small plots'. It also notes 'most parcels in the sample fell below the legally prescribed minimum size of one hectare for land transactions'.
claims.figure: Flat RwF 20,000 fee = >25% of value of small plots; 1 ha legal minimum for transfer
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger & Goldstein, World Bank Case Study No. 73154
claims.why_it_matters: Two lessons a portal designer will otherwise get wrong. (1) A FLAT fee is steeply regressive on small parcels — a flat ₹ charge per 7/12 extract hits a 20-guntha holder far harder than a 20-acre holder. (2) Formalisation can make the ordinary transaction of the poor technically illegal, so they route around the system entirely.

claims.claim: Rwanda's national roll-out was evaluated with a randomised design — 100 sectors randomly selected, half assigned 'early' and half 'late', 3,600 households from 300 villages. It REVERSED the pilot's negative gender finding: 'women without legal marriage certificates also significantly benefit from the LTR program (albeit to a lesser extent than those with civil marriage certificates)', which the authors attribute to Government action taken in response to the pilot evidence (intense sensitisation campaigns on female rights). Perceived right of married women to be registered as a claimant rose from 33% at baseline to about 94% in early-programme areas. Effect on being registered as owner alone or jointly: 19 to 34 percentage points.
claims.figure: 33% → 94%; +19 to +34 pp; RCT n=3,600 households / 100 sectors
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger, Goldstein & La Ferrara, 'Empowering Women through Land Tenure Regularization: Evidence from the Impact Evaluation of the National Program in Rwanda', World Bank (No. 97833)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the best story in the whole assignment for product thinking: they measured a harm at pilot, published it, changed the programme, and measured the fix. It is the model for how a hackathon submission should frame its own limitations — as instrumented and correctable, not hidden.

claims.claim: Rwanda's national LTR registered more than 10.7 million parcels (of an estimated 11.5 million in the country) and delivered about 6.7 million titles in under three years, at a cost of about USD 5 per parcel, using aerial photography and satellite imagery with locally recruited para-surveyors demarcating GENERAL boundaries rather than GPS-measured ones.
claims.figure: 10.7m parcels / 11.5m estimated; 6.7m titles; <3 years; USD 5 per parcel
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger, Goldstein & La Ferrara, World Bank No. 97833, citing Republic of Rwanda (2014)
claims.why_it_matters: The 'general boundaries' choice is the key engineering decision — they deliberately accepted imprecise geometry to get national coverage cheaply and fast. Gujarat's village maps are rasterised with no parcel geometry; Rwanda is the precedent for saying 'approximate, adjudicated, and complete beats precise and partial'.

claims.claim: Rwanda LTR field-process weaknesses, from the national evaluation: physical presence of the landowner's household at demarcation occurred in only 80% of cases (72% for female-headed households); only 71% received a claims receipt; only 38% of landowners had paid the nominal RwF 1,000 (~USD 1.7) fee, and the Government later lifted that fee for poorer rural households; attendance at sensitisation meetings was 86% for female-headed households vs 93% for male-headed, and only 68% of women in male-headed households attended.
claims.figure: 80% present at demarcation; 71% got a receipt; 38% paid the fee
claims.source_name: Ali, Deininger, Goldstein & La Ferrara, World Bank No. 97833, Tables 1–2
claims.why_it_matters: Even the world's most-praised programme left a fifth of owners absent from their own demarcation and a third without a receipt. A receipt/acknowledgement is a cheap, high-value feature: it is the citizen's only proof that they engaged with the system at all.

claims.claim: Georgia's registry reform produced these measured before/after figures: registering property took 39 days in 2005 and 2 days by 2011–12; cost fell from 2.5% of property value to 0.1%; procedures fell from 8 to 1; documents required fell from six to two and later one (the sale-and-purchase agreement). NAPR's budget rose from about $300,000 in 2004 to $7 million in 2006 to about $25 million in 2011, on a self-financing model.
claims.source_name: World Bank, 'Fighting Corruption in Public Services: Chronicling Georgia's Reforms', Ch. 7 'Making Public and Civil Registries Work'
claims.why_it_matters: The headline Georgia numbers, from the primary World Bank publication rather than a blog. Note the source is the Bank chronicling a government it was praising — treat as well-documented but not independently audited.

claims.claim: Georgia's registry reform was primarily an INSTITUTIONAL purge, not a technology project. At the end of 2004 all 2,200 public registry employees were fired in a single day; a few thousand candidates competed for 630 positions and about 400 of the old staff were rehired. Salaries rose almost twentyfold, from about $20/month in 2003 to about $400/month in 2005. Nine regional coordinating offices were eliminated ('When we analyzed their function, we saw that most of their activity was about coordinating corruption'). The Bureaus of Technical Inventory (survey and cadastre) were disbanded and replaced by ~25 competing private survey firms. Fees are collected by commercial banks, not by registry staff.
claims.source_name: World Bank, 'Fighting Corruption in Public Services: Chronicling Georgia's Reforms', Ch. 7
claims.why_it_matters: The most important corrective in this whole research pack. The famous 39-days-to-2-days number was bought with mass dismissal, a 20× pay rise, abolishing offices, privatising survey, and taking cash out of officials' hands. A UI redesign cannot buy any of that. Be explicit in the submission that the portal addresses the access layer and NOT the adjudication layer, and say which Georgia levers are out of scope.

claims.claim: The often-quoted Georgian trust reversal — '97 percent of Georgians believed the civil registry was one of the most corrupt agencies' in a 2004 poll, and '97 percent of respondents believed that there was no corruption in the agency' in a similar survey at end-2006 — is reported in the World Bank volume WITHOUT naming the polling organisation, sample, or question wording for either survey. The independently sourced figure in the same passage is the EBRD/World Bank Life in Transition Survey 2010, in which only 1% of Georgian respondents felt unofficial payments were needed to obtain official documents.
claims.source_name: World Bank, 'Fighting Corruption in Public Services: Chronicling Georgia's Reforms', Ch. 7, 'Greater Trust in Registries'
claims.why_it_matters: A famous number that does not survive scrutiny. A 97%-to-97% mirror-image reversal across two unnamed surveys is a rhetorical artefact. Cite the Life in Transition 1% figure instead — it is a real, repeatable, cross-country instrument.

claims.claim: Georgia's much-cited 'blockchain land registry' is a notarisation layer added in 2016, more than a decade AFTER the measured gains (39→2 days, 2.5%→0.1%) were achieved between 2004 and 2011. The most-cited account of it is a conference paper authored by Georgian government officials (Data Exchange Agency / e-Governance), i.e. a self-report, not an independent evaluation, and it presents no before/after measurement of the blockchain layer itself.
claims.source_name: Goderdzishvili, Gordadze & Gagnidze, 'Georgia's Blockchain-powered Property Registration', ICEGOV 2018
claims.why_it_matters: Judges may ask 'why not blockchain?'. The correct, evidence-based answer: the country everyone cites as the blockchain success story got 100% of its measured improvement before blockchain existed there, from institutional and process reform. Blockchain is not the lever.

claims.claim: Doing Business 2020 'Registering Property' comparator data (data current to 1 May 2019; standardised case = transfer of a warehouse already registered and free of title dispute, between two domestic limited liability companies, in the largest business city): New Zealand rank 2, score 94.6, 2 procedures, 3.5 days, 0.1% of property value, quality of land administration 26.5/30. Rwanda rank 3, score 93.7, 3 procedures, 7 days, 0.1%, quality 28.5/30. Georgia rank 5, score 92.9, 1 procedure, 1 day, 0.0% cost, quality 21.5/30. Singapore rank 21, score 83.1, 6 procedures, 4.5 days, 2.9%, quality 28.5/30. India rank 154, score 47.6 — Mumbai: 9 procedures, 68 days, 7.4% of property value, quality 14.0/30; Delhi: 9 procedures, 49 days, 8.1%, quality 8.0/30.
claims.figure: India rank 154/190; NZ 2, Rwanda 3, Georgia 5, Singapore 21
claims.source_name: World Bank, Doing Business 2020 economy profiles (archived)
claims.why_it_matters: The comparator table for the pitch. Rwanda outranking Singapore, and Georgia scoring LOWER on quality (21.5) than Rwanda (28.5) despite 1-day transactions, is the interesting story: speed and quality are different axes. Caveat every use: this measures a company buying a warehouse in Mumbai, not a farmer in Kheda pulling a 7/12.

claims.claim: Doing Business 2020's detailed India assessment records structural facts that explain the incumbent system: India runs a Deed Registration System (not title registration); registry and cadastral data are held in SEPARATE databases (score 0.0); the Geographic Coverage index is 0.0 out of 8 — not all privately held plots in the largest business city, nor in the economy, are formally registered OR mapped; maps of land plots are consultable by 'only intermediaries and interested parties' (0.0), not the public; there is NO specific and independent mechanism for filing complaints about the property registration agency (0.0); the registration system carries NO state or private guarantee (0.0); there is NO out-of-court compensation mechanism for losses caused by erroneous registry information (0.0); and a first-instance land dispute takes 'more than 3 years' (0.0).
claims.figure: Geographic coverage 0/8; no guarantee; no compensation; >3 years to first-instance judgment
claims.source_name: World Bank, Doing Business 2020 — India economy profile, 'Details – Registering Property in Mumbai – Measure of Quality'
claims.why_it_matters: This is the whole product brief in one table. The 7/12 is presumptive, unguaranteed, uncompensated, unmapped and unlinked to registration. The portal must therefore NEVER present a record as proof of title; it must present it as 'what the revenue record currently says', with provenance, date, and a route to challenge. That framing alone differentiates the submission.

claims.claim: Doing Business 2020 recorded that India has NO publicly available statistics on the number of land disputes at economy level in the first-instance court (score 0.0, 'Number of land disputes in the economy in 2018:' left blank). Georgia, by contrast, does publish them (score 0.5).
claims.source_name: World Bank, Doing Business 2020 — India and Georgia economy profiles
claims.why_it_matters: This is the evidentiary kill-shot on the folklore. The famous 'two-thirds / 66% / 70% of civil cases in India are land disputes' claim cannot be derived from published court statistics, because the World Bank's own data collectors recorded that India publishes no such statistics. Say so, and cite this.

claims.claim: The claim 'more than 70 percent [of] disputes in courts are land based' appears in the World Bank's own flagship Bhoomi case study WITH NO CITATION OF ANY KIND — no study, no court statistics, no footnote. It sits in the same document as a footnoted claim, so the omission is not a formatting artefact.
claims.source_name: Chawla & Bhatnagar, 'Online Delivery of Land Titles to Rural Farmers in Karnataka, India', World Bank Scaling Up Poverty Reduction case study (Shanghai, May 2004), p.10
claims.why_it_matters: You can now show the exact document where a World Bank publication launders an uncited assertion into the global literature. This is a far better slide than repeating the number. Frame: 'the most-quoted statistic about Indian land litigation has no traceable origin, and we refuse to use it.'

claims.claim: The famous 'India loses 1.3% because of bad land records' claim is attributed in the same World Bank Bhoomi paper to 'Mckenzie Report, India the growth Imperative' (i.e. McKinsey Global Institute, 'India: The Growth Imperative', 2001) — but the SAME nine-page document states it two different ways: on p.2, 'India loses 1.3 percent of its potential GROWTH because of badly maintained land records'; on p.10, 'India looses 1.3 percent of potential INVESTMENTS because of its poor land record system'.
