Growth and investment are not the same quantity. The drift is visible within a single primary document.
claims.figure: 1.3% (of growth? of investment? — stated both ways)
claims.source_name: Chawla & Bhatnagar, World Bank Bhoomi case study, pp. 2 and 10 and footnote 6
claims.why_it_matters: Demonstrable citation drift caught in the act. I could not obtain the 2001 McKinsey report itself to verify what it actually said, so the underlying figure remains unverified — mark it unverified, and note that the version repeated everywhere ('1.3% of GDP') matches NEITHER of the two phrasings in the citing document.

claims.claim: The most-repeated Bhoomi impact figure — 66% of manual-system users paid bribes vs only 3% of Bhoomi users — comes from a report-card survey by the Public Affairs Centre, Bangalore (field work by AC Nielsen–ORG–MARG, July/November 2002) with a total sample of 198 Bhoomi users across six districts and a control sample of just 59 users of non-computerised facilities.
claims.source_name: Chawla & Bhatnagar, World Bank Bhoomi case study, pp.12–13 and footnote 8, reporting Lobo & Balakrishnan, Public Affairs Centre
claims.why_it_matters: The number is real and sourced, but the control group is 59 people. It is not an impact evaluation. Quote it with the sample size attached — doing so is itself a credibility signal to judges.

claims.claim: In the same Public Affairs Centre survey, 66% of Bhoomi users reported that they did NOT get a receipt for the Rs 15 fee they paid, and 18% reported their document was not signed by the appointed Village Accountant operating the kiosk.
claims.source_name: Chawla & Bhatnagar, World Bank Bhoomi case study, pp.12–13
claims.why_it_matters: The celebrated anti-corruption system had an off-books cash leak in two thirds of transactions. Receipts and signed provenance are not bureaucratic decoration — they are the anti-corruption mechanism. Any fee or request in the new portal must emit an immutable, retrievable acknowledgement.

claims.claim: Independent fieldwork on Bhoomi (six of eight taluks in Bangalore Rural district, intensive interviews in seven villages) reported the opposite of the official narrative: after Bhoomi, all categories of landowners felt a mutation took 3–4 months; correcting a misspelt name or wrong survey number required a khata-change-like process with multiple taluk visits and 'extra bribes'; bribes were re-centralised at the back office where agents dealt directly with the caseworker; and 'most respondents, especially small and medium farmers, mentioned that bribes had increased substantially after the launch of Bhoomi'.
claims.source_name: Benjamin, Bhuvaneswari, Rajan & Manjunatha, 'Bhoomi: E-Governance, Or, An Anti-Politics Machine Necessary to Globalize Bangalore?', CASUM-m Working Paper
claims.why_it_matters: Qualitative and openly polemical, so weight accordingly — but it names the exact failure the incumbent Gujarat system also has: reading a record is easy, CORRECTING one is not. If the portal only optimises retrieval, it optimises the half that was already working.

claims.claim: The same fieldwork identifies a specific harm from open searchability: because Bhoomi could be queried by survey number, and 'most large farmers and other elites have easy access' to survey numbers, records could be used to locate small farmers in order to 'poach on entitlements meant for small farmers, and more important, on their land'. Small farmers reported their survey numbers being used by larger farmers to claim small-farmer subsidies, seeds and fertiliser.
claims.source_name: Benjamin et al., CASUM-m Working Paper, Table 1 discussion
claims.why_it_matters: The sharpest design tension in the brief. The same openness that stops a corrupt Village Accountant hides a targeting capability for land scouts. This is the ONLY serious argument for the AnyRoR CAPTCHA — and the CAPTCHA does not actually implement it, because it blocks the farmer and not the scraper. The right answer is asymmetric access design, not a CAPTCHA.

claims.claim: Bhoomi's own reported operational figures: 20 million land ownership records covering 6.7 million farmers, 177 taluk kiosks, RTC delivered in 5–30 minutes for a Rs 15 fee; mutations rose 85% after computerisation (about 1 million in one year versus a manual-system average of 0.55 million per year); user-fee revenue reached Rs 270 million by end-April 2004, stabilising at about Rs 8 million per month. Under the manual system a typical bribe for a certificate ranged from Rs 100 to Rs 2,000, and up to Rs 10,000 to have details written ambiguously.
claims.source_name: Chawla & Bhatnagar, World Bank Bhoomi case study
claims.why_it_matters: The mutation-volume jump is the most interesting metric: when updating became cheap, people updated. It is a usable success metric for the Gujarat portal that is not vanity — 'did the rate of recorded changes rise?' means the record is tracking reality better.

claims.claim: New Zealand's Landonline rebuild (STEP programme) was NOT delivered against its original budget. Primary LINZ reporting to Ministers shows: original Programme Business Case approved funding (QRA 85) of NZ$128.2m capital plus NZ$51.7m operating over 12 years; an approved programme re-forecast of NZ$175.7m capital plus NZ$76.1m operating, agreed in August 2022; actual spend of NZ$104.1m capital (59%) and NZ$50.1m operating to 31 March 2024. The widely reported 'on budget' completion is against the 2022 re-forecast — a 37% increase on the original capital budget.
claims.source_name: LINZ, 'Modernising Landonline – Survey and Title Enhancement: STEP update to joint Ministers, Programme Increment 21'
claims.why_it_matters: Rebuilding a national land registry from a working legacy system cost NZ$176m and took from November 2018 to 2025–26 for 2.4m titles. Cite this whenever the submission is asked 'why is your version mocked?' — because honest scoping is the correct answer, and here is what the unmocked version costs.

claims.claim: LINZ's reported benefits from the Landonline rebuild: financial benefits of NZ$124.7m enabled over the programme's 12-year life to 2030; 45% of surveyed titles and web-search customers and 42% of surveyed survey customers reported over 20% productivity improvement; 94% of all respondents reported equal or improved productivity; 100% uptake of new digital services. Titles customers migrated March 2025; legacy access switched off for external customers in 2025; remaining internal functions and database migration due December 2026.
claims.source_name: LINZ 'Modernising Landonline' project page and Reseller News reporting of LINZ figures
claims.why_it_matters: Note what is measured: PROFESSIONAL productivity (surveyors, conveyancers). Almost no public-facing citizen metric is reported. Even the best-run rebuild in the Commonwealth measured the intermediaries, not the landowners. A Gujarat portal that publishes citizen-side metrics would be doing something LINZ does not.

claims.claim: LINZ operating scale and pricing: 2.4 million property titles, ~2.9 million property searches per year, ~500,000 property transactions per year, ~15,000 registered users and ~5,000 daily users (2022/23). From 3 February 2025, title and survey plan searches cost NZ$8 each (up from NZ$6), the most common titles transaction NZ$122 (up from NZ$90), and the most common survey transaction NZ$1,130 (up from NZ$850), all GST inclusive.
claims.source_name: LINZ 'Modernising Landonline' and 'Changes to survey and title fees 2025'
claims.why_it_matters: Even the world's #2 registry charges per search — free-at-point-of-use is not the differentiator. What NZ sells is a single authoritative record retrievable in seconds with no session, no CAPTCHA and no cascade. That is the thing to copy.

claims.claim: Australia solved the multi-jurisdiction fragmentation problem with a model-law federation rather than a single national system. ARNECC (Australian Registrars' National Electronic Conveyancing Council) was formed in 2011 under an Intergovernmental Agreement; the Electronic Conveyancing National Law (ECNL) is enacted separately in each State and Territory; ARNECC maintains one national set each of Model Operating Requirements (for Electronic Lodgment Network Operators) and Model Participation Rules (for Subscribers), which each Registrar then determines locally and must publish at least 20 business days before they take effect. Waivers and current interoperability reforms are also published centrally. All eight states/territories participate.
claims.source_name: ARNECC, 'Regulation' and 'Key objectives'
claims.why_it_matters: The single most transferable governance idea for India, where land is a State subject. You do not need one national land portal; you need a national model spec (record schema, API contract, service standards, publication rules) that each State enacts. Frame the Gujarat portal as a reference implementation of a model spec, not a one-off.

claims.claim: NSW Land Registry Services' prices are set by an independent economic regulator, the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART), following the 2017 concession of the NSW land titles registry to a private operator. ARNECC's own homepage carries IPART notices, confirming the regulator sits inside the e-conveyancing governance stack.
claims.source_name: ARNECC homepage news; IPART land registry services industry pages
claims.why_it_matters: If registry services are outsourced or monetised, a price regulator is a required part of the architecture, not an afterthought. Relevant if the Gujarat design proposes any paid API tier. NOTE: I could not load IPART's own pages (site blocked automated fetch), so the concession terms and regulated price levels are UNVERIFIED here.

claims.claim: Ontario's registry runs as a long-term public-private concession: Teranet launched Teraview in 1995, completed Ontario title automation and legal conversion by 2011, and reports securely handling 'over 10 million remote land related transactions each year' with search and registration access to 'almost 7 million property titles in Ontario'. The Province divested its ownership stake in 2004, an IPO followed in 2006, OMERS Infrastructure acquired Teranet in 2008, and a 50-year extension to the agreements with the Province was granted in 2010.
claims.source_name: Teranet, 'About Us'
claims.why_it_matters: Ontario shows a registry can be run at scale by a private concessionaire — and also shows the risk: a 50-year exclusive licence over the public record of who owns what. Use as the cautionary counterweight to any 'monetise the API' proposal. Company self-reported figures; treat the volumes as marketing-grade.

claims.claim: Singapore separates the geospatial layer from the legal layer and makes only the former free. The Singapore Land Authority's e-services split into Properties, Geospatial (OneMap — 'browse detailed and current geospatial information such as land ownership, the nearest schools and demographic data'; GNSS reference network; cadastral survey submission) and Regulatory ('Find property or land info' = INLIS, for property ownership information and survey plans; 'Lodge your property title'). Singapore's Doing Business 2020 quality of land administration score was 28.5/30 — tied highest among the comparators — while its rank was only 21 because of 6 procedures and 2.9% cost.
claims.source_name: Singapore Land Authority, 'E-services'; World Bank Doing Business 2020 Singapore profile
claims.why_it_matters: The right split for a Gujarat portal: a free, open, API-first map/geospatial layer that anyone can build on (OneMap), and a separate, identity-gated, fee-bearing legal-instrument layer (INLIS). Gujarat currently has neither — it has one CAPTCHA-gated blob. NOTE: I could not extract INLIS fee schedules or confirm Singpass gating; both services are JavaScript SPAs that returned no content.

claims.claim: The World Bank discontinued Doing Business on 16 September 2021 after an external investigation by WilmerHale into data irregularities in Doing Business 2018 and 2020. The investigation collected roughly five million documents, reviewed 80,000, and interviewed more than [dozens of] current and former staff. The improper changes concerned China (DB2018) and Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan (DB2020). Critically for land work: the China changes 'affected the Starting a Business, Legal Rights – Getting Credit, and Paying Taxes indicators', boosting China's score by nearly a point and moving it seven places to rank 78. REGISTERING PROPERTY WAS NOT AMONG THE MANIPULATED INDICATORS.
claims.figure: 5m documents collected, 80,000 reviewed; China moved 7 places to 78
claims.source_name: Machen, Jones, Varghese & Stark (WilmerHale), 'Investigation of Data Irregularities in Doing Business 2018 and Doing Business 2020: Investigation Findings and Report to the Board of Executive Directors'
claims.why_it_matters: Settles whether the historical Registering Property data is citable. YES, with disclosure: the documented manipulation touched Starting a Business, Getting Credit and Paying Taxes for four countries, not the property indicator. Cite the indicator, disclose the scandal, name the indicators actually affected. That is a defensible, checkable position — and it demonstrates exactly the rigour criterion 6 rewards.

claims.claim: The successor product, Business Ready (B-READY), covers ten topics — Business Entry, Business Location, Utility Services, Labor, Financial Services, International Trade, Taxation, Dispute Resolution, Market Competition, Business Insolvency — and does NOT include a 'Registering Property' topic. Property/land issues are folded into 'Business Location'. The first three editions of the pilot report will gradually cover about 170 economies.
claims.source_name: World Bank, Business Ready (B-READY)
claims.why_it_matters: There is no continuing internationally comparable Registering Property series. The DB2020 numbers are the LAST comparable global snapshot, frozen at 1 May 2019. Say the vintage every time you cite them; the honest framing is 'the last comparable global measurement, now six years stale'.

claims.claim: The World Bank's Land Governance Assessment Framework (LGAF), developed by Klaus Deininger, Harris Selod and Tony Burns (book published November 2011, revised 2013), scores land governance on 116 dimensions (originally 80) across nine technical panels covering tenure recognition, forest rights, urban planning, public land management, land information systems, valuation, taxation and dispute resolution. It has been applied in over 40 countries.
claims.source_name: World Bank, Land Governance Assessment Framework programme page
claims.why_it_matters: LGAF is the right diagnostic frame to cite instead of Doing Business, because it scores things Doing Business ignored — completeness of the record, recognition of customary/informal rights, dispute resolution, and public accessibility of land information. If the submission needs an evaluation rubric for its own design, use LGAF's land-information-systems panel.

claims.claim: Doing Business 2020 recorded 2,249,874 property transfers in Mumbai in 2018 — India's largest business city publishes transaction counts even though it publishes no land-dispute counts.
claims.source_name: World Bank, Doing Business 2020 — India economy profile, Transparency of information index
claims.why_it_matters: Proof that Indian land agencies can and do publish operational statistics when asked. A 'system status / volumes served' page on the Gujarat portal is therefore not a novel demand, it is an existing practice being extended.

design_rules.rule: Never present a 7/12 extract as proof of ownership. Label every record with a persistent, unmissable status line: what it is (a revenue record), who maintains it, the date it was last updated, and the fact that Indian land records are presumptive, carry no state guarantee, and no compensation exists for errors. Put this on the record itself, not in a footer or a terms page.
design_rules.rationale: Doing Business 2020 scored India 0.0 on 'is the system of immovable property registration subject to a state or private guarantee' and 0.0 on 'is there a specific, out-of-court compensation mechanism to cover for losses incurred by parties who engaged in good faith… based on erroneous information certified by the registry'. India runs a Deed Registration System. A UI that renders the record as authoritative is making a legal claim the state itself does not make.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Every existing land-record portal, which presents the extract as a clean authoritative document with no epistemic status at all — and the instinct to make the redesigned output look MORE official and certificate-like.

design_rules.rule: Design the record view around three states, not one: HELD (there is a record and here it is), DISPUTED/PENDING (there is a live entry, mutation or objection — show it prominently, with its date and stage), and ABSENT (no record found for this parcel — with an explicit 'this does not mean no one owns it' and a route to raise a claim). Never let ABSENT render as a blank, a zero, or a 404.
design_rules.rationale: The Cambodia Inspection Panel found 19.6% of households in 13 surveyed adjudication areas were adversely affected by systematic titling, 'usually through the refusal to register land in household possession or use'. A silent absence in a digital register is read by banks, buyers and officials as an absence of right. The Rwanda pilot's -8pp finding for unmarried women is the same mechanism at record-field granularity.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Standard web practice of showing an empty-state or error for 'no results', and the incumbent AnyRoR behaviour of returning nothing distinguishable from a session failure.

design_rules.rule: Make CORRECTION a first-class journey with equal prominence to SEARCH, with a tracked case number, a visible SLA, a stage-by-stage status, and a downloadable acknowledgement issued at submission. Measure and publish median correction turnaround as a headline metric.
design_rules.rationale: Independent Bhoomi fieldwork found that after computerisation, correcting a misspelt name or wrong survey number required a khata-change-like process with multiple taluk visits and extra bribes, and that mutations took 3–4 months — i.e. reading got faster while fixing got harder, which re-concentrated rents at the back office. Separately, 66% of Bhoomi users reported getting no receipt for the fee they paid.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The near-universal e-governance pattern of shipping read-only access first and treating write/correction paths as phase two — which is precisely the pattern that produced Bhoomi's measured backsliding.

design_rules.rule: Issue a signed, retrievable, verifiable acknowledgement for EVERY citizen interaction that costs money or asks for a change — with a QR/short code that any third party can verify against the portal without logging in. Treat the receipt as an anti-corruption control, not a UX nicety.
design_rules.rationale: Two independent data points: 66% of Bhoomi users got no receipt for their Rs 15; and in Rwanda's national LTR only 71% of landowners received a claims receipt while 38% had paid the fee. In both cases the missing receipt is where the leakage lived.

design_rules.rule: Reject flat per-document fees. If any charge exists, make it either free for the landowner's own parcels or proportional to holding size/value, and state the basis on the fee screen. Publish the complete fee schedule as a public page with no login.
design_rules.rationale: Rwanda's switch from a 6%-of-value transfer fee to a flat RwF 20,000 fee produced a charge that 'could easily exceed 25 percent of the land value of small plots', and land-market activity measurably fell. Doing Business's Transparency of Information index explicitly scores whether the fee schedule is published online — India's Maharashtra registry scores on this only because a PDF exists.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The default instinct that a flat small fee (₹15, ₹20) is obviously fair because it is small.

design_rules.rule: Replace the CAPTCHA with asymmetric access design: parcel-keyed lookup (village + survey number → record) stays open and unauthenticated; person-keyed reverse lookup (name → all holdings statewide) requires identity, is rate-limited, and is logged with the requester's identity disclosed to the landowner. Publish the access policy.
design_rules.rationale: Bhoomi fieldwork found that open search by survey number — which large farmers and elites could easily obtain — was used to locate small farmers in order to 'poach on entitlements meant for small farmers, and more important, on their land'. That is the only serious argument for restricting access, and a CAPTCHA does not implement it: it blocks the semi-literate farmer while a CNN solves it in milliseconds. Meanwhile Georgia scores 1.0 on 'freely accessible by anyone' for ownership information and India scores only for 'anyone who pays the official fee'.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Both the incumbent position (CAPTCHA everything) and the naive open-data position (expose everything to everyone with no logging).

design_rules.rule: Publish the parcel geometry and map layer separately, free, and API-first — and keep the legal instrument layer distinct, gated and fee-bearing. Two products, two access models, one identifier.
design_rules.rationale: Singapore's SLA splits exactly this way: OneMap (free geospatial, including land ownership overlays, schools, demographics) versus INLIS (regulatory: property ownership information, survey plans, title lodgement). Singapore scores 28.5/30 on quality of land administration. India scores 0.0 on 'is the information recorded by the property registration agency and the cadastral agency kept in a single database' and 0.0 on public consultability of maps ('only intermediaries and interested parties').

design_rules.rule: Prefer general boundaries over precise geometry. Ship an approximate, adjudicated, complete parcel layer rather than waiting for surveyed accuracy, and label the precision explicitly on the map ('indicative extent, not a survey').
design_rules.rationale: Rwanda registered 10.7 million of an estimated 11.5 million parcels in under three years at USD 5 per parcel by using aerial and satellite imagery with locally trained para-surveyors demarcating GENERAL boundaries rather than GPS measurements — and still scored 28.5/30 on Doing Business quality of land administration, third in the world. Precision was traded for coverage, deliberately.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The engineering instinct to withhold a map layer until the geometry is survey-grade — which, given that all 881 Kheda+Anand sheets are rasterised exports with no geometry, would mean shipping nothing.

design_rules.rule: Do not use a 'records digitised' or 'coverage %' number as a headline success metric without publishing its denominator and its exclusions. If parcels are skipped because they are contested, say how many and why.
design_rules.rationale: The Cambodia Panel found the project's one-million-titles target was interpreted as 'the Project will not title lands in areas where disputes are likely' — internally described as 'going for the low-hanging fruits' — with 'no reference in any key project documents to principles for determining "areas where disputes are likely"'. A coverage KPI mechanically selects against the parcels that most need attention.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Every government dashboard and every hackathon pitch deck, which lead with a coverage percentage.

design_rules.rule: Choose measurable, citizen-side success metrics and instrument them from day one: median time from landing page to correct record retrieved; successful-retrieval rate on the first attempt; % of sessions completed without assistance; median correction turnaround; rate of recorded mutations. Do NOT promise credit access, investment, land-market activity or GDP effects.
design_rules.rationale: The World Bank's IEG systematic review of 103 studies found registering property to be an evidence gap 'where the reforms have little or no rigorous evidence', and found registering-property interventions 28 percentage points LESS likely to succeed than other reform areas (p<0.01). Meanwhile LINZ's own benefit reporting measures professional productivity, not citizen outcomes — a gap a new portal can credibly fill. Bhoomi's most defensible measured outcome was the 85% rise in mutation volume: people updated once updating became cheap.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The standard land-tech pitch, which claims unlocked credit and unlocked GDP.

design_rules.rule: Design the schema so that rights which do not fit a legal category are still RECORDABLE as claims, distinct from adjudicated entries. Give tenants, sharecroppers, unpartitioned heirs, co-widows and consensual-union partners a place to appear, flagged as unadjudicated, rather than no place at all.
design_rules.rationale: Rwanda's pilot cut documented ownership for legally unmarried women by 8 percentage points precisely because Rwandan law recognised only registered marriages, so the registry had no slot for consensual unions, customary or religious marriages, or polygamous unions. Cambodia's project design excluded informal settlers from titling by construction. In both cases the harm came from schema, not from software.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Data-modelling hygiene, which says do not store unverified claims in an authoritative register — the answer is a separate, clearly-typed claim table, not omission.

design_rules.rule: Show provenance on every field: which register the value came from (VF-7 / VF-12 / VF-6 / VF-8A), the entry number and date, and a link to the mutation entry that produced it. Render unknown metadata as an explicit em-dash, never as a blank or a plausible default.
design_rules.rationale: Doing Business scored India 0.0 for keeping registry and cadastral information in separate databases and 0.0 for any independent complaints mechanism against the registration agency; there is no compensation for erroneous certified information. When the state guarantees nothing, provenance is the only thing standing between the citizen and an unfalsifiable claim. The Cambodia case shows what happens when a reclassification is invisible to the person it dispossesses.

design_rules.rule: Frame the submission's national ambition as a MODEL SPEC that any state can adopt — a record schema, an API contract, service standards, and a rule that changes are published a fixed period before taking effect — with Gujarat as the reference implementation. Do not propose one national portal.
design_rules.rationale: Australia's ARNECC (formed 2011 under an Intergovernmental Agreement) does exactly this: the Electronic Conveyancing National Law is enacted separately in each State and Territory, while ARNECC maintains one national set each of Model Operating Requirements and Model Participation Rules that each Registrar determines locally and must publish at least 20 business days before they take effect. Eight jurisdictions, one interoperable market, no single system. Land is a State subject in India for the same federal reasons.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The reflex to propose 'one India land portal', which ignores that land administration is constitutionally a State subject.

design_rules.rule: Publish an operations page: transaction volumes served, uptime, median response time, and outstanding correction backlog. Make it a public URL with no login.
design_rules.rationale: Doing Business's Transparency of Information index scores 'are there publicly available official statistics tracking the number of transactions at the immovable property registration agency' — India scores on it, with Mumbai reporting 2,249,874 property transfers in 2018 — but scores 0.0 for publishing land-dispute counts and 0.0 for an independent complaints mechanism. Publishing operations data is already established Indian practice; extending it to backlog and dispute counts is the cheap, high-credibility increment.

design_rules.rule: Do not build on blockchain, and pre-empt the question with the evidence: Georgia's entire measured improvement (39 days → 2 days, 2.5% → 0.1% of value, 8 procedures → 1) was achieved between 2004 and 2011; the blockchain notarisation layer arrived in 2016, after the fact, and its most-cited account is a self-report by the responsible government agency with no before/after measurement.
design_rules.rationale: Traced primary sources: the World Bank's 2012 chronicle of Georgia's reforms attributes the gains to institutional restructuring (2,200 staff dismissed, 630 rehired, salaries up ~20×, nine regional offices abolished, survey privatised, fees collected by banks); the blockchain paper (ICEGOV 2018) is authored by Georgian e-government officials and reports no measured effect.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The single most common judge question in a land-records hackathon.

design_rules.rule: State explicitly, in the submission, which parts of the incumbent problem the portal CANNOT fix: adjudication quality, staff incentives, the presumptive-title regime, the >3-year first-instance dispute timeline, and the absence of a state guarantee. Name Georgia's non-software levers as out of scope.
design_rules.rationale: Georgia's transformation required mass dismissal and rehiring, a twentyfold salary increase, abolishing offices whose function was 'coordinating corruption', privatising cadastral survey, and removing cash from officials' hands. Doing Business 2020 records that a first-instance land dispute in India takes more than three years. IEG found land-registry interventions to be the WORST-performing reform area it evaluated. A portal that claims to fix any of this is making a claim the evidence contradicts.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Hackathon incentives to claim maximum impact — but criterion 6 explicitly rewards the opposite, and this is the cheapest way to win it.

design_rules.rule: Use the DB2020 comparator table (India rank 154, 68 days in Mumbai, 7.4% of property value, quality index 14/30 and geographic coverage 0/8 versus New Zealand 2, Rwanda 3, Georgia 5) to establish that the problem is real — but always caption it with what it actually measured: a warehouse transfer between two domestic companies in Mumbai or Delhi, data frozen at 1 May 2019, from an index the World Bank discontinued on 16 September 2021.
design_rules.rationale: The WilmerHale investigation found the documented manipulation affected Starting a Business, Getting Credit–Legal Rights and Paying Taxes for China, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Azerbaijan — NOT Registering Property. The historical property data is therefore citable with disclosure. B-READY, the successor, has no Registering Property topic, so DB2020 is the last comparable global snapshot.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Both extremes: citing Doing Business rankings as clean fact, and refusing to cite them at all because the report was discontinued.

design_rules.rule: Refuse to use the two famous Indian land statistics — 'two-thirds/70% of civil cases are land disputes' and 'India loses 1.3% of GDP to bad land records' — and say why, in the deck.
design_rules.rationale: The '>70 percent [of] disputes in courts are land based' claim appears in the World Bank's own flagship Bhoomi case study with no citation whatsoever, in a document that footnotes its other claims. The '1.3%' claim is attributed there to McKinsey Global Institute's 'India: The Growth Imperative' (2001) but is stated two incompatible ways nine pages apart in that same document — once as 1.3% of potential GROWTH, once as 1.3% of potential INVESTMENTS. Independently, Doing Business 2020 recorded that India publishes NO statistics on the number of land disputes in first-instance courts, so no share-of-litigation figure can be derived from published data.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Essentially every Indian land-tech pitch deck, policy note and news article — which is exactly why refusing them is a differentiator.

gaps: McKinsey Global Institute's 'India: The Growth Imperative' (September 2001) itself could not be obtained. I traced the '1.3%' claim to that citation and documented its internal inconsistency in the World Bank Bhoomi paper (growth vs investment, nine pages apart), but I could NOT verify what MGI originally wrote, whether the figure concerned land specifically or a bundle of product-market barriers, or whether '1.3% of GDP' — the form repeated everywhere — appears in the source at all. Treat the underlying figure as unverified, not merely drifted.

The original Public Affairs Centre / Lobo & Balakrishnan Bhoomi report card (November 2002) was not obtained directly. All figures reported here (66%→3% bribes, 198 treated / 59 control, AC Nielsen–ORG–MARG fieldwork) come from the World Bank case study's summary of it. The control-group sample of 59 is stated in that summary and should be re-verified against the original before being used as a headline.

Singapore INLIS fee schedules, Singpass gating, and whether a guest/anonymous search path exists could NOT be established — app.sla.gov.sg/inlis and onemap.gov.sg/apidocs are JavaScript single-page applications that return no server-rendered content, and I did not interact with the live services. The Singapore section of Part A is therefore structural only, with no cost or identity figures.

NSW Land Registry Services and Victoria's Land Registry: I could NOT verify the concession terms (widely reported as a 35-year NSW concession in 2017 and a Victorian sale in 2018, with dollar figures I did not confirm), IPART's regulated maximum prices, transaction volumes, or the Torrens assurance-fund arrangements. nswlrs.com.au, rg.nsw.gov.au and ipart.nsw.gov.au all returned empty bodies or blocked automated fetches; land.vic.gov.au returned a Cloudflare interstitial. Any Australian privatisation figures in the deliverable must be re-sourced before use.

ePlan / digital cadastre: icsm.gov.au now redirects to anzlic.gov.au/ICSM, which timed out. I could not confirm the ePlan data model (LandXML-based), which jurisdictions have mandated it, adoption dates, or any measured benefit. Part A item 2's cadastral-modernisation half is unsupported.

New Zealand's public-facing search economics: I confirmed LINZ charges NZ$8 per title/survey-plan search from 3 February 2025, but could not establish what, if anything, the 'Land Record Search' interface exposes free of charge to a member of the public, nor any citizen-side (as opposed to professional-productivity) benefit measurement. LINZ's published benefits are entirely conveyancer/surveyor-facing.

No independent audit of the LINZ programme was located. The $124.7m benefits figure and the 45%/42%/94% productivity percentages are LINZ's own self-reported survey results; the assurance provider named in the primary document (IQANZ) publishes nothing public. The cost re-baselining ($128.2m → $175.7m, August 2022) IS primary-sourced and solid.

Georgia's post-2016 systematic land registration reform (the programme that addresses its weak geographic coverage — DB2020 scored Georgia only 2.0/8 there) has no impact evaluation I could locate. All the strong Georgia numbers describe 2004–2011 transaction reform; the coverage problem it left behind is documented only by the DB2020 sub-index, and the 120m GEL / 660 surveyors / 262 registrars figures reported in Georgian press were not verifiable against a primary source.

GRAIN's 'The digitalisation of land: more data, less land' and Rodima-Taylor's Geoforum 2021 paper 'Digitalizing land administration: The geographies and temporalities of infrastructural promise' were both inaccessible (Cloudflare block; paywall). The critique side of Part C rests instead on the Cambodia Inspection Panel, the Rwanda gender finding and the IEG evaluation — which is a stronger evidence base, but means the specifically anti-digitisation NGO/critical-geography literature is unrepresented here.

No impact evaluation of any Indian state's land-records digitisation with a credible counterfactual was found beyond Bhoomi. Subramanian & Kumar (JDE 2023) is a genuine experiment on Indian land TITLING (nudging farmers to obtain formal titles; finds increased agricultural investment, crop productivity, paddy profits, and released locked-in family labour) but I did not obtain its effect sizes, sample or state. DILRMP and SVAMITVA have no located impact evaluation at all.

Research method degraded partway through: the Firecrawl account returned HTTP 402 (out of credits) on the first call, and the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted after four searches. Everything after that point was gathered by direct WebFetch and curl against URLs I could derive, plus the open OpenAlex, Crossref and World Bank Documents & Reports APIs. Discovery was therefore constrained — the sources here are strong and primary, but the search was not exhaustive, and Part A items 2 and 4 suffered most.

topic: Rural India device, network, language/script and accessibility constraints for a Gujarat 7/12 land-records citizen web portal (2025–2026)

claims.claim: The entire Gujarat geographic cascade — 33 districts, every taluka, and all 16,044 village names — serialises to 189 KB raw, 67 KB gzip, 58 KB brotli. A single district (Anand, 357 villages) is 2 KB gzipped. This is the exact data AnyRoR spends four sequential server round trips delivering.
claims.figure: 58 KB brotli for all 16,044 villages; 2 KB gzip per district
claims.source_name: Own measurement over assets/maps/villages.json in this repo (built from eJamin catalogue, generatedAt 2026-08-10)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the single biggest end-to-end design decision available. It kills the chained-dropdown architecture outright: ship the geography as one cacheable static asset and the whole cascade becomes local and instant, reducing the journey from 6 network round trips to 1.

claims.claim: AnyRoR's CAPTCHA image (id=ContentPlaceHolder1_i_captcha_1) carries no alt attribute, and the page contains no audio or other non-visual CAPTCHA alternative. All 3 images on the cascade page and both images on the result page lack alt entirely.
claims.figure: 0 of 5 images have alt; 0 non-visual CAPTCHA alternatives
claims.source_name: Own audit of anyror/recon-page.html and anyror/detail-page.html (local captures in this repo; live site not touched)
claims.why_it_matters: A hard WCAG 2.1 SC 1.1.1 (Level A) failure on the single control that gates the entire service. A blind Gujarati landowner cannot obtain their own legally-public record. This is the strongest single 'the problem is real' exhibit you have, and it is verifiable, not rhetorical.

claims.claim: Neither AnyRoR page declares a language: the cascade page is <html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"> and the 7/12 result page is bare <html>. Zero aria-* attributes on either page. Four <select> elements and one text input with zero <label for=>.
claims.figure: 0 lang attributes, 0 aria-* attributes, 0 labels for 5 form controls
claims.source_name: Own audit of anyror/recon-page.html and anyror/detail-page.html
claims.why_it_matters: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.1 (A), 1.3.1 (A), 3.3.2 (A) and 4.1.2 (A) all fail. Missing lang specifically breaks Gujarati: it is what a screen reader uses to pick a Gujarati voice and what a browser uses to pick a Gujarati font. Setting lang="gu" costs one attribute and is your cheapest demonstrable improvement.

claims.claim: AnyRoR's 7/12 result page is 311.0 KB raw / 113.1 KB gzipped, of which the ASP.NET __VIEWSTATE hidden field alone is 121,624 bytes — 38% of the page. The cascade page is 37.0 KB raw / 15.3 KB gzip with a 6,828-byte __VIEWSTATE.
claims.source_name: Own measurement of local AnyRoR captures
claims.why_it_matters: Concrete, quotable evidence of server-side session fragility having a byte cost. ViewState is downloaded and re-uploaded on every postback; it is also why a lost session forces a restart.

claims.claim: The AnyRoR journey is 6 sequential full-page round trips before a record appears. All four dropdowns (record type, district, taluka, village) are AutoPostBack selects that call __doPostBack. The page loads jQuery 1.8.3 (released November 2012), AjaxControlToolkit 3.5.40412.0 (a .NET 3.5-era build), bootstrap.min.js, slick.js, and two ScriptResource.axd + two WebResource.axd blobs.
claims.source_name: Own measurement of anyror/recon-page.html
claims.why_it_matters: Shows the bottleneck is ROUND TRIPS, not bytes. At India's P75 RTT of 85 ms the network floor is only ~1.4 s; at a rural cell-edge RTT of 300 ms the same six trips cost ~3.6 s of pure latency before a single useful byte, and any one dropped request restarts the session.

claims.claim: In 15 real AnyRoR 7/12 extracts from Anand district in this repo, the Gujarati LETTER PA (પ, U+0AAA) appears 514 times inside numeric runs where the Gujarati DIGIT FIVE (૫, U+0AEB) belongs. Digit five occurs only 379 times — by far the rarest digit (every other digit occurs 900–3,264 times). So roughly 58% of all 'fives' in the official record text are typed as a letter, not a digit.
claims.source_name: Own measurement across output/*/anyror_*.html in this repo
claims.why_it_matters: A genuine, previously-unreported data-integrity defect in Gujarat's land record. Any exact-match search, numeric sort or parse over survey numbers, mutation numbers and areas silently fails on more than half the fives. Your backend MUST normalise homoglyphs before indexing — and saying so is exactly the end-to-end/backend thinking the judges asked for.

claims.claim: Real 7/12 extracts mix two digit systems inside one document and even inside one token. Across 15 records: 16,222 Gujarati digits and 6,952 Latin digits (70/30), with 197 tokens containing both — e.g. the survey identifier '222/૨/p(935)' has a Latin survey number, a Gujarati sub-division, a Latin part letter and a Latin mutation number.
claims.figure: 16,222 Gujarati vs 6,952 Latin digits; 197 mixed-digit tokens
claims.source_name: Own measurement across output/*/anyror_*.html
claims.why_it_matters: Settles the 'which numerals?' question empirically for your data: you cannot pick one, you must normalise both on ingest and then render one consistently. It also means a citizen typing '૪૫૨' will not match a record stored as '૪પ૨' or '452'.

claims.claim: CLDR/ICU declares the default numbering system for the Gujarati (gu) locale to be 'latn' — Latin digits — with 'gujr' as the native alternative. Verified directly: Intl.NumberFormat('gu-IN').resolvedOptions().numberingSystem returns 'latn', and CLDR's own Gujarati long date format renders '20 ઑગસ્ટ, 2026' with a Latin year. Marathi (deva) and Bengali (beng) by contrast default to native digits; Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil default to Latin.
claims.source_name: Unicode CLDR v47 locale summary for gu, verified against local ICU via Node Intl
claims.why_it_matters: This is the closest thing to an authoritative answer on Gujarati numeral comprehension, and it contradicts the incumbent. The internationalisation standard says a Gujarati reader's default expectation is Latin digits; AnyRoR renders 70% Gujarati digits. Resolve this by rendering Latin digits by default with a Gujarati-numeral toggle — and say in your write-up that CLDR, not taste, decided it.

claims.claim: India's 75th-percentile mobile network is 6.2 Mbps down / 2.1 Mbps up / 85 ms RTT — slower than Indonesia (6.4) and well below the global P75 of 9 Mbps / 3 Mbps / 100 ms. Derived from Cloudflare Radar country data, November 2024 – November 2025.
claims.figure: India P75: 6.2 Mbps down, 2.1 Mbps up, 85 ms RTT
claims.source_name: Alex Russell, 'The Performance Inequality Gap, 2026', infrequently.org (Chrome team; Cloudflare Radar underlying data)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the number to build the performance budget against. It is methodologically explicit and country-specific, which almost no other public figure is. Note it is a P75 of Cloudflare-observed sessions, i.e. biased toward users who already have working connectivity — rural Gujarat is worse.

claims.claim: At the global P75 baseline (9 Mbps / 3 Mbps / 100 ms) on a Samsung Galaxy A24 4G, a three-second load allows 2.0 MiB total with 0.3 MiB JavaScript in a JS-light page (15% JS), or 1.2 MiB total with 0.62 MiB JS in a JS-heavy page. Opening four TLS connections instead of two cuts the three-second budget by 350 KiB.
claims.figure: 3 s / JS-light: 2.0 MiB total, 0.3 MiB JS
claims.source_name: Alex Russell, 'The Performance Inequality Gap, 2026'
claims.why_it_matters: The only maintained, published, methodologically-transparent web performance budget. Scale it by India's 6.2/9 bandwidth ratio to get your P75-India figure.

claims.claim: The author of that budget explicitly states: 'Services trying to scale, and anyone trying to build for emerging markets, should be anchoring P90 or P95, not P75.'
claims.source_name: Alex Russell, 'The Performance Inequality Gap, 2026'
claims.why_it_matters: Justifies your using a budget roughly half of the India-P75 figure. Quote it directly — it pre-empts a judge asking why you did not just use the standard budget.

claims.claim: In rural Gujarat, only 65.2% of persons aged 15 and above used the internet at least once in the previous three months (rural men 74.3%, rural women 56.1%). Roughly one rural Gujarati adult in three, and nearly one rural woman in two, is not an internet user at all.
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, Comprehensive Modular Survey: Telecom 2025 (NSS 80th Round, Jan–Mar 2025), MoSPI/NSO — Table 3, age 15+
claims.why_it_matters: Sets the honest ceiling on any web-only solution and directly supports designing an assisted/proxy path (a relative, a VLE, a shop) rather than assuming the landowner operates the portal themselves.

claims.claim: In rural Gujarat, only 61.9% of persons aged 15+ own a mobile phone — rural men 82.5%, rural women 41.7%. Among Gujarati mobile owners of any age 15+, 20.0% of rural owners have a feature phone only (no smartphone) and a further 2.2% have both.
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, CMS:T 2025 — Table 2 and Table 2.1, age 15+
claims.why_it_matters: One in five rural Gujarati phone owners cannot open a web page on any device they own. It also demolishes the 'everyone has a smartphone' framing — and the 41.7% female ownership figure is the strongest argument for an SMS/IVR or delegated-access fallback.

claims.claim: 98.4% of rural Gujarati internet users reach the internet via mobile phone + mobile data. Only 1.3% use mobile phone + WiFi; 0.2% tablet. Nationally, of rural households with internet, 98.8% use a mobile network and only 9.1% have any fixed/WiFi network; just 3.2% have fibre.
claims.figure: 98.4% mobile-data-only in rural Gujarat; 3.2% rural fibre nationally
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, CMS:T 2025 — Table 5 (rural person) and Statement 14
claims.why_it_matters: There is effectively no unmetered, low-latency path to your rural user. Every byte is cellular. It also means you can assume a Save-Data-relevant context but cannot assume WiFi for a large first download.

claims.claim: All-India digital-skill rates for persons aged 15+ are far below the headline youth figures: able to send/receive email 43.5% (rural 36.9%); able to perform an online banking transaction 48.9% (rural 42.0%); has used copy-and-paste in last 3 months 62.3% (rural 57.9%); has sent a message with an attached file 63.6% (rural 59.1%). In Gujarat, rural 15+ copy-and-paste is 61.3% (men 72.7%, women 50.1%).
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, CMS:T 2025 — Statements 6, 7, 11, 12 and Figs 4.1, 5.1, 9.1, 10.1; Table 7 for Gujarat
claims.why_it_matters: Directly rules out several common UI patterns: 'copy this reference number', 'we emailed you the link', and 'pay online to download'. Four in ten rural adults cannot copy-paste; six in ten cannot use email.

claims.claim: The single most common reason Indian households give for having no internet at home is not cost or coverage: 39.2% say 'do not know how to use it', 21.3% 'do not need the internet', 11.4% 'service available but does not meet household needs'. 13.7% of all Indian households had no internet at the premises.
claims.figure: 39.2% 'do not know how to use it'
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, CMS:T 2025 — Statement 14 and Fig 11.1
claims.why_it_matters: Reframes the problem from infrastructure to comprehension, which is the argument for your redesign. It also matches GSMA's global finding that the usage gap is roughly nine times the coverage gap.

claims.claim: CAUTION: the widely-quoted CMS:T 2025 headlines — '96.8% of rural persons used a mobile phone', '92.7% used the internet', '95.5% own a smartphone', '85.5% of households have a smartphone' — are all for the 15–29 age band (or households), not for adults generally. The 15+ figures are 15–25 percentage points lower, and the typical 7/12 holder is 45–70.
claims.figure: 15–29 band vs 15+: e.g. rural internet 92.7% vs 64.9% all-India
claims.source_name: NSS Report No. 593, CMS:T 2025 (compare Statement/Table headers 'Age: 15-29 years' vs 'Age: 15 years and above'); PIB press release PRID 2132330
claims.why_it_matters: This is the trap in this dataset. Almost every news write-up quotes the youth number as if it were the population number. Flagging it in your honesty section is cheap credibility, and the 15+ number is the one that describes your actual user.

claims.claim: TRAI's quarterly indicators for the quarter ending 31 December 2025: average wireless data usage 25.70 GB per data subscriber per month; average revenue realisation Rs 7.87 per GB; monthly wireless ARPU Rs 194.57; all-India rural tele-density 59.63%; rural internet subscribers 434.27 million, or 47.63 per 100 rural population. Gujarat's rural tele-density is 72.44%, above the national average.
claims.source_name: TRAI, The Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicators, Quarter Ending 31 December 2025 (QPIR)
claims.why_it_matters: CONTRARIAN: at Rs 7.87/GB a 500 KB page costs about 0.4 paise. Data price is NOT the binding constraint in India, and any pitch that leans on 'data is expensive' will be wrong. The real constraints are latency, coverage variability, device capability and comprehension. Budget for round trips, not for rupees.

claims.claim: India's average mobile data traffic per smartphone was 36 GB/month in 2025 (up from 33 in 2024, forecast 65 by 2031) against a global average of 21 GB in 2025. India+Nepal+Bhutan had 600 million LTE and 395 million 5G subscriptions out of 1,230 million total, implying roughly 235 million (~19%) still on 2G/3G. India's 5G population coverage was ~95% at end-2025. The report notes traffic demand in dense urban locations can be up to 1,000 times that of rural areas.
claims.figure: India 36 GB/month vs 21 GB global; ~19% still on 2G/3G; 1000x urban:rural traffic density
claims.source_name: Ericsson Mobility Report, November 2025 (regional key figures tables; Figures 13–14)
claims.why_it_matters: The 36 GB average is video-dominated and tells you nothing about your user's page budget — do not quote it as evidence that bandwidth is plentiful. The useful figures are the ~19% still on 2G/3G and the 1000x urban:rural density gap, which is why '95% 5G population coverage' does not mean a usable connection in a field.

claims.claim: India, July 2026, by page views: mobile is 66.04% of traffic (desktop 33.39%); the dominant mobile viewport is 360x800 CSS px at 18.2%, followed by 393x873 (8.45%) and 360x804 (4.65%); Chrome for Android is 84.6% of the mobile browser market.
claims.source_name: StatCounter GlobalStats, India, July 2026
claims.why_it_matters: Gives you the exact design width (360 px) and tells you Chromium is effectively the only rendering engine you must satisfy. Weakness: StatCounter is page-view-weighted, so it over-represents heavy users on better devices — treat 360x800 as a floor, not a median.

claims.claim: Android version share in India, July 2026 (page-view weighted): Android 15 = 23.73%, Android 16 = 23.42%, Android 13 = 14.03%, Android 14 = 12.31%, Android 12 = 9.43%, Android 11 = 8.82%. So roughly 18% of tracked Indian traffic is Android 12 or older.
claims.source_name: StatCounter GlobalStats, Android Version Market Share India, July 2026
claims.why_it_matters: Chrome on Android auto-updates independently of the OS, so OS version mostly constrains system WebView-in-app and system fonts, not CSS/JS features. Because the tail is page-view weighted it understates old devices — the real device tail is older than this.

claims.claim: HTTP Archive's 2025 Web Almanac: the median mobile page is 2,164 KB (p10 516 KB, p25 1,127 KB, p75 4,119 KB, p90 8,337 KB) across ~72 requests. Median mobile composition: images 911 KB, JavaScript 632 KB, fonts 122 KB, CSS 77 KB, HTML 22 KB. Median mobile page weight grew 202.8% in ten years, from 845 KB (July 2015) to 2,362 KB (July 2025).
claims.figure: median mobile page 2,164 KB; p10 516 KB
claims.source_name: HTTP Archive, Web Almanac 2025, Page Weight chapter
claims.why_it_matters: Gives you the comparison bar. If your portal lands under 500 KB you are below the 10th percentile of the web — a claim you can make with a citation rather than an adjective.

claims.claim: HTTP Archive's 2025 Web Almanac accessibility chapter: median Lighthouse accessibility score is 85%; only 30% of sites pass colour-contrast checks; 86% of sites have a valid lang attribute; 19% of mobile sites restrict zoom/scaling; 25% of form inputs rely on placeholder text alone with no label; 67% of sites remove default focus outlines (up 14 points in one year).
claims.figure: 30% pass contrast; 19% block zoom; 86% have lang
claims.source_name: HTTP Archive, Web Almanac 2025, Accessibility chapter
claims.why_it_matters: Note AnyRoR fails the lang check that 86% of the web passes. It also gives you the specific things to get right (contrast, no zoom lock, real labels, visible focus) that most sites get wrong.

claims.claim: GIGW 3.0 (NIC/MeitY) mandates conformance to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, adding 17 new guidelines (12 at A/AA) for touch-gesture and mobile accessibility. It comprises 25 Quality + 50 Accessibility + 3 Security + 10 Lifecycle guidelines, each classed MUST (mandatory) / SHOULD (advisory) / MAY (voluntary), certified by STQC. Quality guideline 13 makes Unicode use and multi-browser testing of Hindi/regional-language fonts a MUST. Lifecycle guideline 10 requires the website to be bilingual with a prominent language-selection link.
claims.source_name: Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps (GIGW) 3.0, NIC/MeitY — 'New features' and conformity matrix
claims.why_it_matters: Your portal has a named national standard to conform to, and AnyRoR visibly fails several of its MUSTs (no lang, no labels, no bilingual language switch). Building to GIGW 3.0 and saying so is a cheap, checkable claim.

claims.claim: GIGW 3.0 contains no requirement of any kind for page load time, page weight, request count, bandwidth, low-bandwidth variants, or mobile data efficiency — checked across all 25 Quality, 10 Lifecycle, 50 Accessibility and 3 Security guidelines in the published conformity matrix.
claims.source_name: GIGW 3.0 conformity matrix (Annexure II), guidelines.india.gov.in
claims.why_it_matters: A real gap in the national standard and a strong product-thinking point: a fully GIGW-3.0-compliant government site can still be unusable on a rural 4G edge connection, because nothing in the standard measures speed. Proposing a performance clause is a legitimate policy contribution from your submission.

claims.claim: In Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (Supreme Court of India, 8 November 2024), the Court held Rule 15 of the RPwD Rules 2017 ultra vires the RPwD Act 2016 because Section 40 requires mandatory accessibility standards while Rule 15 prescribes only 'self-regulatory guidelines' using discretionary language. It directed the Union to frame mandatory rules within three months and identified IS 17802 (Parts 1 and 2, 2021–2022) as the ICT accessibility standard incorporated by Rule 15(1)(c). As of the 4 April 2025 hearing the rules had not been notified and the committee sought a further six months.
claims.figure: Rule 15 struck down; 3-month deadline missed as of April 2025
claims.source_name: Supreme Court of India, Rajive Raturi v. Union of India, 8 Nov 2024, and daily order of 4 Apr 2025 (Indian Kanoon)
claims.why_it_matters: Accessibility for Indian government digital services is currently in a legal gap: the binding rules were ordered but not yet made. Building to WCAG 2.1 AA / IS 17802 voluntarily, and saying honestly that the enforcement regime is still pending, is both correct and a strong honesty-and-limitations point.

claims.claim: The NALSAR Centre for Disability Studies report relied on by the Supreme Court found 75% of the (sports-sector) websites it surveyed non-compliant with accessibility requirements, alongside findings such as only 2 of 30 High Court benches having tactile guiding strips.
claims.source_name: NALSAR-CDS report, as cited in Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (SC, 8 Nov 2024)
claims.why_it_matters: A court-endorsed, sector-specific non-compliance figure. Do NOT generalise it to all Indian government websites — the 75% is for sports-sector sites in that survey, and reporting it as an all-of-government number would be exactly the kind of laundering you asked me to avoid.

claims.claim: Medhi et al. (ACM TOCHI 2011), from an ethnographic study of 90 low-literacy subjects in India, Kenya, the Philippines and South Africa plus quantitative testing with over 70 Indian participants, found that textual interfaces are unusable by first-time low-literacy users and error-prone for literate but novice users; that a live human operator is up to ten times more accurate than a text-based interface; and that task completion is highest with a graphical interface, though users who understand a spoken-dialog system complete tasks faster.
claims.figure: live operator up to 10x more accurate than text UI
claims.source_name: Medhi, Patnaik, Brunskill, Gautama, Thies, Cutrell, Toyama — 'Designing Mobile Interfaces for Novice and Low-Literacy Users', ACM TOCHI 18(1), 2011
claims.why_it_matters: The canonical primary study on this user group, 306 citations. It supports a graphical/spoken primary path and a human-assisted fallback rather than a purely textual redesign. Caveat: it is 15 years old and predates ubiquitous smartphones and voice assistants — say so.

claims.claim: The widely-repeated '536 million Indian-language internet users' figure is NOT a measurement. It originates in KPMG in India + Google, 'Indian Languages – Defining India's Internet' (April 2017): a KPMG projection to 2021 applying an 18% CAGR to a measured base of 234 million at end-2016. The underlying Nielsen survey (n=7,060; 4,612 urban, 2,448 rural) screened respondents to ALREADY be Indian-language internet users, restricted to ages 15–50, socio-economic classes NCCS A/B/C only, with a 70:30 male:female quota. Gujarati was projected at 31 million users (6% of the total), and Gujarati's 'propensity to adopt internet in future' was 43% — joint-lowest of the eight languages studied with Marathi.
claims.figure: 536 million = 2017 projection to 2021, not a count; n=7,060 pre-screened users
claims.source_name: KPMG in India & Google, 'Indian Languages – Defining India's Internet', April 2017 (Annexure: Nielsen methodology)
claims.why_it_matters: You asked to be told when a famous number is hollow. This one is: it is a nine-year-old projection whose horizon has already expired, from a sample that by construction excluded non-users and the poorest classes — i.e. it excluded precisely your target user. Do not cite it. If you must reference Indian-language demand, use the CMS:T 2025 figures instead.

claims.claim: Measured directly from the font binaries in this repo: Noto Sans Gujarati Regular has ascent 896 / descent -408 per 1000 upem (OS/2 winAscent 1076, winDescent 408) giving a natural line box of 1.304 em (1.484 em on win metrics). Space Grotesk has ascent 984 / descent -292 (win 1150/292), 1.276 em (1.442 em). Gujarati's descent is 40% deeper than the Latin face's.
claims.figure: Gujarati descent 408 vs Latin 292 per 1000 em; min mixed line-height ~1.56
claims.source_name: Own measurement of head/hhea/OS-2 tables in android/app/src/main/res/font/*.ttf
claims.why_it_matters: Explains and quantifies the 'mixed strings box out' problem already noted in this project's CLAUDE.md. The safe line-height for a mixed Gujarati/Latin line is max(1150,1076)+max(292,408) = 1558/1000, i.e. 1.6. Any fixed-height row or button sized from Latin metrics will clip Gujarati matras and descenders.

claims.claim: AOSP's system font configuration ships Noto Sans Gujarati in Regular (400) and Bold (700) only for the sans family (plus NotoSansGujaratiUI compact variants and a NotoSerifGujarati variable font). There is no bundled 500 or 600 weight for Gujarati sans.
claims.source_name: AOSP platform/frameworks/base, data/fonts/fonts.xml (main branch)
claims.why_it_matters: If you specify font-weight 500 or 600 for Gujarati and rely on the system font, Android synthesises a fake bold or snaps to 400/700, which shifts metrics and can break your layout. Restrict Gujarati to 400 and 700, or self-host and subset a variable face.

claims.claim: The Save-Data client hint (Save-Data: on) is documented by MDN as 'Limited availability — not Baseline' and marked experimental; the related prefers-reduced-data CSS media feature has similarly narrow support.
claims.source_name: MDN Web Docs, Save-Data header
claims.why_it_matters: You cannot rely on detecting data-saver mode. Serve the light experience to everyone by default and offer an explicit in-app 'low data' toggle you control, rather than branching on a hint that may never arrive.

claims.claim: Two peer-reviewed studies specifically audit Indian e-government websites for accessibility and usability: Paul & Das, 'Accessibility and usability analysis of Indian e-government websites' (Universal Access in the Information Society, 2019/2020, ~60 citations) and Agrawal, Kumar & Singh, 'Assessing the usability, accessibility, and mobile readiness of e-government websites: a case study in India' (UAIS, 2021/2022, ~33 citations). Both are paywalled and I could not verify their reported figures.
claims.source_name: Universal Access in the Information Society (Springer), via OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar metadata
claims.why_it_matters: These exist and are citable as 'prior work exists', but do not quote numbers from them without reading them. If you have institutional access, these are the two to read — the second explicitly covers mobile readiness, which is your axis.

design_rules.rule: Budget the whole first view at 500 KB compressed over the wire, with a hard sub-budget of 100 KB JavaScript, 150 KB for the critical HTML+CSS+font needed to paint the first useful screen, and 50 KB on repeat visit. Enforce it in CI and fail the build on regression.
design_rules.rationale: Global P75 (9 Mbps/3 Mbps/100 ms) allows 2.0 MiB total and 0.3 MiB JS for a 3-second JS-light load. India's P75 is 6.2 Mbps/2.1 Mbps/85 ms, i.e. 69% of the global bandwidth, scaling that to ~1.4 MiB / ~200 KiB JS. Russell explicitly instructs emerging-market builders to anchor P90/P95 rather than P75; halving again for a rural cell edge (~3 Mbps, ~300 ms RTT) lands near 450–500 KB. For reference, the 10th-percentile mobile page on the whole web is 516 KB, so this budget puts you below 90% of the web.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The median mobile page is 2,164 KB and the median site ships 632 KB of JavaScript. Any React/Next default template blows the JS budget before you write a line of product code.

design_rules.rule: Budget ROUND TRIPS before bytes: at most 1 network round trip between 'the user has chosen their village and survey number' and 'the record is on screen', and at most 2 for the entire journey including the initial page load. No request may depend on the response of a previous request except that one.
design_rules.rationale: Measured: AnyRoR needs 6 sequential full-page loads. At India's P75 RTT of 85 ms the network-only floor is ~1.4 s, but at a rural cell-edge RTT of 300 ms the same six trips cost ~3.6 s of pure latency before any useful byte, and every trip is another chance for the ASP.NET session to die and force a restart. Bytes are cheap in India (Rs 7.87/GB); serialised latency is not.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The universal government-portal pattern of chained dependent dropdowns, each of which is a server round trip. Also conflicts with the instinct to 'optimise the page' — the page size is not the problem.

design_rules.rule: Ship the whole Gujarat geography as one static, immutable, long-cached asset (district → taluka → village names), and do all cascade filtering client-side with zero network calls. Lazy-load per-district (2 KB gzip) if you want to shave the first load further.
design_rules.rationale: Measured from this repo: all 33 districts, every taluka and all 16,044 village names serialise to 189 KB raw, 67 KB gzip, 58 KB brotli. Anand alone is 2 KB gzipped. Four of AnyRoR's six round trips exist solely to deliver data that fits in one cacheable file smaller than the median page's font payload (122 KB).
design_rules.conflicts_with: The assumption that reference data must be fetched from the server because it 'might change'. Village lists change on a timescale of years; version the asset and revalidate with an ETag.

design_rules.rule: Design at 360 CSS px wide as the primary target and make every layout work there without horizontal scroll. Never render the 7/12 as an HTML table on a phone; transform each row into a labelled block.
design_rules.rationale: 360x800 is the single most common mobile viewport in India at 18.2% of page views, and mobile is 66.04% of Indian traffic. The AnyRoR result page uses 8 <table> elements to lay out the 7/12, which is a desktop artefact reproduced on a 360 px screen.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The instinct to preserve the visual fidelity of the paper form. The paper form's grid is the thing that fails on a phone.

design_rules.rule: Set lang="gu" on <html> and mark any English helper text with lang="en" on the element. Never omit it.
design_rules.rationale: Both AnyRoR pages omit lang entirely (<html> and <html xmlns=...>), failing WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.1 (Level A) — a check that 86% of the web passes. lang is what a screen reader uses to select a Gujarati voice and what the browser uses to select a Gujarati font when your webfont fails to load. It is a one-attribute fix.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Nothing. This is free.

design_rules.rule: Render all numbers — survey numbers, sub-divisions, areas, dates, khata and mutation numbers — in Latin digits by default in the Gujarati interface, with an explicit user toggle to Gujarati numerals for those who prefer the form they know from the paper record. Store canonical values in Latin digits.
design_rules.rationale: CLDR/ICU sets the default numbering system for the gu locale to 'latn' — verified directly, Intl.NumberFormat('gu-IN') resolves to latn, and CLDR's own Gujarati date format writes a Latin year. Marathi and Bengali default to native digits; Gujarati does not. Meanwhile the incumbent's real output is 70% Gujarati digits and mixes both systems inside single tokens ('222/૨/p(935)'), so no single rendering is faithful to the source anyway — which frees you to pick the one the internationalisation standard says Gujarati readers expect.
design_rules.conflicts_with: AnyRoR itself, and this project's current design handoff, which specifies that land data 'always keeps its Gujarati numerals'. Worth reopening on the CLDR evidence — but note the counter-argument that a farmer matching a screen against a paper 7/12 may want the digits to look identical, which is exactly what the toggle is for.

design_rules.rule: Normalise Gujarati-digit homoglyphs on ingest, before indexing: map પ (U+0AAA LETTER PA) to ૫ (U+0AEB DIGIT FIVE) when it occurs inside a run of Gujarati digits, and transliterate all Gujarati digits to Latin for the search index while preserving the raw string for display. Make search match across both digit systems.
design_rules.rationale: Measured across 15 real Anand-district 7/12 extracts in this repo: the letter પ appears 514 times inside numeric runs, while the actual digit ૫ appears only 379 times and is by far the rarest digit (all others 900–3,264). Roughly 58% of all 'fives' in the official record text are typed as a letter. Exact-match search, sorting and numeric parsing silently fail on those records today.
design_rules.conflicts_with: This project's own hard rule that you must never strip characters out of a survey number (a rule that exists because stripping fused 250 distinct surveys). The resolution: normalise only into the SEARCH INDEX and only for this specific homoglyph pair; never mutate the stored identity string, and add a probe test asserting zero fused surveys, exactly as tools/identity/probe-tokenizer.mjs already does.

design_rules.rule: Set line-height to at least 1.6 on any line that can contain both Gujarati and Latin, and never give a text-bearing container a fixed pixel height. Use min-height plus padding.
design_rules.rationale: Measured from the font binaries: Noto Sans Gujarati has descent 408/1000 em (winDescent 408) against Space Grotesk's 292/1000, and winAscent 1076 vs 1150. The safe mixed line box is (1150 + 408)/1000 = 1.558 em, so 1.6. A container sized from Latin metrics clips Gujarati matras and descenders — the 'boxing out' already observed in this project.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Compact/'comfy' density targets and any design system whose default line-height is 1.4 or 1.5.

design_rules.rule: Use only font-weight 400 and 700 for Gujarati text. If you need an intermediate weight, self-host a subset variable Gujarati face rather than relying on the system font.
design_rules.rationale: AOSP's fonts.xml ships Noto Sans Gujarati in Regular (400) and Bold (700) only for the sans family. Requesting 500 or 600 triggers synthetic bolding or a snap, which changes advance widths and breaks measured layouts.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Design systems that use 500/600 as their default body/label weights.

design_rules.rule: Subset and self-host the Gujarati webfont to the characters your UI actually uses, and always declare a real fallback stack ending in the system Gujarati font. Give the font a font-display value that never blocks first paint.
design_rules.rationale: The full Noto Sans Gujarati Regular is 196 KB per weight; two weights would consume 392 KB — 78% of a 500 KB total budget on fonts alone, against a median-web font payload of 122 KB. Chrome for Android is 84.6% of the Indian mobile market and every Android build ships a system Gujarati font, so a fallback always exists.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Loading two or three custom families (as the current design specifies Space Grotesk + IBM Plex Mono + Noto Sans Gujarati) — that combination cannot fit the budget unsubset.

design_rules.rule: Never require copy-and-paste, email, or an online payment to complete the main journey. Do not put a reference number on screen and ask the user to type it somewhere else.
design_rules.rationale: MoSPI CMS:T 2025, persons aged 15+: nationally only 62.3% have used copy-and-paste in the last three months (rural 57.9%; Gujarat rural 61.3%, rural women 50.1%), only 43.5% can send or receive email (rural 36.9%), and only 48.9% can perform an online banking transaction (rural 42.0%).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Almost every government portal's 'note down your application number' and 'a link has been sent to your registered email' pattern.

design_rules.rule: Design an explicit assisted/delegated path as a first-class flow, not an afterthought: one person (a son, a neighbour, a village entrepreneur, a shopkeeper) fetching and sharing a record on behalf of the landowner, with a shareable low-byte artefact at the end.
design_rules.rationale: In rural Gujarat only 61.9% of adults 15+ own a mobile phone at all (women 41.7%), 20.0% of rural mobile owners have a feature phone only, and only 65.2% used the internet in the last three months. Medhi et al. (TOCHI 2011) found a live human operator up to ten times more accurate than a text interface for this population. The realistic unit of access is a household or a village, not an individual.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Aadhaar/OTP-gated 'the record holder must log in themselves' designs — and note the data is legally public, so no login is warranted for viewing.

design_rules.rule: Replace the CAPTCHA with rate limiting, caching and a signed short-lived token. If a challenge is unavoidable, it must have a text alternative and a non-visual alternative form.
design_rules.rationale: AnyRoR's CAPTCHA image has no alt attribute and no audio or other non-visual alternative — a WCAG 2.1 SC 1.1.1 (Level A) failure on the single control that gates the entire service, meaning a blind landowner cannot obtain their own legally-public record. GIGW 3.0 makes WCAG 2.1 AA mandatory, and RPwD Act 2016 s.40/s.42 obligations were reinforced by the Supreme Court in Rajive Raturi (Nov 2024). The data being protected is public by law, so the CAPTCHA protects only server capacity — which caching solves better.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The standard government answer that a CAPTCHA is needed to stop scraping. It does not stop scraping (this repo's own CNN solves it at 98.7%); it only stops disabled and low-literacy citizens.

design_rules.rule: Build to GIGW 3.0 and WCAG 2.1 AA explicitly, and add a performance clause GIGW does not have: publish your own page-weight and round-trip budget alongside the compliance claim.
design_rules.rationale: GIGW 3.0 mandates WCAG 2.1 AA across 50 accessibility guidelines plus MUST-level Unicode and multi-browser regional-font testing (Quality 13) and mandatory bilingualism with a prominent language switch (Lifecycle 10) — which AnyRoR lacks. But across all 88 guidelines there is no requirement for load time, page weight, request count or low-bandwidth support, so full compliance does not imply usability on a rural connection.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Treating GIGW certification as sufficient. It is necessary, not sufficient — and saying so is a product-thinking point in your favour.

design_rules.rule: Serve the light experience to everyone by default rather than branching on Save-Data or the Network Information API; offer an explicit in-product 'low data / slow connection' toggle you control, and persist it.
design_rules.rationale: MDN documents Save-Data as 'Limited availability — not Baseline' and experimental, and prefers-reduced-data has similarly narrow support. Meanwhile 98.4% of rural Gujarati internet users are on mobile data with no WiFi path, so the constrained case is the normal case, not the exception.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Progressive-enhancement advice that recommends detecting connection quality and adapting — the detection is unreliable and the adaptation would fire for nearly everyone anyway.

design_rules.rule: Make the record itself the cacheable artefact: once fetched, a 7/12 must be readable offline, and re-opening it must cost zero network. Treat the fetch as the expensive, resumable step and never lose user input across a failed request.
design_rules.rationale: AnyRoR's 119 KB __VIEWSTATE encodes server-side session state that is lost on any interruption, forcing a restart through all six round trips. In rural areas Ericsson notes traffic density can be 1,000x lower than dense urban, and TRAI puts rural internet subscribers at only 47.63 per 100 rural population — connections drop. A stateless, idempotent, bookmarkable URL for every record makes retry free.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Server-rendered form-postback architectures generally, and any design that puts the record behind a POST rather than a GET.

design_rules.rule: Report your device baseline honestly as a Samsung Galaxy A24 4G class device at P75 and something like a Moto E15 / Galaxy A07 at the low end, and test on a throttled 3 Mbps / 300 ms profile rather than Chrome's 'Slow 4G' preset.
design_rules.rationale: Russell's 2026 baseline names the Galaxy A24 4G as the P75 device and notes budget-device CPUs have not meaningfully improved since 2022, that the median smartphone now lives more than two years with P75 devices near three years old, and that even 2025's low-end (Moto E15) still ships a 4G-only radio. India's P75 network is 6.2 Mbps / 85 ms and rural is worse.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Demoing on a flagship over office WiFi, which is how most hackathon submissions are judged and why an explicit throttled demo is differentiating.

gaps: No published P90 or P95 network figure exists for India that I could find. Cloudflare Radar country data via infrequently.org publishes India only at P75 (6.2 Mbps / 2.1 Mbps / 85 ms). My rural P90 estimate of ~3 Mbps / ~300 ms RTT is an extrapolation, not a measurement — label it as such in your write-up.

No source found for typical RAM, internal storage, or storage-pressure statistics for phones actually in use in rural India. Counterpoint publishes shipment ASPs and price bands (India ASP $279 in 2025, sub-Rs 20,000 value share fell from 38% to 29% in two years) but not an installed-base RAM distribution. GSMA, TRAI and IAMAI do not publish it either. Treat any '2 GB RAM is typical' claim as unsourced-folklore.

I could not find any measured evidence on whether showing Gujarati AND English together helps or hurts comprehension for Gujarati-first users. The HCI literature on this population (Medhi et al.) is about text vs graphics vs voice, not about bilingual text pairing. Your 'both' language mode is a reasonable design hypothesis but is currently unevidenced — this is a good candidate for a small user test you can report honestly.

No study found on native-script versus Roman-transliteration preference for Gujarati specifically. Evidence exists for Hindi/Romanised code-mixing in the NLP literature but not as a user-preference finding, and I found nothing for Gujarati. Do not assert a preference.

No experimental evidence found on Gujarati NUMERAL comprehension — i.e. whether a rural Gujarati adult reads ૪૫૨ faster or more accurately than 452. The CLDR/ICU default (latn) is a strong standards signal and the incumbent's 70/30 Gujarati/Latin mix is strong evidence that the data itself is inconsistent, but neither is a comprehension study. This is a genuine open question and worth stating as one.

No reliable evidence found on Gujarati font rendering failures on cheap Android devices beyond what I could verify directly (AOSP bundles Noto Sans Gujarati at 400/700; the metric mismatch I measured). Claims about no-name devices shipping stripped system images with missing Indic fonts are plausible but I found no source. The line-height and weight rules above are measured; a 'tofu' risk claim would not be.

The two peer-reviewed audits of Indian e-government websites (Paul & Das 2019; Agrawal, Kumar & Singh 2021, both in Universal Access in the Information Society) are paywalled. I confirmed they exist and their citation counts but could NOT verify any figure they report. Do not quote numbers from them second-hand.
