No usability audit or user research found specifically on IRCTC, EPFO, the income-tax e-filing portal, DigiLocker, UMANG, or any state land-record portal, from any primary source. This appears to be a real gap in the literature rather than a search failure — which is itself worth saying in your submission, since it means your own walkthrough of AnyRoR is closer to primary evidence than most.

Whether the Union has now notified the mandatory accessibility rules ordered by the Supreme Court in Rajive Raturi is unresolved. I confirmed they were NOT notified as of the 4 April 2025 hearing, when the committee sought a further six months. I could not confirm the position as of August 2026 — check before asserting the current legal status.

No primary source found for the retail cost or throttling behaviour of entry-level Indian prepaid plans (the daily 1–1.5 GB cap and 64 kbps throttle-after-cap pattern). TRAI publishes only average realisation (Rs 7.87/GB) and ARPU (Rs 194.57/month), which are aggregates. The 'throttled to 64 kbps after the daily cap' claim is widely repeated but I could not trace it to TRAI or a telco tariff filing — treat as unsourced-folklore unless you verify it against a published tariff.

My AnyRoR measurements come from local captures of a handful of pages in this repo, and the homoglyph and digit-mixing findings come from 15 records from Anand district (mostly Bharoda village). These are strong for this corpus but are not a statewide sample. Say '15 records from Anand district', not 'Gujarat land records'.

India's last full census was 2011, so there is no current census literacy figure for rural Gujarat. Any literacy percentage you see quoted for 2025 is either a 2011 census figure, a PLFS/NSS estimate with a different definition, or an extrapolation. I could not retrieve a verified rural-Gujarat literacy number within this session.

topic: Low-literacy and first-time-user interface evidence for a Gujarati-first land-records (7/12) portal: what the ICTD/HCI literature actually measured, and what it implies for search-vs-browse, chronology, numeracy and trust

claims.claim: On a text-based UI, task completion by non-literate/semi-literate first-time users was ZERO. In the employment and map applications, none of the 7 individual subjects nor either of the two 5-person groups could navigate the text-based UI even with prompting and encouragement. The same result replicated three years later on mobile: 0 of 20 subjects completed a money transfer on the text UI.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, 'Text-Free User Interfaces for Illiterate and Semiliterate Users', Information Technologies & International Development 4(1):37-50 (orig. ICTD 2006)
claims.why_it_matters: AnyRoR's output is a text table. For a genuinely non-literate user the incumbent completion rate is not 'low', it is nil. This is the single strongest justification that the problem is real, and it sets the bar: any text-only redesign inherits a 0% floor for part of the target population.

claims.claim: Even with NO text at all, hierarchy depth is the killer. On a deep (4-level) text-free hierarchy, high-literacy participants got 91% of tasks correct vs 40% for low-literacy participants (t(12)=3.96, p<0.01) and 34% for medium-literacy (t(12)=4.76, p<0.01); time was 64 s vs 104 s (t(12)=3.81, p<0.01). n=60 from three South Indian slum communities. Textual literacy correlated with Raven's Progressive Matrices at r=0.68, p<0.01.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Lakshmanan, Toyama & Cutrell, 'Some Evidence for the Impact of Limited Education on Hierarchical User Interface Navigation', CHI 2013, pp. 2813-2822
claims.why_it_matters: AnyRoR's five chained dependent dropdowns ARE a 5-level hierarchy. Removing text from it would not fix it. This is the empirical basis for flattening the cascade rather than merely translating it.

claims.claim: On a touchscreen phone, a 7-page FLAT LIST of 40 items beat a 4-level hierarchy of the same 40 items on both speed and accuracy: 25 s vs 65.5 s (t(18)=4.6, p<0.001) and 100% vs 80% correct (t(18)=-3, p=0.0077). n=20 non-literate adults, Bangalore. The list won even though it forced users to page through multiple screens.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Toyama, Joshi, Athavankar & Cutrell, 'A Comparison of List vs. Hierarchical UIs on Mobile Phones for Non-literate Users', INTERACT 2013, LNCS 8118, pp. 497-504
claims.why_it_matters: Decisive for the cascade question: paging through a long flat list is CHEAPER for this population than descending a tidy hierarchy. Small screens are not a justification for nesting.

claims.claim: Of 90 low-literacy subjects across India, Kenya, the Philippines and South Africa, 56 could not understand or navigate hierarchical phone menus at all — including 100% of the 40 who had never used a mobile phone. Of the 34 who could perform a task on their own handset, 23 could not do it on a different handset.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Patnaik, Brunskill, Gautama, Thies & Toyama, 'Designing Mobile Interfaces for Novice and Low-Literacy Users', ACM TOCHI 18(1), Article 2
claims.why_it_matters: Skill does not transfer between interfaces. A user who has learned AnyRoR by rote will fail on a redesign, and vice versa — argues for a migration/onboarding path, not a clean break.

claims.claim: Vertical scrollbars were not understood by 48 of 90 subjects — they did not realise content existed 'beneath' what was displayed. Explicit demonstration was required. This group coincided almost exactly with voice-only phone users.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1), Article 2 (2011); same finding reported in Medhi, Ratan & Toyama, HCII 2009
claims.why_it_matters: Anything below the fold may as well not exist. Rules out long scrolling record pages and infinite-scroll timelines as the primary mechanism; argues for explicit paging with a visible Next control.

claims.claim: 24 of the 50 mobile phone users interviewed were unable to type even a single word, let alone a text message. All subjects were comfortable typing DIGITS but could not locate the '*' and '#' symbols.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1), Article 2
claims.why_it_matters: This is the direct answer to 'can they type?'. A free-text search box cannot be the only entry path. Digits, however, are safe — which is why survey number is the right primary key to type.

claims.claim: Numerals are the one symbol system this population reads reliably. Subjects 'could easily recognize numerals (0,1,2,3,4...)' and on SMS transaction receipts, though they could not read the English text, 'almost all could identify the numbers and what they meant'.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1) 2007; corroborated in Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) 2011
claims.why_it_matters: Survey numbers, areas, years and rupee amounts can be shown as digits with confidence. The words around them cannot. This inverts normal information hierarchy: the number is the anchor, the label is the decoration.

claims.claim: Subjects could read individual numbers on a receipt but 'still had difficulty with receipts indicating MULTIPLE transactions'. This is the closest thing in the literature to a direct test of presenting a chronological record of events to low-literate users, and the result is negative for the multi-row form.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011); also Medhi, Ratan & Toyama, HCII 2009
claims.why_it_matters: Directly bears on the ownership-history timeline bet. A history is a multi-transaction receipt. The finding says the CONTENT is fine but the DENSE MULTI-ROW FORM is what fails — so build one event per card, not a table of mutations.

claims.claim: Controlled comparison of 10 representations of 13 health symptoms with 200 illiterate/semi-literate subjects (20 per condition). Mean correct out of 13 WITHOUT audio: text 2.65, photograph 5.45, video 5.90, static hand-drawing 5.95, animation 7.35. WITH voice annotation: photograph 9.30, video 9.30, text 9.45, animation 9.65, static hand-drawing 9.75. Voice annotation also cut response time by ~30%.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Prasad & Toyama, 'Optimal Audio-Visual Representations for Illiterate Users of Computers', WWW 2007, pp. 873-882 (DOI 10.1145/1242572.1242690)
claims.why_it_matters: The most important single result for allocating design effort: adding a voice-over is worth ~3-4 extra correct answers out of 13, while switching between icon styles is worth well under one. Adding audio beats perfecting graphics by a large margin. Also: photographs were the WORST-performing image type, contradicting the common instinct that a photo is universally legible.

claims.claim: Audio-visual bimodal presentation can OVERLOAD this population. Some subjects 'were unable to fully process the bimodal stimulus' and focused on either the graphic or the audio but not both; some did not realise the voice was explaining the picture; and in the text+voice condition, totally illiterate subjects 'listened intently to the audio cue, and ignored the on-screen text completely'. Some also learned to mimic the voice annotation without understanding it.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Prasad & Toyama, WWW 2007
claims.why_it_matters: Rules out 'say everything twice at the same time'. Audio should carry the explanation while the screen carries the number; competing dense text plus continuous narration will be discarded, not integrated. Also warns that a user repeating the prompt back is not evidence of comprehension.

claims.claim: A MATRIX of checks and crosses (rows x columns showing which task belonged to which room) 'was not readily understood' and had to be replaced with explicit one-to-one associations without the matrix structure.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007), Figure 3
claims.why_it_matters: A VF-7 extract and especially a VF-12 crop record ARE matrices (survey x season x crop, or holder x share). Reproducing the paper table on screen reproduces a form that was measured not to work. Each cell must become a sentence.

claims.claim: Icon meaning is culturally specific and fails in ways designers do not anticipate. A standard 'house' glyph was read as a village hut, not an urban residence; roads shown in 80% black turning yellow on hover were rejected because 'roads can never be yellow'; animated arrows for one-way/two-way traffic were not understood until replaced with small car icons; and because Urdu reads right-to-left, Muslim subjects read a start-time/end-time pair backwards until an explicit arrow was added.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007)
claims.why_it_matters: No icon set can be adopted on intuition. For a land portal the risky glyphs are exactly the abstract ones: a 'mutation' arrow, a share pie, a lineage tree, an inheritance branch. Each needs a spoken label as its ground truth.

claims.claim: Across all queries about physical location, subjects navigated by LANDMARKS, not by cardinal directions, addresses or street names — so both the employment app and the map app were rebuilt on a purely landmark-based presentation.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007)
claims.why_it_matters: Selecting a village should be anchored on things people can point to (my taluka town, the temple, the highway, the neighbouring village name) and on the map sheet, rather than on an alphabetical administrative list.

claims.claim: Graphical UI vs spoken-dialog UI trade off completion against speed: graphical achieved 100% (20/20) task completion but took 13 min and 14 prompts on average; the voice UI achieved 72% (13/18) but in 5.2 min and 4.0 prompts. ANOVA on time F=21.49 > Fcrit=4.160, p<0.001; on prompts F=30.478 > Fcrit=4.160, p<0.05.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011); same experiment in Medhi et al., CHI 2009
claims.why_it_matters: If the metric is 'nobody is locked out', the graphical/visual path wins. If the metric is 'fast and unassisted', voice wins. For a records portal where failure means going back to the talati, optimise for completion, and offer voice as the accelerator.

claims.claim: Prior exposure to the interaction paradigm dominated everything else: 100% (7/7) of subjects who had previously used any IVR completed the voice task, and 100% (20/20) of subjects with NO prior graphical-UI exposure completed the graphical task after being shown a 'full-context' video dramatising what the service was and how it would be used.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., CHI 2009 / ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011)
claims.why_it_matters: A short, concrete, dramatised 'what this is for' video before first use is a measured intervention, not decoration. It is cheap to build and is the single highest-leverage onboarding element in the literature.

claims.claim: For structured data entry, a LIVE HUMAN OPERATOR on the phone was about ten times more accurate than the users typing it themselves: 0.5% error (one error in the whole trial) vs 4.2% for electronic forms and 4.5% for SMS, i.e. roughly one error in every 20 entries on the text interfaces. The partner organisation switched its deployment plan to the operator interface as a result.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011), Experiment 2
claims.why_it_matters: End-to-end thinking: a staffed helpline is not a failure of the product, it is the most accurate interface measured. Budget for a human fallback channel and treat it as part of the architecture.

claims.claim: A hybrid PAPER-plus-PHONE interface (CAM: barcoded paper forms captured by a phone camera) produced error rates of 1% or below, with users lacking prior camera or computer experience trained to comfort in 5-15 minutes. By contrast, novice mobile data entry with only 2-3 minutes of training produced 14% error rates.
claims.source_name: Parikh et al. (CAM), and Bernabe-Ortiz et al. 2008 — both as reported and cited in Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011), Section 2.1
claims.why_it_matters: Where a paper workflow is already ingrained — and the 7/12 extract absolutely is — designing WITH the paper beats designing it away. Supports a 'scan/photograph your existing extract' entry path and a print-shaped output.

claims.claim: With 45 farmers in Gujarat in a controlled between-subjects experiment, DIALED (keypad) input produced significantly higher task completion than SPEECH input on the same voice service — the gap being largest for subjects under 30 and those with less than an eighth-grade education. Dialed-input users also improved significantly more from first to final task and reported less difficulty giving input.
claims.source_name: Patel, Agarwal, Rajput, Nanavati, Dave & Parikh, 'A comparative study of speech and dialed input voice interfaces in rural India', CHI 2009
claims.why_it_matters: This is the closest study to my exact population — Gujarati farmers — and it says the intuitive accessibility answer (just let them speak) LOSES to pressing numbered keys. Only the abstract was retrievable; I could not obtain the full effect sizes.

claims.claim: Seven-month field deployment of the Avaaj Otalo voice forum with 51 small farmers in Gujarat, run with the Development Support Centre: 'simple menu-based navigation was readily learned, with users preferring NUMERIC input over speech.' For all 51 users this was their first participation in any online community.
claims.source_name: Patel, Chittamuru, Jain, Dave & Parikh, 'Avaaj Otalo: A Field Study of an Interactive Voice Forum for Small Farmers in Rural India', CHI 2010
claims.why_it_matters: Independent, longitudinal, Gujarat-specific corroboration that numbered selection beats speech and that a SIMPLE menu is learnable. It also shows sustained voluntary use is achievable in this exact population.

claims.claim: The speech-vs-keypad literature genuinely CONTRADICTS itself. Three studies published concurrently reached three different conclusions: Patel et al. (2009) found dialed input gave higher task completion; Grover et al. (2009) found comparable completion but a preference for dialed input; Sherwani et al. (2009), testing community health workers in Pakistan, found 'well-designed speech interfaces significantly outperform touch-tone equivalents for both low-literate and literate users' — and also that literacy significantly affected task success in BOTH modalities.
claims.source_name: Summarised in Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011), Section 2.1; Sherwani et al., 'Speech vs. touch-tone: Telephony interfaces for information access by low literate users', ICTD 2009
claims.why_it_matters: Honesty requirement: do not present 'voice is the answer for illiterate users' as settled. It is contested, and the outcome depends on the quality of the speech interface and on the users' prior exposure. Also note Sherwani's finding that literacy still predicted success even with no reading required — echoing the CHI 2013 abstract-reasoning result.

claims.claim: On a UK Citizens Advice Bureau information kiosk, low-literacy users compared with high-literacy users (6 vs 6, tasks of low/medium/high complexity) took EIGHT times longer to complete an information search and were still significantly less accurate; spent one third more time per page without being informed by it; visited eight times more pages; back-tracked 13 times more often; were four times more likely to revisit a page; and were 13 times more likely to be lost.
claims.source_name: Kodagoda & Wong, 'Effects of Low & High Literacy on User Performance in Information Search and Retrieval', BCS HCI 2008 (DOI 10.14236/ewic/hci2008.17)
claims.why_it_matters: The only quantified low-vs-high literacy comparison I found on an e-government information-seeking task. The direction is unambiguous — exploratory search is catastrophic for low-literacy users — but n=12 total, in the UK, on a kiosk. Directional, not a citable multiplier.

claims.claim: In a before/after redesign of a pharmaceutical website tested double-blind with 50 users, task success for lower-literacy users rose from 46% to 82% while higher-literacy users rose from 68% to 93%; time on task fell from 22.3 min to 9.5 min for lower-literacy users and from 14.3 to 5.1 min for higher-literacy users. Lower-literacy users 'often simply pick the first hit on the list, even if it's not the most appropriate', and 'having to scroll breaks lower-literacy users' visual concentration because they can't use scanning to find the place they left off'.
claims.source_name: Nielsen Norman Group (Jakob Nielsen), 'Lower-Literacy Users: Writing for a Broad Consumer Audience' — study described as conducted by NN/g, sponsored by Pfizer
claims.why_it_matters: Two useful things: (a) simplification helps BOTH groups, so plain design is not a compromise, and (b) low-literacy users cannot re-find their place after scrolling and do not evaluate result lists — they take hit #1. That is a direct argument against ranked search results as the primary navigation.

claims.claim: Rural Indian numeracy, measured on 34,745 youths aged 14-18 across 28 rural districts in 26 states: 25% cannot fluently read a Std II text in their own regional language; only 43.3% can do 3-digit-by-1-digit division; ~85% can measure with a ruler when the scale starts at 0 cm but this collapses to 39% when the starting point is moved; about 50% can calculate elapsed time, add weights, or apply the unitary method. Among the subset who can at least subtract, over 60% manage a budget task, about 37% can apply a percentage discount, and only about 10% can calculate a loan repayment.
claims.figure: 39% ruler with moved origin; 37% discount; 10% interest
claims.source_name: ASER Centre, 'ASER 2023 Beyond Basics' — Main Findings
claims.why_it_matters: This is the numeracy ceiling, measured on the YOUNGEST and most-schooled rural cohort — landowners aged 40-70 will be worse. It says: never ask the user to convert units, apply a percentage, read a value off an offset scale, or compute interest. Present every derived number pre-computed, with its inputs shown separately.

claims.claim: Rural Indian digital baseline, same survey: close to 90% of 14-18-year-olds have a smartphone in the household and know how to use it, but males are more than twice as likely as females to own one (43.7% vs 19.8%). Of those who could bring a smartphone: about 80% could find a specific YouTube video, ~90% of those could share it, 70% could browse the internet to find the answer to a question, about two thirds could set an alarm, and a little over one third could use Google Maps to find travel time between two points.
claims.figure: 90% household access; 70% can browse to find an answer; 43.7% vs 19.8% ownership
claims.source_name: ASER Centre, 'ASER 2023 Beyond Basics' — Main Findings, digital section
claims.why_it_matters: Corrects the canonical literature's 2006-2013 feature-phone baseline. The 2020s reality is high device access, real YouTube/WhatsApp fluency, and a strong gender gap in device OWNERSHIP — which means the phone in the household is often not the landowner's own, reinforcing shared and mediated use.

claims.claim: CAPTCHAs are hard for motivated, literate, paid humans. Across 318,000 CAPTCHA solves from the 21 most popular schemes: image CAPTCHAs took a mean 9.8 s; three independent human solvers agreed on a single answer for only ~71% of image CAPTCHAs (perfect three-way agreement on all schemes just 31% overall, and only 35% for the hardest image scheme). Audio CAPTCHAs took 28.4 s, produced three-way agreement only 31.2% of the time with everyone giving a different answer 33.6% of the time, and had a ~50% give-up rate. Non-native English speakers were slower and less accurate on English-centric schemes.
claims.source_name: Bursztein, Bethard, Fabry, Mitchell & Jurafsky, 'How Good Are Humans at Solving CAPTCHAs? A Large Scale Evaluation', IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2010
claims.why_it_matters: AnyRoR gates legally-public data behind a Latin-alphanumeric CAPTCHA. If literate paid workers disagree ~29% of the time on image CAPTCHAs and non-native English speakers do worse, then for a Gujarati-first user of whom roughly half cannot type a word, the CAPTCHA is not a speed bump, it is the wall. Note the paper also found eBay's real-world eventual success rate was 98.5%, i.e. success comes from RETRIES — which a fragile server-side session destroys.

claims.claim: Intermediated interaction — a digitally skilled person operating the device for or with a non-literate person — is a PREVALENT mode of information access in low-income communities, not an edge case. The ethnography in two Bangalore slums identifies three distinct forms: proximate enabling (the intermediary inputs intent), proximate translation (the intermediary interprets the output), and surrogate usage (both).
claims.source_name: Sambasivan, Cutrell, Toyama & Nardi, 'Intermediated technology use in developing communities', CHI 2010
claims.why_it_matters: The design target is not one person and one phone. It is a landowner plus a son/neighbour/talati/CSC operator around one screen. That changes what 'simple' means: the output must be READ ALOUD-able and hand-off-able, and the input must be delegable.

claims.claim: Collaborative use outperformed solo use in the text-free UI trials: individual subjects averaged 50% (no help feature) and 75% (with help) task completion, while five-person groups averaged 100% in both conditions and were markedly faster (e.g. 1.5 vs 4.5 units of interaction, 5.5 vs 12.6 min on the same task). In individual tests subjects 'appeared nervous and uncomfortable'; groups 'seemed more confident, suggesting ideas to one another'.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007), Tables 1-2 and qualitative section
claims.why_it_matters: Counterintuitive but consistent with the intermediation finding: designing for a single isolated user is designing for the worst-performing configuration. Small samples, so treat as directional.

claims.claim: A consistent, always-available HELP feature was identified as a design element that prior work on illiterate-user UIs had OVERLOOKED, and it measurably improved completion (individual subjects: 50% without help vs 75% with help on the employment task).
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007)
claims.why_it_matters: A persistent spoken help affordance on every screen is a measured intervention, not polish. Cheap to build; contributes a large fraction of achievable completion.

claims.claim: A CLICK-FREE interface (actions triggered by a 3-second hover) was tried and abandoned: novice illiterate subjects were 'as confused by this as experienced PC users'. Hover was retained only for supplementary information (photo reveal, voice on mouse-over), never for the primary action.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Sagar & Toyama, ITID 4(1):37-50 (2007)
claims.why_it_matters: No long-press, swipe-to-reveal, pull-to-refresh or gesture affordances for primary actions. Every action must be a visible tappable target.

claims.claim: Specialised vocabulary fails even in the local language. Because most subjects were unbanked, 'View last transaction', 'Get balance' and 'Change PIN' were 'all alien concepts, in the absence of detailed explanation'. Local-language instruction manuals existed but were 'complex and laden with banking jargon'; most subjects did not even attempt to read them, and 'human mediation was critical for most successful transactions'.
claims.source_name: Medhi et al., ACM TOCHI 18(1) Article 2 (2011); Medhi, Ratan & Toyama, HCII 2009
claims.why_it_matters: Translating 'mutation register', 'khata', 'record of rights' or 'encumbrance' into Gujarati does NOT make them comprehensible. Land-revenue jargon is exactly the banking-jargon case. Every legal term needs a one-sentence spoken gloss in ordinary speech.

claims.claim: Trust in a new digital financial channel was mediated by RECOURSE and by TRUSTED LOCAL HUMANS, not by interface polish. 7 of 30 subjects in the Philippines and 6 of 23 in South Africa were 'concerned about the money transfer not reaching the recipient's phone and were wary about whether it would be possible to RETRACE lost money'. By contrast M-PESA adopters in Kenya trusted the channel 'primarily due to the clear marketing by the provider and the strong pre-existing ties with the local prepaid talktime agents, who sold the new service as a trustworthy channel'.
claims.source_name: Medhi, Ratan & Toyama, 'Mobile-Banking Adoption and Usage by Low-Literate, Low-Income Users in the Developing World', HCI International 2009
claims.why_it_matters: Directly answers the trust question: an official-LOOKING page is not what builds trust. What builds trust is (a) a visible, credible route to fix or dispute a wrong record, and (b) endorsement by a person the user already trusts locally. Design for both explicitly.

claims.claim: In South Asian bureaucracy, authority is carried by the MATERIALITY of the document — signatures, seals, stamps, the parchi (chit), the petition and the physical file — and these graphic artefacts are the mechanism through which citizens make and contest claims, including over land expropriation. Related ethnography frames the state's signature as simultaneously authoritative and forgeable, a paradox that shapes how the poor relate to official papers.
claims.source_name: Matthew S. Hull, 'Government of Paper: The Materiality of Bureaucracy in Urban Pakistan' (UC Press, 2012); Veena Das, 'The Signature of the State: The Paradox of Illegibility' (2004)
claims.why_it_matters: Ethnographic, not experimental — but it is the best-grounded account of WHY a screenshot feels weaker than a stamped paper. Implication: preserve the visual grammar of officialdom (issuing office, record number, date of issue, verification route) rather than stripping it out in the name of minimalism.

claims.claim: Event History Calendar survey methods, which anchor recall on landmark personal events and allow sequential and parallel retrieval across life themes, improve the quality of retrospective reports compared with standard segmented survey questions, because they mirror the hierarchical/thematic structure of autobiographical memory.
claims.source_name: Robert F. Belli, 'The Structure of Autobiographical Memory and the Event History Calendar', Memory 6(4) (DOI 10.1080/741942610)
claims.why_it_matters: The strongest indirect support for a chronology feature — but only in a specific form: anchored on remembered life events, not on abstract dates. It says a timeline works if each entry can be pegged to something the user lived through ('the year of your father's death', 'when the canal came'), and works poorly as a bare list of dates.

claims.claim: An audio-visual social feed ordered reverse-chronologically on an infinite-scroll page was used successfully by low-literate farmers: over four months 306 farmers registered through the phones of eight agricultural mediators, making 514 posts and 180 replies, including multi-turn conversations. Usage was mediated throughout — all access was through the extension workers' phones.
claims.source_name: Medhi-Thies, Ferreira, Gupta, O'Neill & Cutrell, 'KrishiPustak: A Social Networking System for Low-Literate Farmers', CSCW 2015
claims.why_it_matters: The only field evidence I found that low-literate Indian farmers will consume a newest-first ordered list of dated items. It supports the chronology bet — but note the items were audio/photo, one per card, and access was mediated. It is not evidence that a reverse-chron TABLE of text works.

claims.claim: Design rules extracted from an 11-week IVR deployment in rural India: prompts recorded in the local accent with slow clear diction; every possible action explained BEFORE the corresponding key press; keys given consistent meanings across all menus; multi-digit inputs avoided as much as possible; and invalid inputs answered with explanatory error messages rather than rejection.
claims.source_name: Vashistha, Cutrell, Borriello & Thies, 'Sangeet Swara: A Community-Moderated Voice Forum in Rural India', CHI 2015
claims.why_it_matters: Transfers straight to any voice/IVR fallback channel for a land-records service, and the 'explain the action before requiring it' and 'same control means the same thing everywhere' rules transfer to the touch UI too.

claims.claim: The widely-repeated figure that '30% of Web users have low literacy' is Jakob Nielsen's own estimate, extrapolated from a US adult-literacy survey statistic ('43% of the U.S. population has low literacy'), and is projected forward without a study behind the projection.
claims.source_name: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Lower-Literacy Users: Writing for a Broad Consumer Audience'
claims.why_it_matters: Flagged per the rigour requirement: this number circulates in UX writing as if measured. Do not cite it. The underlying NAAL 43% figure is real and US-specific; the web-user extrapolation is not.

design_rules.rule: Do NOT replace the five chained dropdowns with a search box as the primary path. Replace them with a FLAT, PAGED, TAPPABLE LIST at each level, and collapse the five levels to at most two decisions before results. Keep a search box only as a secondary accelerator for literate users and intermediaries.
design_rules.rationale: Typing is the binding constraint: 24 of 50 mobile users could not type a single word (Medhi TOCHI 2011). And low-literacy users who do search take the first hit without evaluating it (NN/g) and get lost 13x more often on exploratory search (Kodagoda & Wong). But hierarchy is equally fatal — a 4-level text-free hierarchy dropped low-literacy accuracy to 40% vs 91% (CHI 2013), and on a phone a 7-page flat list beat a 4-level hierarchy 100% vs 80% correct and 25 s vs 65.5 s (INTERACT 2013). Flat browse is the only option both bodies of evidence endorse.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The near-universal modern UX instinct that a single search box is the accessible, low-friction replacement for a cascade of dropdowns. For this population it swaps one failure mode (hierarchy) for a worse one (text entry).

design_rules.rule: Make the SURVEY NUMBER the one thing the user is ever asked to type, and give it a numeric keypad, never a text field.
design_rules.rationale: Digits are the single symbol system this population reads and enters reliably: 'subjects could easily recognize numerals' and were 'comfortable typing the digits' while unable to type words or even locate * and # (Medhi ITID 2007, TOCHI 2011); on SMS receipts 'almost all could identify the numbers and what they meant' even when the surrounding English was unreadable.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Generic 'search everything' inputs that accept names, villages and numbers in one box — which forces the keyboard into alphabetic mode and immediately excludes half the users.

design_rules.rule: Persist the user's district/taluka/village after the first successful lookup and make the second visit start at the survey-number step. Traverse the geography hierarchy ONCE, ever.
design_rules.rationale: Every unit of navigation is disproportionately expensive here (8x time, 8x pages visited, 13x more likely to be lost for low-literacy users — Kodagoda & Wong), and skill does not transfer between screens or handsets (23 of 34 subjects who succeeded on their own handset failed on a different one — TOCHI 2011). The cheapest navigation is the navigation you delete.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Stateless government portals that require the full cascade on every visit, and the privacy-by-default instinct to store nothing locally.

design_rules.rule: Never render a land record as a table or matrix. Explode every row into a one-fact-per-line labelled statement, and every mutation into its own card.
design_rules.rationale: A matrix of checks and crosses 'was not readily understood' and had to be replaced with explicit one-to-one associations (Medhi ITID 2007). Separately, users could read the numbers on a receipt but 'still had difficulty with receipts indicating MULTIPLE transactions' (TOCHI 2011). A VF-7 or VF-12 extract is exactly a multi-row matrix.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The fidelity instinct — 'reproduce the official extract layout so it looks authentic' — and the data-viz instinct that a dense table lets users compare rows at a glance.

design_rules.rule: Put a spoken Gujarati voice-over on every screen and every field, replayable on tap, before you spend any effort optimising icon style.
design_rules.rationale: In the 200-subject controlled comparison, adding voice annotation moved mean comprehension from 2.65-7.35 out of 13 up to 9.30-9.75 out of 13 across ALL visual styles, and cut response time by about 30%. The spread between the best and worst image style once audio was present was 0.45 out of 13 — under half a question. Audio is worth roughly ten times what the graphic choice is worth.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Standard design-effort allocation, which spends heavily on illustration/iconography and treats audio as an accessibility afterthought. Here the ratio is inverted.

design_rules.rule: Let audio carry the explanation and the screen carry the number. Keep on-screen text to short labels; do not narrate a wall of text while displaying it.
design_rules.rationale: Some subjects 'were unable to fully process the bimodal stimulus' and attended to either the graphic or the audio but not both; totally illiterate subjects 'listened intently to the audio cue, and ignored the on-screen text completely' (Medhi WWW 2007). Redundant simultaneous channels are not additive for this population.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The accessibility convention that every visual element should have a matching, complete audio equivalent presented at the same time.

design_rules.rule: Do not treat a user repeating the prompt back as evidence of comprehension. Verify understanding with a concrete confirmation question ('is this your land?') rather than an acknowledgement.
design_rules.rationale: Medhi et al. observed that 'some subjects quickly learned to mimic the voice annotation without thoroughly understanding what was being said or depicted' — notably in the text+voice condition where they did not know the term but repeated it (WWW 2007).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Usability-test practice that scores a task as passed when the participant produces the right utterance or taps the right control.

design_rules.rule: Never require scrolling to discover that content exists. Paginate with an explicit, large, labelled Next/Previous control, and put every required action above the fold.
design_rules.rationale: 48 of 90 subjects did not understand vertical scrollbars and 'did not realise that there were functions beneath what was displayed' (TOCHI 2011), and 'avoid menus that require scrolling' is one of the eight formal design recommendations from that ethnography. NN/g independently reports that scrolling 'breaks lower-literacy users' visual concentration because they can't use scanning to find the place they left off'. Meanwhile a 7-page paged list outperformed a hierarchy (INTERACT 2013), so paging costs nothing.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Mobile-first orthodoxy that infinite scroll is natural and pagination is legacy. For a long ownership history in particular, infinite scroll is the wrong container.

design_rules.rule: One decision per screen, zero nested menus, and a Back control that sits in the same place on every screen with a spoken label.
design_rules.rationale: Participants 'did not seem to understand the concept of nesting, that the top graphic in a hierarchy represented a group of pages, or that selecting items corresponded to progress' and, once down a wrong branch, 'did not remember how to navigate back to higher levels' despite video instruction (CHI 2013, INTERACT 2013). Sangeet Swara's field-tested rule is that keys have consistent meanings across ALL menus (CHI 2015).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Progressive disclosure and information-architecture grouping, which are normally taken to REDUCE cognitive load. The evidence says grouping is itself the load.

design_rules.rule: Show numeric progress ('2 of 4') using digits, not a dots-and-bars progress indicator.
design_rules.rationale: Digits are reliably read (Medhi ITID 2007; TOCHI 2011) while abstract graphical conventions are not — animated directional arrows were not understood until replaced by literal car icons (ITID 2007).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Minimal progress dots and unlabelled step indicators, which are standard in modern wizards.

design_rules.rule: Design for two people around one phone. Make every result read-aloud-able in one pass, hand-off-able to a helper, and shareable to WhatsApp as a self-contained image/PDF plus an audio summary.
design_rules.rationale: Intermediated interaction is a prevalent mode, in three named forms (Sambasivan et al. CHI 2010). In the text-free UI trials, five-person groups reached 100% task completion vs 50-75% for individuals, and did so 2-3x faster (Medhi ITID 2007). ASER 2023 shows household smartphone access at ~90% but female ownership at 19.8% vs 43.7% male — the device is often not the landowner's own.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The single-user mental model behind almost all consumer UX, and privacy-first designs that make sharing or reading over someone's shoulder deliberately hard.

design_rules.rule: Remove the CAPTCHA from the citizen path entirely. Move abuse control server-side (rate limiting, signed session tokens, proof-of-work, or an authenticated bulk tier for professionals).
design_rules.rationale: Three human solvers agreed on a single answer for only ~71% of image CAPTCHAs and it took literate paid workers 9.8 s each; audio CAPTCHAs took 28.4 s with only 31.2% three-way agreement and a ~50% give-up rate; non-native English speakers were slower and less accurate on English-centric schemes (Bursztein et al. 2010). Layered on a population of whom ~half cannot type a word (TOCHI 2011), and on data that is legally public, a Latin-alphanumeric CAPTCHA is a categorical exclusion, not friction.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The standard government-IT assumption that a CAPTCHA is a cheap, neutral anti-scraping measure. It is neither cheap nor neutral, and it is being applied to public data.

design_rules.rule: If any challenge must remain, make it survivable across retries: never invalidate a session, never rotate the challenge on re-render, and always allow an unlimited, instant retry with the previous answers preserved.
design_rules.rationale: Bursztein et al. found eBay's real-world eventual success rate was 98.5% despite per-attempt human agreement near 71% — i.e. in the field, success comes from RETRIES. A fragile server-side session that discards the user's cascade selections on a failed attempt converts a recoverable error into abandonment.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Security hardening that expires or rotates a challenge on every failure, which is correct against bots and catastrophic against a slow, semi-literate human.

design_rules.rule: Build the ownership timeline — but as a vertical stack of one-mutation-per-card, newest first, each card a full spoken sentence with the year in digits, and never more than one event visible per card.
design_rules.rationale: This is the honest verdict on the chronology bet. Direct evidence is thin, and the closest measurement is NEGATIVE for the dense form: users could read the numbers but 'still had difficulty with receipts indicating multiple transactions' (TOCHI 2011). But the card form is supported: KrishiPustak's newest-first audio-visual feed was used by 306 low-literate farmers over four months (CSCW 2015), and matrices specifically failed while explicit one-to-one associations worked (ITID 2007). So chronological ORDER is fine; chronological TABLES are not.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The instinct to visualise history as a horizontal timeline axis, a Gantt-like band, or a sortable table of mutation entries. All three are matrix/axis forms with no supporting evidence for this population.

design_rules.rule: Anchor each history event to something the user lived through, not only to a date: '1998 — 27 years ago — when the land passed to your father'. Where the record supports it, name the relationship, not the legal instrument.
design_rules.rationale: Event History Calendar research shows that anchoring on landmark personal events, with sequential and parallel retrieval across life themes, improves retrospective recall over segmented date-based questions, because it mirrors autobiographical memory structure (Belli 1998). Separately, only ~50% of rural 14-18-year-olds can calculate elapsed time (ASER 2023), so 'how long ago' must be computed FOR the user.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Records-fidelity design that presents the mutation date and entry number as the primary identifiers because that is what the register holds.

design_rules.rule: Never ask the user to convert a unit, apply a percentage, read a value off an offset scale, or compute interest. Pre-compute every derived figure and show its two inputs as separate, labelled, spoken numbers beside it.
design_rules.rationale: ASER 2023, on the youngest and most-schooled rural cohort: ruler reading collapses from ~85% to 39% when the scale's starting point moves; only about 50% can apply the unitary method; among those who can at least subtract, only ~37% can apply a percentage discount and ~10% can compute a loan repayment. A 40-70-year-old landowner is on the wrong side of these numbers.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Interactive unit-toggle widgets and calculators, which look like empowerment but are exactly the operation the evidence says fails.

design_rules.rule: Print the customary unit AND the official metric side by side, each with its own digits and its own spoken label, and state the customary unit's local basis in words beside the number (e.g. '16.4 vigha (at 20 guntha)' / '1.66 hectare').
design_rules.rationale: Numerals are read reliably (ITID 2007, TOCHI 2011) but conversions are not performed reliably (ASER 2023). Since the vigha varies by region, an unlabelled customary figure is not merely imprecise — it is a number the user cannot check. I found NO study measuring comprehension of customary vs metric land units among Indian farmers, so this rule is derived, not measured.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Metrication policy and the tidy-design instinct to pick one canonical unit. Both discard the unit the user actually thinks in.

design_rules.rule: Never present a rupee valuation (area x jantri rate) without showing the area and the rate as two separate spoken numbers, and labelling the result explicitly as a stamp-duty floor rather than a market value.
design_rules.rationale: Only ~10% of the ASER 2023 cohort could compute a loan repayment and ~37% a discount, so the multiplication cannot be reproduced or checked by the user. Combined with the finding that specialised financial vocabulary is 'alien' even in the local language (TOCHI 2011), an unexplained rupee figure will be read as an authoritative valuation.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Product instinct to surface a single headline 'your land is worth X' number as the hook.

design_rules.rule: Gloss every legal and revenue term in ordinary spoken Gujarati at first use. Translating 'mutation register' or 'record of rights' into Gujarati is not sufficient.
design_rules.rationale: 'View last transaction', 'Get balance' and 'Change PIN' were 'all alien concepts, in the absence of detailed explanation' among unbanked subjects, and local-language manuals 'laden with banking jargon' went unread (TOCHI 2011). Land-revenue vocabulary is the same case. Medical terms behaved similarly — some were more recognisable in English than in a formal Hindi translation.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The assumption that vernacular localisation solves comprehension. Register matters more than language.

design_rules.rule: Open first-time use with a short, concrete, dramatised video showing a person like the user getting their own extract and what they then do with it — not a feature tour.
design_rules.rationale: 100% (20/20) of subjects with no prior graphical-UI exposure completed the task on the graphical UI, and post-trial interviews credited the 'full-context video' — which included dramatisations of what the service was and how one would register and use it — with better understanding of the concept than an equivalent verbal explanation (Medhi CHI 2009 / TOCHI 2011). Conversely, when instruction was abstract, participants failed to transfer it: 'But that was about animals and birds, and this is about clothes and TV sets' (CHI 2013).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Onboarding orthodoxy that favours short interactive coach-marks over video, and that teaches the interface rather than the scenario.

design_rules.rule: Put a persistent, identically-placed, spoken HELP control on every screen, and make invalid input produce an explanatory spoken message rather than a rejection.
design_rules.rationale: The consistent help feature was singled out as an element prior work had overlooked, and individual completion rose from 50% without it to 75% with it (Medhi ITID 2007). Sangeet Swara's deployed rule set likewise requires explanatory error messages on invalid input and explaining an action BEFORE requiring it (CHI 2015).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Contemporary minimalism that hides help behind an overflow menu or assumes a self-evident interface needs none.

design_rules.rule: Every primary action must be a large, visible, tappable target. No hover, long-press, swipe-to-reveal, pull-to-refresh or gesture affordances.
design_rules.rationale: A click-free hover interface was built and abandoned because novice illiterate subjects were 'as confused by this as experienced PC users'; hover was retained only for supplementary information, never for primary actions (Medhi ITID 2007). Soft keys — controls whose meaning changes with context — defeated 45 of 90 subjects (TOCHI 2011), and gestures are the touchscreen equivalent of a soft key.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Modern mobile gesture vocabulary, which is treated as learned and universal.

design_rules.rule: Field-test every icon with actual Gujarati village users before shipping it, and give each icon a spoken label as its ground truth. Prefer semi-abstract line drawings over photographs.
design_rules.rationale: Icons failed in unforeseeable ways: a 'house' read as a village hut; roads 'can never be yellow'; abstract traffic arrows unintelligible until replaced by car icons; start/end times read backwards by right-to-left readers until an explicit arrow was added (ITID 2007). And in the controlled 200-subject test, photographs were the WORST-performing image type without audio (5.45/13 vs 7.35 for animation and 5.95 for hand-drawing).
design_rules.conflicts_with: The widespread belief that a photograph is the most universally legible representation, and that a well-known icon set can be adopted without testing.

design_rules.rule: Reproduce the official marks of the paper extract — issuing office, record/entry number, date of issue, a scannable verification code, and a signature/seal block — rather than stripping them out in the name of clean design. Make the shareable artefact look like the document the user already trusts.
design_rules.rationale: South Asian bureaucratic authority is carried by the materiality of the document: signatures, seals, stamps, the parchi and the file (Hull 2012; Das 2004). This is ethnographic rather than experimental, but it is corroborated by the CAM result — where a paper workflow was already ingrained, a paper-plus-phone hybrid achieved <=1% error (cited in TOCHI 2011).
design_rules.conflicts_with: Modern minimalist e-government design, which removes seals, ornate borders and reference numbers as visual noise. Here they are the trust-bearing content.

design_rules.rule: Build trust through RECOURSE and LOCAL ENDORSEMENT, not through official-looking chrome: a visible 'this record is wrong — here is exactly what to do' path naming the office, the form and the person, plus material the local talati / CSC operator / sarpanch can vouch for.
design_rules.rationale: Non-adopters' stated fear was specifically about traceability — 'whether it would be possible to retrace lost money' — while M-PESA's adoption was attributed to clear marketing plus 'strong pre-existing ties with the local prepaid talktime agents, who sold the new service as a trustworthy channel' (Medhi, Ratan & Toyama, HCII 2009). Trust came from the human network and from recourse, not the screen.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The product assumption that trust is a visual-design and copywriting problem solved by security badges and testimonials.

design_rules.rule: Budget for a staffed human fallback channel — a phone number a user or an intermediary can call to have the lookup done for them — and present it as part of the architecture, not as a failure.
design_rules.rationale: The live-operator interface was about TEN times more accurate than users entering data themselves: 0.5% error vs 4.2% (electronic forms) and 4.5% (SMS), which caused the research partners to switch their deployment plan to operators, noting call-centre cost-effectiveness in India (TOCHI 2011, Experiment 2). And 'human mediation was critical for most successful transactions' in the ethnography.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Self-service-first product thinking, and the assumption that a helpline is a cost centre indicating design failure. The measurement says it is the most accurate interface available.

design_rules.rule: Offer an entry path that starts from the paper the user already holds: photograph the existing 7/12 extract, read the survey number from it, and skip the cascade entirely.
design_rules.rationale: CAM's barcoded paper-plus-phone hybrid achieved error rates of 1% or below with users lacking prior camera or computer experience trained to comfort in 5-15 minutes, and the authors explicitly flag this as the right design point 'in cases where paper forms are already ingrained into the workflow' (cited in TOCHI 2011). Nothing is more ingrained in this workflow than the paper 7/12.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Digital-transformation framing that treats the elimination of paper as the goal rather than paper as the highest-accuracy input device available.

design_rules.rule: Use audio OUTPUT liberally; never make speech RECOGNITION the only input path. Where a voice channel is offered, use numbered keypad selection.
design_rules.rationale: The evidence is genuinely contradictory (Patel 2009: dialed beats speech; Grover 2009: comparable but dialed preferred; Sherwani 2009: speech beats touch-tone), but the two studies conducted with GUJARAT FARMERS specifically both favour numeric input: dialed input gave significantly higher completion, especially for those with less than eighth-grade education (Patel CHI 2009, n=45), and across a 7-month deployment with 51 Gujarat farmers 'users preferr[ed] numeric input over speech' (Avaaj Otalo, CHI 2010).
design_rules.conflicts_with: The strong contemporary intuition — reinforced by voice assistants and by Indian-language voice-search marketing — that speech input is THE accessibility answer for non-literate users. In the population closest to this project it lost.

design_rules.rule: Instrument and publish your own funnel: step-level drop-off, retry counts, time-to-first-record, and helpline volume. Do not claim an abandonment improvement you have not measured.
design_rules.rationale: I could find no published abandonment or funnel data for AnyRoR or any Indian land-records portal, and the canonical completion-rate literature is 2006-2015, on feature phones and PCs, with sample sizes between 12 and 90. ASER 2023 shows a materially different 2020s baseline (~90% household smartphone access, 70% able to browse to find an answer), so pre-2015 completion rates should be treated as lower bounds, not as your predicted numbers.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The hackathon temptation to quote a 20-year-old lab completion rate as if it were your product's measured before/after.

gaps: NO study found that directly tests a TIMELINE or chronology visualisation with low-literate users. The chronology recommendation is assembled from three indirect sources: a negative result on dense multi-record displays (multi-transaction receipts were hard, TOCHI 2011), a positive field result on newest-first one-item-per-card audio feeds (KrishiPustak, CSCW 2015), and survey-methodology research on landmark-anchored recall (Belli 1998). Treat the timeline as a testable hypothesis, not an evidence-backed feature, and put it in front of five real users before you build it out.

NO evidence found on comprehension of GUJARATI NUMERALS. Every 'non-literate people can read numbers' finding in this literature refers to Indo-Arabic digits 0-9. AnyRoR renders Gujarati digits. Whether a semi-literate Gujarati farmer reads 900 as fluently as it is an untested assumption sitting under my strongest design rule. Show both, and test it.

NO study found measuring comprehension of customary Indian land units (vigha, bigha, guntha) versus metric among farmers. The unit rule is derived from general numeracy data (ASER 2023), not from a measurement of unit comprehension.

Jan Chipchase's non-literacy field work could NOT be verified to a primary source. His personal site's PDFs are 404 and the Internet Archive was returning 503 during this research. Its existence and topic are attested by a citation in Medhi et al. TOCHI 2011 ('work that looks beyond the UI at coping mechanisms of illiterate and semi-literate users' — Chipchase 2005, 2006), but I could not retrieve a single figure. Any specific statistic attributed to Chipchase should be treated as unsourced until the primary is obtained.

SEARCH-vs-BROWSE evidence in an INDIC SCRIPT is essentially absent. I found no study of query typing, spelling errors, transliteration errors, or autocomplete behaviour by low-literate users in Gujarati, Hindi or any Indian script. The typing evidence I rely on (24/50 could not type a word) is from feature-phone SMS in 2009-2011, not from a 2020s Android soft keyboard with predictive text, transliteration and voice dictation. This is the single weakest link in an otherwise strong argument, and it is the link my central design decision rests on.

Kodagoda & Wong's dramatic multipliers (8x time, 13x lost) come from n=6 low-literacy vs n=6 high-literacy users on a UK kiosk. Directionally consistent with everything else, but not a citable statistic.

The NN/g lower-literacy figures (46%->82% success) come from a study described as NN/g's own, sponsored by Pfizer, with no peer-reviewed methodology published; it overlaps in sponsor and period with Summers & Summers' two-year Pfizer-funded study (ASIST 2005). I could not disentangle whose data it is. Cite it as an industry redesign study, not as a controlled experiment. NN/g's related claim that '30% of Web users have low literacy' is an unsourced extrapolation and should not be cited at all.

NO published abandonment-rate or funnel data exists for AnyRoR or, as far as I could find, for any Indian land-records portal. There is no baseline to claim an improvement against. Anyone quoting an AnyRoR drop-off percentage is inventing it.

The full text of three directly relevant papers was PAYWALLED and only their abstracts could be obtained: Patel et al. CHI 2009 (speech vs dialed, 45 Gujarat farmers), Patel et al. CHI 2010 (Avaaj Otalo), and Sherwani et al. ICTD 2009 (speech vs touch-tone). The claims from these are the authors' own abstracts, so the direction is reliable, but I do not have their effect sizes or confidence intervals.

The speech-vs-keypad question is UNRESOLVED in the literature — three concurrent 2009 studies reached three different conclusions, as Medhi et al. themselves note. Do not present either side as settled.

Almost the entire canonical evidence base predates the smartphone era for this population (2006-2015, feature phones, styluses, Tablet PCs, soft keys). ASER 2023 shows ~90% household smartphone access and 70% of rural 14-18-year-olds able to browse the internet to answer a question. Nobody has re-run the Medhi hierarchy or scrolling experiments on a WhatsApp-fluent 2020s rural Indian user. The direction of the findings is very likely to hold; the magnitudes almost certainly do not.

NO evidence found on how slow or intermittent connectivity specifically affects abandonment among low-literate users (as distinct from users in general), which matters for a portal whose incumbent depends on fragile server-side sessions.

NO evidence found on legibility thresholds (font size, weight, contrast, line length) for Gujarati script with older, low-vision rural readers. Latin-script accessibility guidance may not transfer to a script with dense conjuncts and a shirorekha-free but diacritic-heavy form.

THREE CLAIMS WILL NOT SURVIVE SCRUTINY AND SHOULD BE PULLED OR REWRITTEN BEFORE PUBLICATION:

1. Claim 7 is the dangerous one. "48.8% of women in Gujarat have ever used the internet — among the five lowest states" is wrong twice over. 48.8% is TRIPURA's figure in NFHS-6, quoted in the very FACTLY article cited (published 3 July 2026) as the LOWEST state. Gujarat's NFHS-5 figure is 30.8% (NFHS-5 Table 3.7, FR375 p.104), and Gujarat is roughly 11th-lowest of 36 states/UTs, not fifth. Worse, the whole framing is superseded: the cited article exists precisely to report that women's ever-use of the internet rose from 33.3% (NFHS-5) to 64.3% (NFHS-6), and rural women's from 24.6% to 58.6%. Citing "fewer than 3 in 10 rural women have ever used the internet" from an article whose headline is "Women's Internet Use Nearly Doubles" is the kind of error that discredits an entire argument.

2. Claim 11 (PRS/DILRMP) is quoted with perfect accuracy but the figures are labelled in PRS's own Table 1 as "data updated till September 2017". They are nine years old and DILRMP has since replaced its whole MIS (MIS 4.0, launched 15 Oct 2024). Any of these numbers presented as today's picture invites an immediate, fatal correction.

3. Claim 10 inherits a garble from Vidhi. The NCAER primary data (via Ideas for India, 6 Aug 2018) shows OWNERSHIP variation of 34% in rural Shimla and 6% in Baddi — and separately POSSESSION variation of 38% and 60%. Fusing them into "ownership-and-possession discrepancies of 34% and 6%" makes Baddi look nine times better than it was. Sample sizes are also tiny (100 parcels in HP, 102 in Maharashtra) and never mentioned.

TWO SMALLER TRAPS: Claim 3 contains a quoted phrase — "expediters who understand the system" — that does not appear anywhere in the Benjamin et al. paper (I grepped the full text; the only hit for any form of "expedite" is an unrelated table cell). Claim 2 rests partly on an arithmetic impossibility in the source: Article 14's "2.58 lakh sq km" of rural Gujarat surveyed exceeds Gujarat's entire geographical area (~1.96 lakh sq km), and the Rs 370 crore is the reporter's own extrapolation from a single Vadodara contract rate, not a measured spend.

THE STRONGEST MATERIAL, safe to lean on: the Jitendra Singh judgment (claim 1, verbatim and good law), Toyama 2011 (claim 4, every phrase verbatim including "the greater one's capacity, the more technology delivers" and the "appropriate design / participatory design / human-centered design" banners under the "Myth of Scale" heading), Agarwal et al. 2021 (claim 6, all four numbers verbatim — just say "rural landowning households across nine states, 2014"), and the Pulitzer Center Andhra reporting (claim 12).

ONE USEFUL PRIMARY FIND for the project itself: the AnyRoR free view does carry an explicit disclaimer, in Gujarati, on every VF-7/integrated page — "અહીં દર્શાવેલ જમીનની વિગતો ફક્ત આપની જાણ માટે જ છે જેને સત્તાવાર નકલ તરીકે ગણવામાં આવશે નહી" ("the land details shown here are for your information only and will not be treated as an official copy"). That is a real, quotable primary source, and it is stronger than the invented "not accepted for court, registration or banking" wording. I found it in this repo's own saved scrape at /home/kirtan/Desktop/projects/irmsc/output/43/anyror_43.html and confirmed the live portal at https://anyror.gujarat.gov.in/LandRecordRural.aspx. verdicts.claim: Supreme Court held mutation entry 'does not confer any right, title or interest' and is 'only for the fiscal purpose'; title must be decided by a civil court before mutation follows — Jitendra Singh v. State of MP (SC, 6 Sept 2021)
verdicts.reasoning: Opened the judgment at the cited Indian Kanoon URL and confirmed the case (Jitendra Singh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh, SC Civil Appellate Jurisdiction, bench M.R. Shah and Aniruddha Bose, 6 September 2021). The passages are verbatim: 'mutation entry does not confer any right, title or interest in favour of the person and the mutation entry in the revenue record is only for the fiscal purpose'; 'Entries in the revenue records or jamabandi have only fiscal purpose, i.e., payment of land revenue, and no ownership is conferred'; 'so far as the title of the property is concerned, it can only be decided by a competent civil court'; and on the sequence, the party claiming title 'has to approach the appropriate civil court... and only thereafter on the basis of the decision before the civil court necessary mutation entry can be made'. One nuance worth knowing if challenged: this judgment is an authoritative restatement, not the origin. The proposition runs back through Sawarni v. Inder Kaur (1996), Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh and Bhimabai Mahadeo Kambekar (2013), which the Court itself relies on. That strengthens rather than weakens the citation — it is settled law, not one bench's view. Safe to quote directly.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors., Supreme Court of India, Civil Appeal decided 06.09.2021 — https://indiankanoon.org/doc/104309066/ (the cited URL IS the primary source)

verdicts.claim: Gujarat rural re-survey 2009–2018 covering ~93% of rural Gujarat (2.58 lakh sq km) halted Aug 2018 after ~12,000 of 18,501 villages promulgated; 5.28 lakh survey numbers with complaints by Dec 2021; 1.68 lakh verification applications 2020–21, 90,000+ disposed by March 2022; officials estimated 15–20% of landowners approached offices for corrections; state cost ~Rs 370 crore vs union allocation Rs 54.66 crore
verdicts.reasoning: I pulled the full Article 14 piece (Prudhviraj Rupavath, 9 Dec 2022). Most of it holds exactly: 'records were promulgated in about 12,000 of the total 18,501 villages'; the August 2018 halt; the reliance on old maps instead of the contractually mandated DGPS/ETS (sourced to an anonymous district superintendent of land records); '5.28 lakh survey numbers' (revenue minister Rajendra Trivedi to local media, Dec 2021); '1.68 lakh applications' between 2020 and 2021 with 'more than 90,000... disposed of' (assembly reply, March 2022); and Rs 54.66 crore union allocation, which came from the reporter's own RTI reply — the strongest number in the piece. But two elements will not survive a hostile reading. First, the 15–20% figure is misdescribed. The article attributes it to KP Goswami, one government surveyor at the Ahmedabad district land records office, saying 'about 15-20% of landowners with grievances had approached his office for corrections' — one office, one man's impression, and a percentage of aggrieved landowners, not of landowners generally. Second, the cost figure is built on an impossible number: 2.58 lakh sq km exceeds Gujarat's entire geographical area (~1.96 lakh sq km), and the Rs 370 crore is the reporter's explicit extrapolation ('presuming this rate to have been matched in other deals') from a single 2012 Vadodara contract at Rs 14,295 per sq km. That is a back-of-envelope estimate resting on an area larger than the state. Anyone checking will find it in thirty seconds.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Gujarat's rural re-survey (2009–2018) was halted in August 2018 after records had been promulgated in about 12,000 of the state's 18,501 villages, following mass complaints. Gujarat's revenue minister told local media in December 2021 that complaints had been raised against 5.28 lakh survey numbers, and told the assembly in March 2022 that of 1.68 lakh verification applications received in 2020–21, more than 90,000 had been disposed of. An RTI reply obtained by Article 14 showed the union government allocated Rs 54.66 crore to Gujarat for the resurvey under DILRMP between 2012-13 and 2020-21, with the bulk of the cost borne by the state. Drop the 15–20% figure, or state it precisely as one Ahmedabad district surveyor's estimate of the share of aggrieved landowners who had approached his office. Drop the Rs 370 crore / 2.58 lakh sq km figures entirely — they are a journalist's extrapolation from one district contract, and the area exceeds Gujarat's total geographical area.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Article 14 is itself secondary throughout: the headline numbers are ministerial statements to the Gujarat assembly and to local media, Dec 2021 and March 2022. The only primary document is the RTI reply on the Rs 54.66 crore union allocation, reproduced in the piece. https://tribe.article-14.com/post/how-gujarat-s-rural-land-digitisation-programme-was-botched-starting-a-fresh-trail-of-land-litigation--63929cdfce158

verdicts.claim: Benjamin et al. (2007) found Bhoomi increased corruption and bribery, substantially increased transaction time, and let very large players capture vast quantities of land, via centralisation away from villages; poorer users could not afford the 'expediters who understand the system'; electronic access often slower than paper due to computer malfunction and power cuts
verdicts.reasoning: I read the full CASUM-m working paper (Benjamin, Bhuvaneswari, Rajan, Manjunatha, January 2007). The three headline findings are verbatim in the abstract: 'the digitization of land records led to increased corruption, much more bribes and substantially increased time taken for land transactions. At another level, it facilitated very large players in the land markets to capture vast quantities of land... These consequences have come about via the centralization of both land records and management away from the village panchayat to the district level.' The slowness claim is also supported in the body: mutation went from '2-3 days' pre-Bhoomi to '3-4 months', and farmers visiting the taluk office 'may find that either the computer is down or that there is a power cut'. Two problems. First, the quoted phrase 'expediters who understand the system' does not appear in this paper. I searched the full text; the only occurrence of any form of 'expedite' is an unrelated table cell about expediting a change of records. Publishing that as a quotation from this paper is a misattribution waiting to be found. The paper's actual supporting sentence is that 'poorer people are discouraged from applying for copies of their titles due to the increased bribes, uncertainty, and time taken', in a process 'dominated by a network and system of various agents who have set a market rate'. Second, this is an unrefereed self-published working paper using ethnographic methods, and its central finding is directly contested. The Princeton ISS case study of the same programme, which I also read, concludes 'Corruption decreased and customer service improved.' Presenting Benjamin as settled fact rather than as one contested study invites an easy rebuttal. The fourth author is Manjunatha, not Manjunath.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Solomon Benjamin and colleagues, in a 2007 ethnographic working paper, argued against the consensus that Karnataka's Bhoomi digitisation had increased corruption and bribery, substantially increased the time taken for land transactions (mutations going from 2–3 days to 3–4 months), and helped very large players capture land in Bangalore's booming periphery — all through the centralisation of records away from the village panchayat to the taluk and district level. Poorer farmers, they found, were 'discouraged from applying for copies of their titles due to the increased bribes, uncertainty, and time taken', in a process dominated by paid agents who had set a market rate. Drop the phrase 'expediters who understand the system' — it is not in the paper. Frame the whole finding as a contested minority position: the Princeton ISS case study of the same programme reached the opposite conclusion.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Benjamin, S., Bhuvaneswari, R., Rajan, P. & Manjunatha (January 2007), 'Bhoomi: E-Governance, Or, An Anti-Politics Machine Necessary to Globalize Bangalore?', CASUM-m Working Paper — an unrefereed working paper. The Semantic Scholar link in the citation is only a bibliographic record, not the paper.

verdicts.claim: Toyama's amplification thesis: technology magnifies existing institutional intent and capacity; three mechanisms (differential access, capacity, motivation); 'the greater one's capacity, the more technology delivers... technology helps the rich get proportionately richer, thus widening, not narrowing, the gaps'; names 'appropriate design', 'participatory design', 'human-centered design' under the 'myth of scale'
verdicts.reasoning: I extracted the full text of the cited PDF and every element checks out verbatim. Section 3: 'technology is merely a magnifier of underlying human and institutional intent and capacity'. Abstract: 'Three mechanisms for amplification are identified, arising out of differentials in access, capacity, and motivation', with sections 3.1.1 Differential Access, 3.1.2 Differential Capacity, 3.1.3 Differential Motivation. Section 3.1: 'The greater one's capacity, the more technology delivers; conversely, the lesser one's capacity, the less value technology has. In effect, technology helps the rich get proportionately richer, thus widening, not narrowing, the gaps between rich and poor.' Section 3.2 'The Myth of Scale': believers 'charge in under the banners of appropriate design, participatory design, human-centered design, all in the unshakeable belief that the design of the technology or the larger socio-technical system is what matters.' One small precision worth keeping: Toyama says 'human and institutional intent and capacity', not institutional alone — and he is explicit that 'technology cannot substitute for human intent or capacity where it is lacking'. This is the cleanest claim in the set.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Minor precision only: Toyama describes technology as 'a magnifier of underlying human AND institutional intent and capacity'. Keeping 'human' in matters, because the mechanism he describes runs through individual capacity as much as institutional capacity.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Kentaro Toyama, 'Technology as Amplifier in International Development', Proceedings of the 2011 iConference, ACM — https://www.kentarotoyama.org/papers/Toyama%202011%20iConference%20-%20Technology%20as%20Amplifier.pdf (the cited URL IS the primary source)

verdicts.claim: Heeks: ~35% of e-government projects in developing/transitional countries are total failures, ~50% partial failures, ~15% succeed, attributed to design–reality gaps
verdicts.reasoning: The figures are real and correctly attributed, but the cited URL is the wrong page and the claim carries no date, which is where it will break. The cited page (egov4dev.org/success/evaluation/) contains no such statistics — it is about evaluation methods. The figures live at egov4dev.org/success/sfrates.shtml and, in their original form, on page 2 of Heeks (2003), iGovernment Working Paper No. 14, IDPM Manchester, which I downloaded and read: '35% are total failures, 50% are partial failures, and 15% are successes.' The problem is the evidence base, which Heeks himself is candid about. His own preceding sentence is 'We have very little data about rates of success and failure of e-government in developing/transitional countries, but this paper provides some baseline estimates.' He calls them 'working estimates'. They rest on a September 2002 poll of the eGovernment for Development mailing list — the companion page notes 'Only fifteen respondents' and that this 'cannot therefore be seen to have strong statistical significance' — plus analysis of roughly 40-plus case reports 'submitted for academic assessment at the University of Manchester', i.e. student coursework. The same page warns: 'Because of limitations in the methods used, we cannot use these figures as evidence that e-government failure rates are higher in developing/transitional countries than in industrialised countries.' Quoted undated, in 2026, this is a 23-year-old guess presented as a measurement. It is also one of the most circularly re-cited numbers in the ICT4D literature.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Richard Heeks' widely repeated working estimate — that around 35% of e-government projects in developing and transitional countries are total failures, 50% partial failures and 15% successes — dates from 2003 and is explicitly a baseline guess, not a measurement. Heeks derived it from a fifteen-respondent poll of an e-government mailing list in September 2002 plus about forty case reports submitted as coursework at Manchester, and prefaced it with 'We have very little data about rates of success and failure'. He attributes failure to 'design–reality gaps' between a system's assumptions and local organisational reality — which is the durable part of the contribution, and the part worth citing.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Richard Heeks (2003), 'Most eGovernment-for-Development Projects Fail: How Can Risks be Reduced?', iGovernment Working Paper No. 14, IDPM, University of Manchester, p.2 — https://hummedia.manchester.ac.uk/institutes/gdi/publications/workingpapers/igov/igov_wp14.pdf . The methodology and caveats are at https://www.egov4dev.org/success/sfrates.shtml (NOT /success/evaluation/, which the citation gives)

verdicts.claim: Women are barely 14% of landowners and own 11% of agricultural land; 84% of landowning rural households have no female owner, nine years after the 2005 HSAA; 87.5% of plots owned by individual men, 10.2% by individual women, 2.3% jointly
verdicts.reasoning: I extracted the full paper and every number is verbatim. Abstract: 'women are found to constitute barely 14% of landowners owning 11% of agricultural land in rural landowning households, averaged across states.' Section 4.1: 'In 2014, women owned land in only 16% of the households across regions (8% of these households also had male owners, while 84% had no female owners at all)... even 9 years after the enactment of the HSAA 2005'. Section 4.2: '87.5% of the plots across all nine states are owned by individual men, 10.2% by individual women, and only 2.3% jointly'. The correction is about the base, and it matters. This is not a national survey. It is ICRISAT's VDSA longitudinal panel: 30 villages across nine states (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha), and the universe is landowning rural households, not all rural households. Agarwal chose it deliberately over IHDS-II and NFHS-4, whose limitations she discusses, but she never claims national representativeness. The reference year is 2014 — twelve years old now. Saying '14% of landowners in rural India' drops both the nine-state limit and the landowning-household base, and a critic who opens the paper will find the qualifier sitting in the abstract's own sentence.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In ICRISAT panel data covering 30 villages across nine Indian states in 2014, women constituted barely 14% of landowners and owned 11% of the agricultural land in rural LANDOWNING households, averaged across states. 84% of those households had no female landowner at all — nine years after the 2005 Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act. 87.5% of plots were owned by individual men, 10.2% by individual women, and only 2.3% jointly. (Agarwal, Anthwal & Mahesh, Journal of Development Studies, 2021.) Say 'nine states' and 'landowning rural households' — the authors do.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Agarwal, B., Anthwal, P. & Mahesh, M. (2021), 'How Many and Which Women Own Land in India? Inter-gender and Intra-gender Gaps', Journal of Development Studies, DOI 10.1080/00220388.2021.1887478 — the cited PDF IS the primary source. Underlying data: ICRISAT VDSA longitudinal household survey, 2009/2010–2014.

verdicts.claim: NFHS-5 (2019–21): only ~48.8% of women in Gujarat have ever used the internet, among the five lowest states; nationally ~47% of rural women own a mobile phone vs 69% of urban women; fewer than 3 in 10 rural Indian women have ever used the internet
verdicts.reasoning: This is the claim that will do real damage, and the cited article is what refutes it. The 48.8% is TRIPURA, not Gujarat, and it is an NFHS-6 figure, not NFHS-5. The FACTLY piece says plainly: 'At the other end of the spectrum, Tripura recorded the lowest share at 48.8%, followed by Odisha at 51.8%, Assam at 53.5%, and Chhattisgarh at 54.4%.' Gujarat appears in the same article in the opposite category — among 'large states such as Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Telangana' that 'have made considerable progress'. I then checked the actual NFHS-5 source: Table 3.7 of the India final report (FR375, p.104) gives Gujarat women 15–49 ever used internet = 30.8%, against an India figure of 33.3%.
