Gujarat is roughly eleventh-lowest of 36 states and UTs, well above Bihar (20.6), Tripura (22.9), Odisha (24.9), West Bengal (25.5), Telangana (26.5), Chhattisgarh (26.7), Madhya Pradesh (26.9) and Assam (28.2). Not remotely 'among the five lowest'. The mobile-phone numbers are genuine NFHS-5 — FR375 §14.11: 'Urban women (69%) are more likely than rural women (47%) to own a mobile phone that they themselves use' — and the rural internet figure was 24.6%, so 'fewer than 3 in 10' was true for 2019–21. But the cited FACTLY article (published 3 July 2026) exists specifically to report that NFHS-6 has overtaken all of it: women's ever-use of the internet up from 33.3% to 64.3%, rural women from 24.6% to 58.6%, mobile ownership from 54% to 63.6% with rural at 57.4% and urban at 77.6%. Building a digital-exclusion argument on NFHS-5 while citing the article announcing the doubling is self-refuting.
verdicts.corrected_claim: If the argument needs a Gujarat figure: NFHS-5 (2019–21) recorded that 30.8% of Gujarat women aged 15–49 had ever used the internet, slightly below the all-India 33.3% — but Gujarat was not among the lowest states. If the argument needs a current figure, use NFHS-6 as reported by FACTLY (July 2026): women's ever-use of the internet has risen nationally from 33.3% to 64.3%, with rural women rising from 24.6% to 58.6% and mobile ownership among rural women from 36.9% (NFHS-4) to 57.4%. The honest contrarian point is no longer 'rural women cannot get online' — it is the gap that persists: urban women at 77.6% mobile ownership against rural 57.4%, and states like Tripura still at 48.8% internet use. Do not present the 47%/69% phone split or 'fewer than 3 in 10' as current; both are 2019–21 and superseded.
verdicts.real_primary_source: NFHS-5 India Report (FR375), IIPS/MoHFW, Table 3.7 p.104 and §14.11 — https://dhsprogram.com/pubs/pdf/FR375/FR375.pdf . The FACTLY article cited is about NFHS-6, not NFHS-5: https://factly.in/womens-internet-use-nearly-doubles-but-access-gaps-remain/ (published 3 July 2026)

verdicts.claim: Digital Seva Setu (launched Oct 2020) offers 321 services across 14,112 gram panchayats in 248 talukas, staffed by Village Computer Entrepreneurs; 27,13,079 users in 2023–24 and 34,99,261 in 2024–25
verdicts.reasoning: The cited MyGov blog post does not contain most of these numbers. It is dated July 2022 and says '313+ services', '14000+ Gram Panchayats', '8000 e-Grams centres' and '86 Lakhs+ applications' — no taluka count, no launch date, and no year-by-year user figures. So the citation does not support the claim as written. I did verify the service and panchayat counts independently at the official portal, digitalsevasetu.gujarat.gov.in, which displays 'Services 321' and 'GramPanchayat 14120'. That confirms 321 services but gives 14,120 gram panchayats, not 14,112 — a small discrepancy, but one that shows the figure was copied from somewhere with a date attached that the claim has lost. The 248 talukas and the two user counts (27,13,079 and 34,99,261) I could not trace to any source I could reach; they have the texture of a Gujarat state budget publication or Socio-Economic Review table, but I could not open one to confirm. The qualitative core of the claim — that Gujarat delivers these services through a staffed counter, with Village Computer Entrepreneurs submitting applications on citizens' behalf rather than citizens using websites themselves — IS supported by the MyGov post, which describes VCEs assisting citizens and explaining government processes. That is the part of the argument that actually matters, and it is safe.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Gujarat delivers rural government services primarily through an assisted, staffed counter rather than through citizens using websites directly. The state's Digital Seva Setu portal currently lists 321 services available across 14,120 gram panchayats, delivered at village e-Gram centres by Village Computer Entrepreneurs who submit applications on citizens' behalf. (Official portal, digitalsevasetu.gujarat.gov.in, accessed August 2026.) Drop the 248 talukas and the 27,13,079 / 34,99,261 annual user figures unless you can point at the specific government publication they came from — the MyGov post cited does not contain them.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Official portal https://digitalsevasetu.gujarat.gov.in/ (live counters: 321 services, 14,120 gram panchayats). The cited MyGov blog post is a July 2022 beneficiary story giving 313+ services, 14,000+ gram panchayats and 86 lakh+ applications — it is not the source of the figures in the claim.

verdicts.claim: Gujarat issues a digitally signed, legally usable RoR through iORA for ~Rs 5–15 per village form; the free AnyRoR view is explicitly not accepted for court, registration or banking; Landeed resells the same document for Rs 199 with 1-hour-to-3-day turnaround
verdicts.reasoning: Three parts, verifying differently. The Landeed part is solid: I opened the product page (last updated 31 January 2026) and it states 'The fee is ₹199 per document' and 'Processing time ranges from 1 hour to 3 days, with most orders completed within 6–8 hours.' The digitally-signed-RoR part is solid: both AnyRoR and iORA carry a 'Digitally Signed RoR' entry, and the official Gujarati SOP (anyror.gujarat.gov.in/Download/Digital_RoR_SOP.pdf) confirms the document 'is digitally signed and is a copy recognised by the State Government', verifiable by QR code or by unique number at anyror.gujarat.gov.in/rorverify.aspx, and that it is issued only after online payment. The two failures are the fee and the disclaimer wording. The SOP describes the payment step but never states an amount, and I found no Rs 5–15 figure on any government page I could reach — it appears to come from third-party 'how to' guides, which is exactly the circular sourcing to avoid. And the disclaimer is real but says something narrower than claimed. Every AnyRoR free view carries, in Gujarati: 'અહીં દર્શાવેલ જમીનની વિગતો ફક્ત આપની જાણ માટે જ છે જેને સત્તાવાર નકલ તરીકે ગણવામાં આવશે નહી' — 'the land details shown here are for your information only and will not be treated as an official copy.' It does not enumerate court, registration or banking. The narrower, verbatim version is more useful anyway, because it is quotable and checkable.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Gujarat issues a digitally signed Record of Rights online through AnyRoR/iORA, which the state's own procedure document describes as 'digitally signed and a copy recognised by the State Government', verifiable by QR code or unique number — and it is issued only against an online payment. The free AnyRoR view, by contrast, carries an explicit disclaimer on every record: 'the land details shown here are for your information only and will not be treated as an official copy'. A private company, Landeed, resells a certified Gujarat SatBara/7-12 for Rs 199 per document with a stated turnaround of one hour to three days. Drop the 'Rs 5–15' official fee unless you can source it to a government notification — the state's own SOP does not state an amount. Do not write that the free view is 'explicitly not accepted for court, registration or banking'; the portal does not say that. Quote the actual disclaimer.
verdicts.real_primary_source: AnyRoR/iORA official SOP: https://anyror.gujarat.gov.in/Download/Digital_RoR_SOP.pdf ; the free-view disclaimer is served on every AnyRoR record page (live at https://anyror.gujarat.gov.in/LandRecordRural.aspx and captured in this repo at /home/kirtan/Desktop/projects/irmsc/output/43/anyror_43.html); Landeed pricing at https://web.landeed.com/products/gujarat/certified-satbara-ror . No primary source located for the Rs 5–15 fee.

verdicts.claim: India's titling is presumptive not conclusive; Vidhi cites 34% ownership-and-possession discrepancies in rural Shimla and 6% in Baddi, and Maharashtra area discrepancies vs GPS/ETS in more than half of properties despite near-perfect ownership concordance (101 of 102 parcels)
verdicts.reasoning: The claim reproduces the Vidhi blog accurately — Vidhi does write 'An impact assessment in Himachal Pradesh found ownership and possession discrepancies of 34% and 6% in rural Shimla and Baddi, respectively', and does give '101 of 102 parcels' for ownership concordance and '54 of 102' for inaccurate encumbrance records. But Vidhi is tertiary. It links to Ideas for India without naming the study, so I traced it: the article is 'Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme: Assessing impact in Himachal Pradesh and Maharashtra' by Sudha Narayanan, Gausia Shaikh, Bhargavi Zaveri, Diya Uday and Prerna Prabhakar, 6 August 2018, summarising impact assessments by NCAER (Himachal Pradesh) and IGIDR (Maharashtra). At the primary level the Vidhi phrasing is a garble. NCAER's Real-Time Mirror check reports OWNERSHIP variation of 34% in rural Shimla and 6% in Baddi, and separately POSSESSION variation of 38% in Shimla and 60% in Baddi (plus land use 34%/32% and land area beyond 5% variation 78%/52%). Fusing ownership and possession into a single '34% and 6%' makes Baddi look an order of magnitude cleaner than the study found — its possession discrepancy was the worst number in the table. The sample sizes are also fatal to any statewide reading and go unmentioned everywhere downstream: 50 parcels per tehsil, 100 in total across five villages in Himachal, and about 102 parcels across five villages in two Maharashtra tehsils (Mulshi and Palghar), fieldwork in 2017. Maharashtra's area finding is that roughly half of sample parcels deviated by more than 20% from recorded area — Vidhi's 'more than half' is a slight upgrade on 'approximately half'. The opening proposition, that Indian title is presumptive rather than conclusive, is uncontroversial and is independently supported by claim 1.
verdicts.corrected_claim: India's land titling is presumptive, not conclusive — the state does not guarantee title. DILRMP impact assessments conducted in 2017 found large gaps between records and ground reality even in small samples: NCAER's check of 100 parcels in Himachal Pradesh found ownership variation of 34% in rural Shimla and 6% in Baddi, but POSSESSION variation of 38% in Shimla and 60% in Baddi, and area variation beyond 5% in 78% and 52% of parcels respectively. IGIDR's survey of about 102 parcels across two Maharashtra tehsils found near-perfect ownership concordance with the record office (101 of 102) but area deviations exceeding 20% in roughly half the parcels when measured by handheld GPS and Electronic Total Station. State the sample sizes — 100 and 102 parcels — and never merge the ownership and possession columns.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Narayanan, Shaikh, Zaveri, Uday & Prabhakar, 'Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme: Assessing impact in Himachal Pradesh and Maharashtra', Ideas for India, 6 August 2018 — https://www.ideasforindia.in/topics/macroeconomics/digital-india-land-records-modernisation-programme-assessing-impact-in-himachal-pradesh-and-maharashtra — summarising underlying impact assessments by NCAER (Himachal Pradesh) and IGIDR (Maharashtra), fieldwork 2017. Vidhi is a tertiary retelling and misstates the HP figures. NOTE: the URL Vidhi links to is dead; the live path is /topics/macroeconomics/.

verdicts.claim: Only 39% of spatial data verified and 26% of maps linked to RoR against 86% computerisation of textual records; real-time RoR/map update at 15%; survey/re-survey complete in 9% of villages (35% of area)
verdicts.reasoning: Every figure matches PRS's Table 1 exactly — 'Computerisation of land records: 86%', 'Spatial data verified: 39%', 'Cadastral maps linked to RoR: 26%', 'Real time updation of RoR and maps: 15%', 'Number of villages where survey/re-survey work completed: 9%', 'Area surveyed: 35%' — sourced by PRS to the Department of Land Resources. The problem is not accuracy, it is age. PRS labels the table 'data updated till September 2017'. These are nine-year-old numbers, and the argument they support (that the textual record and the map are largely unreconciled) is exactly the kind of structural claim a critic will test against current data. DILRMP has since been substantially rebuilt — the Department of Land Resources replaced its monitoring system with DILRMP MIS 4.0 on 15 October 2024, retiring the old MIS 3.0, and now reports separately on digitised mapsheets/FMBs/tippans, villages with cadastral maps linked to RoR, geo-referenced villages and ULPIN coverage. I could not extract current national percentages because the new dashboard loads its numbers asynchronously and its top-5/bottom-5 report exports came back empty, so I am not substituting a number I have not seen. But quoting the 2017 table undated is not defensible. Also worth noting: PRS itself is a secondary compiler here, not the origin — the origin is the DoLR monitoring system.
verdicts.corrected_claim: As of September 2017 — the last figures compiled by PRS Legislative Research from the Department of Land Resources — 86% of textual land records had been computerised nationally, but only 46% of cadastral maps had been digitised, 39% of spatial data verified and 26% of maps linked to the Record of Rights; real-time updating of RoR and maps stood at 15%, and survey/re-survey was complete in 9% of villages covering 35% of area. Always attach the September 2017 date. If a current figure is needed, take it from DILRMP MIS 4.0 (dilrmp.gov.in), which replaced the old monitoring system on 15 October 2024 and reports considerably higher progress.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development — DILRMP monitoring data as on September 2017, compiled in PRS Legislative Research, 'Land Records and Titles in India', Table 1: https://prsindia.org/policy/analytical-reports/land-records-and-titles-india . Current data: DILRMP MIS 4.0, https://dilrmp.gov.in/

verdicts.claim: In Andhra Pradesh, digitisation of the Adangal automated Column 13 to show cultivator and owner as the same person, erasing recorded tenancy; tribal and Dalit farmers lost claims and welfare eligibility through altered or deleted record columns, and NRIs claimed tribal land
verdicts.reasoning: I retrieved the full Pulitzer Center story (Sushmita, AI Fellow, 22 October 2025, part of the project 'Digitalized and Dispossessed in India') and every element is supported. On Column 13: 'Column 13 of the Adangal mentions farming practices and names of the cultivators, who may be tenants or landowners. Ajay said that when the records were digitised, Column 13 was reportedly automated to show both cultivator and owner as the same person. The revenue officials told me that when the name of the owner is updated, the name of the cultivator automatically gets updated as that of the owners.' On the system: Meebhoomi (Webland), launched 2015, 'has been automated to show both cultivator and owner as the same person, erasing tenant farmers and others who have been cultivating the land for generations.' On the NRI claim: a Gadaba PVTG farmer's land in Gadabapalam shown as owned and cultivated by a non-resident Indian named in neither physical record. On deleted columns and welfare loss: farmers in Chatterjeepuram found their names had disappeared from records they had downloaded in 2016; twelve Madiga farmers in Kasimkota lost PM Kisan and Rythu Bharosa payments after their names were removed from 1B records; a Revenue Division Officer confirmed 'those [columns] were not useful to the government and hence dropped'. A Libtech India/Manchester/Naples 2025 study found 40% of Rythu Bharosa exclusions traced to land-record mutation problems. One framing caution: the Column 13 automation is an allegation relayed by an activist quoting revenue officials — the story itself says 'reportedly automated'. Present it as reported and attributed, not as an established software specification, and this holds up.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Use 'reportedly automated' or 'according to activists and revenue officials quoted by the Pulitzer Center' for the Column 13 mechanism — the reporting itself hedges it, and the state has not confirmed it. Also name the system: Meebhoomi (Webland), launched 2015. Everything else stands as written.
verdicts.real_primary_source: Sushmita, 'In Andhra Pradesh, Software Flaws Aid Land Grab From Tribal and Dalit Farmers', Pulitzer Center, 22 October 2025, from the project 'Digitalized and Dispossessed in India' — https://pulitzercenter.org/stories/andhra-pradesh-software-flaws-aid-land-grab-tribal-and-dalit-farmers (the cited URL IS the primary reporting)

topic: Indian land-records digitisation — DILRMP, ULPIN/Bhu-Aadhaar, NGDRS, state portals, Bhoomi and Dharani evidence, and the legal status of digitally signed record-of-rights extracts (research for a redesigned Gujarat 7/12 citizen portal)

claims.claim: The famous claim that land disputes are 'two-thirds of all pending court cases in India' traces to the World Bank's 2007 India land report, where it appears as an explicitly hedged aside with NO citation: 'Although detailed figures are hard to come by, with some estimating that land-related conflicts account for two thirds of all pending court cases, the large amount of land related litigation in India is proverbial.' The same report elsewhere gives a different figure — 'almost 40% pertain to land' of ~23 million pending civil cases — also uncited.
claims.figure: two-thirds (66%) vs 40% in the same report
claims.source_name: World Bank, 'India: Land Policies for Growth and Poverty Reduction' (Report No. 38298-IN), 9 July 2007 — full text, pp. 14 and 43
claims.why_it_matters: PRS and dozens of downstream write-ups cite 'World Bank 2007' as if it were a measurement. Using it uncritically in a hackathon submission is the exact failure mode the honesty criterion punishes. Say instead: 'the most-quoted number is an unsourced aside the World Bank itself flagged as an estimate, and the same report gives 40% twenty-nine pages earlier.'

claims.claim: The separate '66% of all civil cases in India are related to land/property disputes' claim is traceable, and its origin is Daksh's Access to Justice Survey 2016 — a litigant-intercept survey, not a court-records census. Namita Wahi's widely-cited 2019 CPR piece states the figure and footnotes it to 'Daksh, Access to Justice Survey, 2016'. Daksh's own published methodology: over 9,000 litigants interviewed across 300 locations, of whom 4,696 had civil disputes pending.
claims.figure: 66% of pending civil cases; n≈9,000 litigants, 300 locations, 4,696 civil
claims.source_name: Namita Wahi, 'Understanding Land Conflict in India and Suggestions for Reform', Centre for Policy Research (footnote 3) — and Daksh, 'The Access to Justice Survey: Decoding Delays, Part I: Civil Cases'
claims.why_it_matters: This is the defensible version of the claim, and it is narrower than how it is normally used: it describes the composition of *pending civil* cases as estimated from a litigant sample — not 'two-thirds of all Indian court cases'. State it that way and the write-up gains credibility instead of losing it.

claims.claim: The 'land disputes take 20 years to resolve' figure is specifically about land ACQUISITION disputes travelling all the way to the Supreme Court, from CPR's Land Rights Initiative review of Supreme Court land-acquisition cases 1950–2016. It is not the average duration of an ordinary 7/12 mutation dispute. The same source states ~25% of all Supreme Court decided cases involve land disputes, of which ~30% concern land acquisition.
claims.figure: 20 years (land acquisition disputes to Supreme Court resolution); 25% of SC cases involve land
claims.source_name: Namita Wahi, CPR Land Rights Initiative (citing Wahi et al., 'Land Acquisition in India: A Review of Supreme Court Cases from 1950 to 2016', CPR 2017)
claims.why_it_matters: Prevents a common misquote. If the portal's problem statement says 'land disputes take 20 years', a judge who knows the literature will mark it down; scoping it to Supreme Court land-acquisition litigation is both accurate and still striking.

claims.claim: Under India's system, registration records the TRANSACTION, not the title. Ownership is presumptive, not conclusive: the onus of verifying title falls on the buyer, not the state. Three statutes govern it — Transfer of Property Act 1882, Registration Act 1908, Indian Stamp Act 1899 — and records are fragmented across three departments (Revenue holds the RoR, Registration holds deeds, Survey & Settlement holds maps) that operate in silos.
claims.source_name: PRS Legislative Research, 'Land Records and Titles in India'
claims.why_it_matters: This is the single most important honest framing for the write-up: a beautiful 7/12 viewer cannot make title conclusive, and claiming otherwise would be the biggest integrity failure available. It also justifies showing 'this is a record of rights, not a title guarantee' on every screen.

claims.claim: The Information Technology Act 2000, First Schedule (read with s.1(4)), expressly excludes from the Act's operation: 'Any contract for the sale or conveyance of immovable property or any interest in such property' (item 5), along with negotiable instruments, powers-of-attorney, trusts and wills. Meanwhile ss.4, 5 and 6 give legal recognition to electronic records, electronic signatures, and the electronic issue of government documents.
claims.source_name: Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended), India Code official text
claims.why_it_matters: This is the precise legal reason a state CAN issue a digitally signed 7/12 (a government-issued record, covered by ss.4–6) but CANNOT let you execute a sale deed online under the IT Act. It gives the prototype a clean, defensible boundary: 'we deliver a legally valid extract; we deliberately do not touch conveyancing, and here is the statute that says why.'

claims.claim: DILRMP's own MIS reported, as on 16 Nov 2024: RoR computerisation 95.6% of villages (6,26,210 of 6,55,333); issuance of DIGITALLY SIGNED RoR in only 67.9% of villages; cadastral maps digitised 59.9% (2.23 cr of 3.73 cr); maps geo-referenced 54.3%; maps linked to RoR 72.0%; REAL-TIME updation of RoR and maps in only 35.7% of villages; SROs computerised 95.7%; SRO–land-record integration 88.6%. Total RoRs in India: 36,94,82,818.
claims.source_name: NCAER, 'Study on Evaluation of Quality of Land Records', submitted to Department of Land Resources, MoRD — Table 1.1, sourced to dilrmp.gov.in dated 16 Nov 2024
claims.why_it_matters: The 35.7% real-time-updation figure is the killer stat for the product: the record you fetch is frequently stale, so the UI must show recency and pending-mutation state rather than presenting a clean 'photo of paper'. The 67.9% digitally-signed figure sets the realistic ceiling for a legally-valid-download feature.

claims.claim: Official DILRMP numbers contradict each other across ministry channels within weeks. PIB's Year End Review (26 Dec 2024) claims '95% of Maps/FMBs have been digitized' and 'ULPIN has been assigned to 23 crore land parcels'; the DILRMP MIS six weeks earlier showed 59.9% of maps digitised; and ThePrint, using ministry data in Oct 2024, reported only 8.4 crore of 28.72 crore parcels (~30%) had ULPIN. The DoLR homepage in Aug 2026 shows 32.59 crore.
claims.figure: maps: 95% (PIB) vs 59.9% (MIS); ULPIN: 23 cr (PIB, Dec 2024) vs 8.4 cr (Oct 2024) vs 32.59 cr (Aug 2026)
claims.source_name: PIB, 'Year End Review 2024: Achievement of the Department of Land Resources' (PRID 2088125); DoLR homepage counters; ThePrint
claims.why_it_matters: Direct answer to 'is the official dashboard credible?' — No, not without stating the denominator. Cite both numbers side by side. It also licenses the prototype to publish its OWN honest coverage metrics rather than a green progress bar.

claims.claim: The DILRMP dashboard is self-reported by states and carries that disclaimer: 'Data presented in this site has been updated by respective State Governments/UT Administration and Department of Land Resources...'. The dashboard was relaunched as 'MIS 4.0' on 15 October 2024, superseding MIS 3.0.
claims.source_name: DILRMP MIS 4.0 public dashboard, Department of Land Resources / NIC
claims.why_it_matters: Explains the contradictions above structurally rather than as an accusation: the centre publishes what states report, with no independent verification layer. A credible product-thinking section can propose exactly that missing verification layer.

claims.claim: NCAER's ground-truth study for DoLR — a census of 1,342 land parcels across 8 villages in Punjab, Chandigarh, Delhi and Rajasthan plus patwaris covering 40 villages, fieldwork 28 Sept–20 Oct 2024 — found that landowner awareness of digital copies is low and that access 'by directly downloading from the web is extremely limited'; that RoRs largely do NOT show ULPIN and landowners and patwaris alike are unaware of the ULPIN scheme; that apart from loan/lien/mortgage, NO other encumbrances (revenue-court proceedings, civil-court proceedings, town-planning restrictions) are reflected in land records; and that 'inconsistencies are reported between DOLR website data and what the survey brought out i.e. ground realities'.
claims.source_name: NCAER, 'Study on Evaluation of Quality of Land Records', Executive Summary (for DoLR, MoRD)
claims.why_it_matters: This is a government-commissioned study saying, in the government's own document, that citizens do not download their own records and that the encumbrance picture is incomplete. It is the best available justification for (a) redesigning access rather than adding more data, and (b) explicitly labelling which encumbrances the record cannot show.

claims.claim: NCAER warns that even a small error rate compounds: 'even a small 2% to 3% occurrence of errors (as would appear from this survey) when multiplied over millions of landowners translates into a very large number of situations that have the potential to generate dispute and litigation.' It also found widespread ignorance of rectification procedures — people do not know whom to approach when a record is wrong.
claims.source_name: NCAER, 'Study on Evaluation of Quality of Land Records' (for DoLR, MoRD)
claims.why_it_matters: Justifies making 'this record looks wrong — what do I do?' a first-class flow rather than a footer link. That single flow is a differentiator no state portal currently offers well.

claims.claim: DILRMP money is far smaller than its rhetoric: Rs 2,428 crore released to States/UTs across 2008-09 to 2024-25 for the whole country; the 2021-22 to 2025-26 extension carries an outlay of just Rs 875 crore; Budget 2024-25 allocated Rs 141 crore. In the earlier NLRMP phase (to 2015-16) States utilised only Rs 525.3 crore of Rs 1,167.4 crore released — about 45%.
claims.figure: Rs 2,428 cr total since 2008-09; Rs 875 cr for 2021-26; Rs 141 cr in BE 2024-25; 45% NLRMP utilisation
claims.source_name: PIB Year End Review 2024 (DoLR) and NCAER §1.3.1 (citing MoRD Annual Report 2023-24 and PRS Demand for Grants analysis)
claims.why_it_matters: Frames the 'end-to-end / infrastructure' section realistically: the national programme spends roughly the cost of a mid-sized enterprise IT project per year across 36 states. A proposal that assumes big central budgets is not credible; one that assumes cheap, reusable delivery is.

claims.claim: DILRMP has a successor already in motion: 'DILRMP 3.0', reviewed by the Union Minister on 8 May 2026, whose components include georeferencing and ULPIN assignment, AADHAAR SEEDING, 'mobile number and address integration in land records databases', computerisation of revenue courts, development of 'Core GIS and Land Stack software', and urban land-records pilots. The stated purpose of Land Stack is 'immediate and accurate valuation of land parcels, thereby helping banks streamline loan approval processes'.
claims.source_name: PIB, 'Land Stack Initiative to Usher in Transparent and Citizen-Centric Land Management...' (PRID 2259050)
claims.why_it_matters: Positions the prototype correctly: the national direction of travel is a credit-and-valuation stack for banks, with mobile numbers and Aadhaar going INTO the land-record database. A citizen-first portal that treats the farmer, not the lender, as the primary user is a genuine differentiator — and the privacy critique writes itself.

claims.claim: ULPIN / Bhu-Aadhaar is a 14-digit identifier derived computationally from the geo-referenced coordinates of a parcel's vertices, following the ECCMA 'Property Natural Identifier Unit' (PNIU) 14-digit format and OGC standards. It is assigned in two stages — a temporary ID from textual records, then a permanent one once geo-coordinates exist. Rolled out in 29 States/UTs, piloted in 4 more.
claims.source_name: Department of Land Resources, 'Bhu-Aadhar: Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN)'
claims.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to the parcel identity layer already built: ULPIN is coordinate-derived and mutable (temporary → permanent), so it is NOT a stable primary key for a client-side identity layer. Treat it as an optional alias attached to a survey-number-based identity, never as the join key.

claims.claim: ULPIN rollout is bottlenecked on geo-referencing century-old cadastral maps, not on software. Only ~30% of parcels (8.4 crore of 28.72 crore) had a ULPIN three years after launch; officials quoted: 'In several districts, the village maps are over 100 years old. It is a challenging process to match two sets of maps.' Ministry also conceded 'the number of land parcels might increase due to sub-division of plots', making the denominator unstable. Deadline: March 2026, with Rs 30–100 crore incentives to states.
claims.figure: 8.4 crore of 28.72 crore (~30%) as of Oct 2024
claims.source_name: ThePrint (Risha Chitlangia), '3 years on, 30% of rural land parcels have Bhu-Aadhaar. Centre pushes for completion by 2026'
claims.why_it_matters: An identity layer that hard-depends on ULPIN will be empty for most of India for years. It also mirrors the project's own finding that Kheda/Anand village map sheets are rasterised with no parcel geometry — the same bottleneck, seen from the other end.

claims.claim: Gujarat is at or near the top on the technical DILRMP metrics: ULPIN assigned to 1.19 crore of ~1.2 crore parcels; 100% of cadastral maps digitised; 99.9% of villages have cadastral maps linked to RoR; 1,19,40,832 RoRs across 18,389 villages; RoR computerisation 100%.
claims.figure: Gujarat: 100% maps digitised, 99.9% map-RoR linkage, ~99% ULPIN
claims.source_name: NCAER, 'Study on Evaluation of Quality of Land Records', Annexure Tables 1.1A/1.2A (DILRMP MIS, 16 Nov 2024); ThePrint for ULPIN
claims.why_it_matters: This is the strongest argument for the whole project: Gujarat's DATA is essentially complete. The failure is entirely in the citizen interface — chained dropdowns, a CAPTCHA on public data, desktop tables. That reframes the submission from 'digitise Gujarat' (done) to 'the last mile is the only mile left', which is a much sharper product thesis.

claims.claim: NGDRS (National Generic Document Registration System) is NIC's uniform deed-registration platform — online data entry, payments, appointments and document search — adopted by 18 States/UTs, with 12 more sharing data with the national portal. e-Court integration with land records has been cleared in 26 States/UTs. It registers DEEDS; it is not a record-of-rights system.
claims.source_name: PIB, '95% of Land Records in Rural India Digitized' (PRID 2068408)
claims.why_it_matters: Lets the write-up draw the record-of-rights vs deed-registration line concretely with named systems: AnyRoR/Bhoomi/Mahabhulekh on one side (Revenue), NGDRS/IGR on the other (Registration), and mutation as the fragile bridge between them.

claims.claim: The Department of Land Resources published a draft 'Registration Bill, 2025' to replace the Registration Act 1908 entirely, with public comments invited until 25 June 2025. Key features: enabling online registration with electronic presentation and admission of documents, electronic registration certificates, digital record maintenance, Aadhaar-based authentication WITH informed consent plus alternatives for non-Aadhaar holders, and electronic integration with other record systems; expanded compulsory registration covering agreements to sell, powers-of-attorney, sale certificates, and equitable mortgages. It does NOT introduce conclusive title.
claims.source_name: Department of Land Resources, MoRD — draft 'The Registration Bill, 2025' overview and public-consultation notice
claims.why_it_matters: Two uses. (1) End-to-end thinking: the legal plumbing for online registration is being rewritten right now, so a portal design can name exactly which of its flows would become lawful under it. (2) Honesty: even the brand-new bill keeps presumptive title, so no portal — yours included — can promise ownership certainty.

claims.claim: Karnataka Bhoomi's positive evaluation is real and specific but thin: of manual-system users, two-thirds paid a bribe, versus 3% of Bhoomi users; weighted average bribe Rs 152.46 (manual) vs Rs 3.09 (Bhoomi); 72% got the RTC in one visit vs 5% manually; 85% rated staff behaviour good vs 0% manually. The headline 'Rs 806 million saved annually / 1.32 million mandays' is an extrapolation from this survey. Sample: 198 Bhoomi users and 59 manual-system users across six districts; the document is marked DRAFT and was funded by the World Bank's Governance Knowledge Sharing Program.
claims.figure: 3% vs 66% paying bribes; Rs 3.09 vs Rs 152.46; Rs 806 million/yr; n=198 vs 59
claims.source_name: Albert Lobo & Suresh Balakrishnan, 'Report Card on Service of Bhoomi Kiosks', Public Affairs Centre, Bangalore, November 2002 (archived World Bank copy)
claims.why_it_matters: The single most-cited e-governance success statistic in India, and it rests on 257 interviews in a draft report. Reporting the sample size alongside the number is exactly the 'honesty about limitations' the rubric rewards — and it is genuinely useful, because the *mechanism* it identifies (removing the intermediary from the counter) is the mechanism a redesigned portal reproduces.

claims.claim: The best-known critical Bhoomi evaluation found the opposite of the report card. Benjamin et al.'s ethnography in six taluks around Bangalore found that after Bhoomi, mutations that had taken 2–3 days at village level took 3–4 months at taluk level; bribes rose and became systematised through a market of 'agents' with set rates (RTC copy Rs 15 fee plus Rs 300 agent charge; mutation bribes Rs 500–5,000, rising to Rs 15,000–20,000 and charged per acre in high-development taluks); small farmers' survey numbers were used by larger farmers to claim small-farmer subsidies; and the effect ran through centralisation — closing village offices and moving all functions to taluk level across four administrative 'tables'. The authors state the report was initially suppressed by its funding institute.
claims.figure: 2–3 days → 3–4 months for a mutation; mutation bribes Rs 500–20,000
claims.source_name: Solomon Benjamin, R. Bhuvaneswari, P. Rajan, Manjunatha, 'Bhoomi: E-Governance, Or, An Anti-Politics Machine Necessary to Globalize Bangalore?', CASUM-m Working Paper, January 2007
claims.why_it_matters: Qualitative, non-random, six taluks, anonymised respondents — so it cannot support a national claim, and I would label it that way. But its causal story (centralisation creates intermediaries; simplified digital forms erase the irregular cases that the poor actually have) is the most useful design warning available, and it is why the portal must work end-to-end without an intermediary and must render unusual survey numbers rather than normalising them away.

claims.claim: The strongest quantitative evidence on registry computerisation in India finds effects that are real but small and urban-only: exploiting the staggered manual-to-digital transition of Andhra Pradesh's 387 sub-registry offices (1999–2005) against credit and transaction data 1995–2007, Deininger and Goyal find 'significant, though quantitatively modest, increases in credit access in urban but not rural areas.'
claims.source_name: Klaus Deininger & Aparajita Goyal, 'Going digital: Credit effects of land registry computerization in India', Journal of Development Economics 99(2), Nov 2012 (also World Bank Policy Research WP 5244, 2010)
claims.why_it_matters: Sets honest expectations. If the best-identified study finds digitisation lifted credit only in urban areas, a rural-farmer portal should not claim credit-unlocking as its headline benefit. Claim access, comprehension and time instead — and say why.

claims.claim: Telangana's Dharani inherited a structural exclusion from the 2017 Land Records Updation Programme: records were split into Part A (undisputed, verified and migrated) and Part B (ownership disputes), and 'part-B records with ownership disputes were ignored under this program'. A field study in four villages across Mulugu and Kumuram Bheem Asifabad districts found only 72.6% of surveyed land (1,493.84 of 2,057.75 acres) was recorded in Dharani at all; 563.91 acres were missing, from RSR discrepancies (38.9%), podu cultivation (32.2%), sada bainama (21.7%) and missing survey numbers (7%). 91.7% of pattadars had never accessed the Dharani portal — 5% among Scheduled Tribes.
claims.figure: 27.4% of surveyed land absent from Dharani; 91.7% never used the portal; ST access 5%
claims.source_name: R. Bhanu Prakash (Centre for Economics and Social Studies, Hyderabad), 'Land Records in Telangana: Issues and Challenges', JNRID 4(3)
claims.why_it_matters: A four-village purposive sample in two tribal districts, in a low-tier journal — so the percentages must be presented as a case study, not a state estimate. But the mechanism is exactly the cautionary tale: a redesign that migrates only the clean records leaves the contested ones — disproportionately tribal and Dalit-held — outside the system entirely, with no screen to appear on.

claims.claim: Dharani's legal architecture removed remedies that had existed since 1971. The Telangana Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books Act, 2020 contains no provision for appeals or revisions equivalent to sections 5(B), 5(5) or 9 of the 1971 Act, and lacks a redressal path for orders passed under the older Act; entire survey numbers were placed on prohibited-property lists even when only part of the land was disputed or under court stay; and applications rejected online carried the bare remark 'rejected' without reasons.
claims.source_name: R. Bhanu Prakash, 'Land Records in Telangana: Issues and Challenges', JNRID 4(3), §B and §E
claims.why_it_matters: The most transferable lesson in the whole research: the failure was not the UI, it was deleting the appeal. Any redesign that replaces a paper process must preserve — and ideally surface — the objection, appeal and revision routes, and must never return an unexplained 'rejected'.

claims.claim: Dharani was replaced by the Bhu Bharati portal in 2025, and the replacement is itself now under investigation. Between March and August 2026 Telangana piloted Bhu Bharati in five mandals (2 April), reported 5.20 crore visits at the one-year mark, then constituted a Special Enquiry Team under Charu Sinha to probe Dharani and Bhu Bharati irregularities (July 2026), ordered a replacement of Bhu Bharati's 'software and architecture', and saw reporting on 'weak Dharani architecture allowing potential access to land data by private persons' and an audit flagging ~10,000 suspicious deals.
claims.figure: 5.20 crore visits in year 1; ~10,000 suspicious deals flagged
claims.source_name: Aggregated dated headlines from The Hindu, The Times of India, Telangana Today, Deccan Chronicle and The New Indian Express, via Google News (Mar–Aug 2026)
claims.why_it_matters: Headline-level evidence only (I could not open the article bodies), so it should be cited as 'as reported by' with dates. But it makes the cautionary tale current rather than historical, and 'the replacement for the failed portal is itself being replaced' is the strongest possible argument for shipping something small, auditable and reversible.

claims.claim: Maharashtra runs the clearest two-tier model in India, and labels it. The free Mahabhulekh 7/12 viewer requires a CAPTCHA and a MANDATORY mobile number, offers 16 languages (Marathi, English, Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Oriya, Urdu, Assamese, Nepali, Konkani, Maithili), and states outright that 'the information displayed on this portal cannot be used for any official or legal purposes'. The separate Digital Satbara (DSLR) service issues digitally signed 7/12, 8A, Property Card, K-Prat and MH DIGI Maps behind a login (regular or OTP) with a CAPTCHA and a non-refundable prepaid deposit, and states 'Digitally signed 7/12, 8A and Property Card can be used for all official and legal purposes.'
claims.source_name: Maharashtra Bhumi Abhilekh (Mahabhulekh) and Digital Satbara (DSLR), Settlement Commissioner & Revenue Department, Government of Maharashtra
claims.why_it_matters: Two directly copyable patterns and one anti-pattern. Copy: the explicit legal-status label on every extract, and the multi-language interface. Do not copy: forcing a mobile number to read a public record, or putting a CAPTCHA in front of both tiers.

claims.claim: Karnataka has already removed the login barrier for paid certified prints: Bhoomi's i-RTC service is described as 'Printing of RTC by citizen by online payment without any login', at Rs 15 per RTC, and printed RTCs carry a reference number that can be verified against an XML record. Dishaank provides GIS parcel lookup with a mobile app.
claims.source_name: Karnataka Land Records portal (Bhoomi), Revenue Department, Government of Karnataka
claims.why_it_matters: Direct existence proof that a state can issue a paid, verifiable land record with NO account, NO OTP and NO CAPTCHA. This defeats the standard objection that authentication is legally required, and gives the redesign a named precedent to point at.

claims.claim: Rajasthan Apna Khata offers all jamabandi copies free, but explicitly as uncertified informational copies; authenticated/certified copies require applying at a designated e-Mitra kiosk. Interface is Hindi-primary. Andhra Pradesh's Meebhoomi requires a login — citizen, official, or Aadhaar-plus-OTP — with a CAPTCHA on every authentication path, in English and Telugu.
claims.source_name: Apna Khata (Rajasthan Revenue Department) and Meebhoomi (Andhra Pradesh)
claims.why_it_matters: Completes the comparison table: free-but-uncertified (Rajasthan), paid-and-certified-without-login (Karnataka), free-and-labelled plus paid-signed (Maharashtra), login-and-Aadhaar-gated (AP), CAPTCHA-gated-free (Gujarat). Gujarat's incumbent sits at the worst corner — gated AND uncertified.

claims.claim: Gujarat does already issue a digitally signed record of rights, but through a different portal from the public viewer: iORA (Integrated Online Revenue Applications) lists 'ડિજિટલી સાઇન્ડ ગામ નમૂના નંબર (Digitally Signed RoR)' and digitally sealed property cards among its services, operates in Gujarati and English, and recommends a 1024x768 screen resolution.
claims.source_name: iORA — Integrated Online Revenue Applications, Revenue Department, Government of Gujarat
claims.why_it_matters: Important for accuracy: the write-up must NOT claim Gujarat has no digitally signed RoR. The accurate claim is that the legally valid extract lives on a separate, desktop-era, Gujarati-form-heavy portal while the public viewer (AnyRoR) hands back an unusable-for-any-purpose page — i.e. the problem is fragmentation and interface, not absence of capability.

claims.claim: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 does not apply to 'personal data that is made or caused to be made publicly available by ... any other person who is under an obligation under any law for the time being in force in India to make such personal data publicly available' (s.3(c)(ii)(B)).
claims.source_name: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — Gazette text (MeitY)
claims.why_it_matters: This is the real, checkable privacy story for a land-records portal — better than any of the vague 'Bhu-Aadhaar surveillance' commentary I could not source. Land records are published under statutory obligation, so the names, shares and (under DILRMP 3.0) mobile numbers and Aadhaar seeds inside them sit OUTSIDE the DPDP Act's protections. Data minimisation therefore has to be a design choice by the portal, because the law will not impose it.

claims.claim: Transliteration of land records into the 22 Schedule VIII languages is live in 17 States/UTs under DILRMP — but it is transliteration (script conversion), not translation of the record's substance.
claims.source_name: PIB, '95% of Land Records in Rural India Digitized' (PRID 2068408)
claims.why_it_matters: Validates the existing project rule ('app chrome respects language; land data is never translated, Gujarati numerals stay with a Latin helper line') as being aligned with national practice — and gives a citation for it in the write-up.

claims.claim: 'Land record digitalisation will boost India's GDP by 1.5%' is a ministerial assertion (Giriraj Singh, then Minister for Rural Development, Feb 2024) reproduced in NCAER's reference list; I could find no published model, dataset or working paper behind it.
claims.source_name: Puja Das, Livemint, 'Land record digitalization to boost India's GDP by 1.5%: Giriraj Singh' (as cited in NCAER's references)
claims.why_it_matters: A second famous number that will show up in every competing hackathon deck. Naming it as unmodelled is cheap credibility, and it protects the submission from being built on a number that cannot be defended in Q&A.

claims.claim: The Land Conflict Watch figures — 7.7 million people affected by conflict over 2.5 million hectares, threatening $200 billion of investment — come from a continuously updated activist-maintained database of reported conflicts, not a survey or a court-records study, and are cited as such in the CPR piece that popularised them.
claims.source_name: Land Conflict Watch, cited as footnote 1 in Namita Wahi, CPR
claims.why_it_matters: Usable, but only if described as 'documented conflicts logged by Land Conflict Watch' rather than 'India has 7.7 million people in land conflict'. The distinction is the difference between a sourced claim and a repeated one.

claims.claim: DILRMP added an urban arm in September 2024: NAKSHA (NAtional geospatial Knowledge-based land Survey of urban HAbitations), a pilot across 150 cities with an outlay of Rs 193.81 crore, intended to be completed in about a year.
claims.source_name: PIB, Year End Review 2024, Department of Land Resources (PRID 2088125)
claims.why_it_matters: Scopes the prototype honestly: rural 7/12 is a mature dataset; urban land records are a pilot. Saying 'we deliberately scope to rural agricultural survey records because that is where the data actually exists' is a defensible product decision with a citation.

design_rules.rule: Serve the record with no CAPTCHA, no login and no mobile number for viewing. Gate only the paid, digitally signed download — and gate it with payment, not with an account.
design_rules.rationale: Karnataka's i-RTC already issues a paid, verifiable RTC 'without any login' at Rs 15, which proves authentication is not legally required for a public record. Maharashtra's free viewer demands a CAPTCHA and a mandatory mobile number for data it then declares legally useless — pure friction for no protection, especially since DPDP s.3(c)(ii)(B) gives that data no statutory protection anyway.
design_rules.conflicts_with: AnyRoR, Mahabhulekh and Meebhoomi all gate free public data behind a CAPTCHA and/or login; the reflex assumption is that a government record needs identity verification to read.

design_rules.rule: Stamp every extract with its legal status in plain Gujarati, on the artefact itself, not in a footer: 'માહિતી માટે જ — કાનૂની હેતુ માટે નહીં' for the free view, and 'ડિજિટલી સાઇન્ડ — તમામ સરકારી અને કાનૂની હેતુઓ માટે માન્ય' for the signed PDF.
design_rules.rationale: Maharashtra runs exactly this two-tier model and labels both tiers explicitly ('cannot be used for any official or legal purposes' vs 'can be used for all official and legal purposes'). Rajasthan gives free copies but only tells you they are uncertified in a disclaimer most users never read. The label is the product.

design_rules.rule: Never claim, imply or design UI that suggests the record proves ownership. Show a persistent, tappable 'આ માલિકીનો પુરાવો નથી' explainer stating that Indian title is presumptive and the entry carries only a rebuttable presumption of correctness.
design_rules.rationale: Registration records the transaction, not the title; the onus of verifying title is on the buyer, not the state (PRS). The draft Registration Bill 2025, written in 2025, still does not introduce conclusive title. A portal that implies certainty is making a legal misstatement.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Almost every land-portal pitch deck frames the product as 'proof of ownership' or 'end land disputes'.

design_rules.rule: Do not build any conveyancing, e-signing or transfer flow. Stop at the extract and hand off to registration, and say in the write-up that IT Act 2000 First Schedule item 5 excludes 'any contract for the sale or conveyance of immovable property' from the Act.
design_rules.rationale: ss.4–6 of the IT Act legally recognise electronic records, electronic signatures and electronically issued government documents — which is precisely what a digitally signed RoR is — but the First Schedule carves out conveyances. The boundary is statutory, not a product choice.

design_rules.rule: Keep the parcel identity layer keyed on (village id + survey number as written), and attach ULPIN only as an optional alias that may be absent, may change, and must never be required to find a parcel.
design_rules.rationale: ULPIN is coordinate-derived and assigned in two stages (temporary from textual data, permanent after geo-referencing), so it is mutable by design. Only ~30% of parcels had one as of Oct 2024, and NCAER's ground survey found ULPIN largely does not appear on RoRs at all and that neither landowners nor patwaris know the scheme exists.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The obvious architectural instinct — 'use the government's official unique ID as the primary key'.

design_rules.rule: Show recency as a first-class field on every parcel tile: date of last entry, and an explicit 'pending mutation' state where known. Treat any record without a recency signal as suspect and say so.
design_rules.rationale: DILRMP's own MIS shows real-time updation of RoR and maps in only 35.7% of villages nationally. A record rendered without a date invites the user to believe it is current when it usually is not.

design_rules.rule: Render an explicit 'what this record does NOT show' block listing the encumbrance types absent from the RoR — revenue-court proceedings, civil-court proceedings, town-planning restrictions — rather than silently displaying only mortgages and liens.
design_rules.rationale: NCAER's four-state ground study found that apart from loan/lien/mortgage, no other encumbrance category is reflected in land records. A clean-looking record therefore actively misleads a buyer about litigation risk.
design_rules.conflicts_with: Standard UX advice to hide empty sections — here the emptiness is the information.

design_rules.rule: Make 'this record is wrong' a primary action on the parcel tile, leading to a concrete, named route: which office, which form, what it costs, what the expected time is. Never dead-end at a phone number.
design_rules.rationale: NCAER reported that 'lack of knowledge on records rectification procedures among land owners was reported extensively' and that people do not know whom to approach. Dharani's rejection messages read simply 'rejected' with no reasons, which the Telangana field study identifies as a transparency failure.

design_rules.rule: Never normalise, strip or reject an unusual survey number in order to fit it into the schema. Render exactly what the record says — Gujarati letters, slashes, plus and minus signs, sub-divisions — and if it cannot be parsed, show it verbatim rather than dropping it.
design_rules.rationale: Benjamin et al. found that Bhoomi's simplified digital forms marginalised 'uncommon situations often encountered by the poor' out of existence. The project's own tokenizer probe found that character-stripping fused 250 distinct surveys onto shared keys. Both are the same failure at different layers.

design_rules.rule: Show contested, incomplete and unmigrated parcels rather than hiding them. If a parcel is known to exist but has no clean record, render an explicit 'record incomplete / disputed' tile with a route to raise it — do not omit it from search results.
design_rules.rationale: Telangana's LRUP split records into Part A (clean, migrated) and Part B (disputed, ignored); a field study in two tribal districts found 27.4% of surveyed land absent from Dharani entirely, disproportionately podu cultivation and sada bainama holdings. Omission from the screen became omission from the state.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The engineering instinct to ship only the records that pass validation.

design_rules.rule: Never let a restriction that applies to part of a survey number propagate to the whole of it. Model restrictions at sub-parcel granularity, or label them as 'applies to part — extent unknown'.
design_rules.rationale: A documented Dharani failure: 'Entire survey numbers are placed under prohibited property lists, even if only part of the land is under dispute or court stay', and entire survey numbers were marked non-agricultural (NALA) when only part had been converted.

design_rules.rule: Preserve and display record history. Keep the prior version of every record visible alongside the current one, and never let a migration overwrite what came before.
design_rules.rationale: Two independent cautionary cases: Benjamin et al. record the deliberate decision to 'make illegal the continuation of old Record of Rights formats in transactions after 2001' and an NIC officer's stated intent to 'kill the old system'; the Telangana ROR Act 2020 left no redressal path for orders passed under the 1971 Act. Both destroyed the evidence people needed to contest an error.

design_rules.rule: Design the entire journey to be completable in one session by one person on a cheap phone, with no step that requires visiting an office or knowing an official. Count and publish the number of taps and the number of required fields.
design_rules.rationale: Bhoomi's measured benefit was the collapse from 3.25 officials met and multiple visits to 1.43 officials and one visit (PAC 2002); its measured harm, in the critical study, was that centralisation created a professional agent market with set rates. Both point at the same variable: how many humans stand between the citizen and the record.

design_rules.rule: Set benefit expectations at access, comprehension and time — not at credit. Do not claim the portal unlocks loans.
design_rules.rationale: The best-identified study of registry computerisation in India (Deininger & Goyal 2012, 387 AP sub-registry offices) found credit effects that were 'significant, though quantitatively modest' and present in urban but not rural areas. A rural-farmer portal claiming credit unlocking is claiming the one effect the evidence rejects for rural India.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The standard land-digitisation pitch, and the stated purpose of the national Land Stack initiative itself ('helping banks streamline loan approval processes').

design_rules.rule: Publish the prototype's own coverage and freshness metrics — records held, last-fetch date, known-missing categories — on a page the judges can open, and show the denominator for every percentage.
design_rules.rationale: The official DILRMP dashboard is state-self-reported with no verification layer, and its numbers contradict PIB within weeks (59.9% vs 95% of maps digitised; 8.4 crore vs 23 crore ULPINs two months apart). Doing the opposite, visibly, is a cheap and legible integrity signal.

design_rules.rule: Treat land-record data as unprotected by law and minimise it by choice: no personal data in URLs or query strings, no server-side log tying a query to an identity, no requirement to supply a phone number to read, and an explicit statement of what the portal stores.
design_rules.rationale: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii)(B) removes from the Act's scope personal data made publicly available under a legal obligation — which is exactly what a published RoR is. Meanwhile DILRMP 3.0 proposes 'Aadhaar seeding, mobile number and address integration in land records databases'. Statutory protection will not arrive; the portal has to supply the restraint.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The assumption that DPDP compliance is the privacy story. For land records it is close to a null set.

design_rules.rule: Keep app chrome bilingual and switchable (gu | both | en) but never translate the land data itself: keep Gujarati numerals and the record's own strings, and add a Latin helper line beside them.
design_rules.rationale: DILRMP's national approach is transliteration into the 22 Schedule VIII languages, live in 17 States/UTs — script conversion, not substantive translation. Maharashtra's free viewer already offers 16 language interfaces over an untranslated record. This is the settled national pattern and matches the project's existing rule.

design_rules.rule: Provide a verification path for any extract the portal issues: a short reference number printed on the document that resolves, on a public URL, to the same data.
design_rules.rationale: Karnataka already does this — printed RTCs carry a reference number verified against an XML record. It is what converts a downloadable PDF from a screenshot into something a bank or a buyer can check, without needing the recipient to have an account.

design_rules.rule: Do not build survey-number search, parcel geometry or adjoining-plot detection on top of village map sheets, and state plainly in the write-up that these are raster exports.
design_rules.rationale: The project's own eJamin survey found all 881 Kheda + Anand sheets are rasterised with no text layer, no parcel geometry and no georeferencing, with only ~5% of sheets vector statewide. Nationally the same constraint appears as the ULPIN bottleneck: geo-referencing century-old village maps is the stated reason ULPIN sat at ~30% after three years.
design_rules.conflicts_with: The natural demo instinct to show a clickable cadastral map.

design_rules.rule: Position the submission as 'Gujarat's land DATA is essentially complete; the last mile is the only mile left' and cite the state's own numbers to prove it.
design_rules.rationale: Per DILRMP MIS (16 Nov 2024): Gujarat is at 100% RoR computerisation, 100% cadastral maps digitised, 99.9% maps linked to RoR, and ~99% ULPIN coverage (1.19 crore of ~1.2 crore parcels). The failure is entirely interface: five chained dropdowns, a CAPTCHA on legally public data, desktop tables, and an unusable-for-any-purpose output, with the legally valid signed extract exiled to a separate 1024x768-era portal.

design_rules.rule: Ship small, auditable and reversible; keep the incumbent reachable and never make the new system the only door.
design_rules.rationale: Telangana replaced Dharani with Bhu Bharati in 2025; by July 2026 the state had constituted a Special Enquiry Team into both portals and ordered a replacement of Bhu Bharati's own software and architecture. Big-bang replacement of a land-records system has now failed twice in one state inside six years.

design_rules.rule: In the honesty section, name the three specific things the prototype cannot do — confer title, guarantee freshness beyond the last fetch, and cover urban or non-agricultural parcels — and pair each with the citation that explains why.
design_rules.rationale: Each has a clean primary source: presumptive title (Registration Act 1908 / draft Registration Bill 2025 which does not change it); 35.7% real-time updation nationally; and NAKSHA, the urban land-record programme, still being a 150-city pilot as of Dec 2024.

gaps: Firecrawl credits were exhausted (HTTP 402) and the session's WebSearch budget ran out early; DuckDuckGo, Mojeek and public SearxNG instances all served CAPTCHA or 429. Everything after that point came from direct URL fetches, PIB by PRID scan, Google News RSS, OpenAlex, Crossref, Wikipedia API and the Wayback CDX index. Coverage is therefore deep on documents I could name and thinner on things only a general search would have surfaced.

I could NOT find a substantive, well-sourced privacy or civil-liberties critique of ULPIN/Bhu-Aadhaar. The IJLLR piece that looks like legal analysis contains none. Treat 'ULPIN privacy concerns' as an unsourced talking point. The defensible privacy argument is structural, not citational: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii)(B) exempts data published under legal obligation, while DILRMP 3.0 proposes Aadhaar seeding plus mobile numbers and addresses inside the land-record database.

The exact fee for Maharashtra's digitally signed 7/12 is unverified. The DSLR portal states payment is required and non-refundable but names no amount; the widely repeated 'Rs 15' figure is Karnataka's i-RTC fee and I could not confirm it for Maharashtra.

Maharashtra's December 2025 grant of 'full legal validity' to digital 7/12 extracts is known only at headline level (The Indian Express, 4 Dec 2025; Hindustan Times, 8 Dec 2025 — both via Google News RSS). I could not open the article bodies or locate the underlying Government Resolution, so the legal instrument behind that specific decision is unconfirmed.

UP Bhulekh could not be characterised: upbhulekh.gov.in renders only a heading without JavaScript, and its record page 404s on direct fetch. UP is therefore missing from the state comparison except for its DILRMP aggregates.

NCAER's Land Records and Services Index (N-LRSI) state rankings for 2019-20 and 2020-21 were not retrieved — only its methodology (60% weight to extent of digitisation, 40% to record quality). The state league table would strengthen the comparison section.

The live DILRMP MIS 4.0 dashboard figures could not be read: the page loads its numbers by JavaScript and I did not call its internal data endpoints. All MIS numbers here come from NCAER's 16 Nov 2024 snapshot of it. Current live values may differ, and given the contradictions documented above, they should be re-checked before publication.

The Telangana Bhu Bharati (Record of Rights) Act 2025 and the Telangana Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books Act 2020 were not read in original. The claim that the 2020 Act removed appeal and revision provisions equivalent to ss. 5(B), 5(5) and 9 of the 1971 Act rests on one low-tier journal article and should be verified against the statutes before being asserted in the write-up.

Dharani quantitative claims rest on a four-village purposive sample in two tribal districts (Mulugu, Kumuram Bheem Asifabad) published in JNRID, a low-tier journal. The percentages (91.7% never accessed the portal, 27.4% of land unrecorded) are plausible and mechanistically consistent with mainstream reporting, but are not state-representative and must not be presented as such.

No CAG performance audit of DILRMP, and no Parliamentary Standing Committee report on it, was located. Either would be the strongest independent check on the official dashboard and is worth one targeted search if budget allows.

Deininger & Goyal (2012) was read from the RePEc abstract, not the full paper; the magnitude of the credit effect is described qualitatively ('significant, though quantitatively modest') rather than as a coefficient.

The Public Affairs Centre 2002 Bhoomi report card is marked '// DRAFT //' on its title page. I could not locate a final published version, so the famous Rs 806 million / 1.32 million mandays figures come from a draft.

Gujarat's digitally signed RoR flow on iORA (fee, registration requirement, whether an OTP is needed, what the signed artefact looks like) was not tested, deliberately: the brief forbids interacting with live government sites, and the project's own memory records AnyRoR WAF/IP-blocking risk. Only the service listing on the iORA landing page was read.

AnyRoR itself was not fetched at all during this research for the same reason. All statements about the incumbent Gujarat citizen experience should be sourced to the project's own prior observations, not to this research.
